chapters.summary: Committee staff welcomes attendees, asks phones and electronic devices to be silenced, and directs testifiers to fill out appearance cards with the Sergeant at Arms. The Chair is told the committee is ready to begin.
chapters.title: Committee staff opens hearing and gives testimony instructions

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Welcome to today's New York City Council hearing for the Committee on Transportation and Infrastructure.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: At this time, please sign to all cell phone and electronic devices.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: If you are testifying today, please fill out an appearance card with the sergeant at arms.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Moving forward, no one is to approach today's.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Chair Brie, we're ready to begin.

chapters.summary: Chair Abreu opens the hearing, introduces himself as Majority Leader and Chair of Transportation and Infrastructure, and frames Vision Zero around the principle that traffic deaths are preventable. He notes 205 traffic fatalities in 2025, a 31% reduction from 2014, but says recent tragedies show more work remains.
chapters.title: Chair Abreu opens Vision Zero oversight hearing

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Good morning and welcome to today's hearing.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: I'm Councilmember Sean Abreu, Majority Leader and Chair of the Committee on Transportation and Infrastructure.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Since its launch in 2014, Vision Zero has fundamentally changed how New York City approaches street safety.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: The central principle is simple.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Traffic deaths and serious injuries are preventable.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: And every New Yorker deserves to travel safely, whether they are walking, cycling, driving, or using another form of transportation.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Over the years, we have meaningful progress towards this goal.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: In 2025, New York City recorded 205 traffic fatalities, a 31% reduction when compared to 2014.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: However, any life lost on our streets is one too many, and recent tragedies remind us that there is still considerable work ahead.

chapters.summary: Abreu says the administration released Vision Zero Reimagined, a 10-year plan he broadly supports, but he demands clear strategies, realistic timelines, and measurable outcomes. He asks what actions will be prioritized, when results will come, and how progress will be measured.
chapters.title: Abreu questions implementation of Vision Zero Reimagined

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Last month, the administration released Vision Zero Re-

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: imagined, a new action plan aimed at eliminating traffic deaths and serious injuries.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: I support the goals outlined in this plan and welcome the administration's renewed commitment to street safety.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: However, ambitious goals must be accompanied by clear strategies, realistic timelines, and measurable outcomes.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Today, we want to better understand how the administration intends to turn these commitments into meaningful improvements on our streets.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: What specific actions will be prioritized?

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: When can New Yorkers expect to see results?

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: And how will we measure whether the city is making sufficient progress towards its goals?

chapters.summary: Abreu flags that NYPD issued nearly 700,000 Vision Zero-related moving summonses annually before the pandemic, but only about 300,000 in FY2021 and just over 413,000 in FY2026. He says this is roughly 40% below pre-pandemic levels and raises serious questions about enforcement strategy.
chapters.title: Abreu flags declining NYPD Vision Zero summonses

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: And essentially part of that discussion is enforcement.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: In fiscal years 2018 and 2019, the NYPD issued nearly 700,000 Vision Zero-related moving summonses annually.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: By fiscal year 2021, that number had fallen to approximately 300,000.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: While enforcement has since increased, with the NYPD issuing just over 413,000 summonses in fiscal year 2026, this is still approximately 40% below pre-pandemic levels.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: These numbers raise serious questions about the city's enforcement strategy.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Why has enforcement remained substantially below previous levels?

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: And what will it take to restore a consistent and effective enforcement presence?

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: We need to ensure that dangerous behavior is addressed across.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: all modes of transportation, including cars, motorcycles, e-bikes, mopeds, and other micromobility devices.

chapters.summary: Abreu calls for fair and consistent enforcement across cars, motorcycles, e-bikes, mopeds, and micromobility, and continued investment in daylighting, safer intersections, protected bike infrastructure, and lower speed limits. He also wants to examine low-traffic neighborhoods and intelligent speed assistance.
chapters.title: Abreu outlines street safety investments and new tools

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Street safety requires fair, consistent enforcement that prioritizes the behaviors posing the greatest risk to New Yorkers.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Beyond enforcement, we must continue investing in improving street safety improvements, including daylighting, safer intersections, protected bicycle infrastructure, and lower speed limits.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: We also want to examine new approaches, such as low-traffic neighborhoods and intelligent speed assistance technology, while ensuring that these initiatives are practical,

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: effective, and responsive to community needs.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: The legislation before us today provides an opportunity to advance these conversations and consider additional tools to prevent dangerous driving and protect vulnerable road users.

chapters.summary: Abreu lists the legislation before the committee: Intro 46 on autism warning plaques, Intro 113 on studying dangerous driving, Intro 613 on protected bike lanes, Intro 1070 on low-traffic neighborhood pilots, Intro 1153 on intelligent speed assistance devices, and Res 687 on drag racing enforcement.
chapters.title: Abreu lists legislation before committee

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: We will be hearing the following legislation.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Introduction number 46, sponsored by Councilmember Areola, in relation to installing child with autism warning plaques on streets.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Introduction number 113, sponsored by Councilmember Brooks Powers, in relation to requiring a study of dangerous driving.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Introduction number 613, sponsored by Councilmember Joseph, in relation to the installation of protected bicycle lanes.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Introduction number 1070, sponsored by myself, in relation to establishing a low-traffic neighborhood pilot program.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Introduction number 11.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: 1153, sponsored by Councilmember Santos Suoso, in relation to establishing a demonstration program for the installation and maintenance of intelligence speed assistance devices.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: And Resolution 687, sponsored by myself, calling on the New York State Legislature to pass and the New York State Governor to sign.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: S-1768A-2585, the Drag Racing and Speed Enforcement Act, which would impose five points on a driver's license for being convicted of participating in speed contests and races.

chapters.summary: Abreu highlights his Intro 1070, a two-year low-traffic neighborhood pilot in five neighborhoods across at least three boroughs, with community input and evaluation of safety, noise, and surrounding streets. He also describes his resolution urging state passage of the Drag Racing and Speeding Enforcement Act.
chapters.title: Abreu promotes low-traffic neighborhood pilot and drag racing resolution

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: I will let the other sponsors discuss their bills, but I am particularly excited about my bill related to low traffic neighborhoods.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Low-traffic neighborhoods use a range of traffic-calming measures to reduce through-traffic on residential streets.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Examples from the United Kingdom suggest that these approaches can reduce traffic volumes without significantly impacting surrounding roads or emergency response times.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Introduction number 1070 would establish a two-year pilot program in five neighborhoods across at least five boroughs.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Three boroughs, my apologies.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: The program would incorporate community input and evaluate impacts on street safety, noise, and surrounding streets.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: We want to better understand where these measures would be most effective and how they can help create safer, more livable neighborhoods.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: In addition, my resolution that we'll be hearing will call on the state to pass S-1768 and A-2585.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: which are known as the Drag and Speed Enforcement Act, which would work to combat illegal drag and speed racing.

chapters.summary: Abreu says the hearing aims to hold the administration accountable to new commitments and ensure they translate into safer streets. He thanks committee staff by name and turns the floor over to bill sponsors.
chapters.title: Abreu frames hearing goal and thanks staff

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Ultimately, this hearing, the goal is to hold the administration accountable to new commitments and to ensure that those commitments translate into safer streets.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: We look forward to working constructively with the administration advocates and community

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: and communities to identify what is working, where improvements are needed, and what additional steps must be taken.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: I want to thank my staff and committee staff for their hard work in preparing for today's hearing.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Jaleesa Quigley, my Deputy Chief of Staff, Jake Borey, my Senior Advisor, Sierra Townsend, Senior Legislative Counsel, Theodore Miller, Legislative Counsel, Kevin Katowski, Senior Policy Analyst, John Bazile, Senior Policy Analyst, and Yates Wong, Finance.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: I look forward to today's testimony and discussion.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: I will now turn it over to the bill sponsors, beginning first with Councilmember Brooks Powers, followed by Councilmember Santos Suazo.

chapters.summary: Council Member Brooks-Powers presents Intro 113, saying streets should be governed by data and progress measured transparently. Her bill would require DOT, NYPD, and other agencies to study driving behavior and report annually on patterns linked to crashes, injuries, and fatalities.
chapters.title: Council Member Brooks-Powers presents Intro 113

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Thank you, Majority Leader and Chair Abreu and members of the Committee on Transportation and Infrastructure for hearing Intro 113 today.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: As we evaluate the administration's Vision Zero plan today, I remain committed to the principle that our streets should be governed by data and that progress should be measured transparently and consistently.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: The work of this committee, including during my time as chair, has shown that safety and fairness go together.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: That work has included...

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: It's citywide daylighting, ending jaywalking enforcement, and overhauling city truck routes.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Enforcement should be focused on the behavior that is injuring and killing New Yorkers.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: To do that, the city must know that behavior better.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: My bill, Intro 113, would require the Department of Transportation, working with the NYPD and other agencies, to study driving behavior and identify the patterns that signal dangerous driving before it ends in a crash.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: The study would draw on data the city already collects but rarely looks at in this way.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Hit and run reports, reckless driving convictions, crash reports, the driving activity of vehicles registered to people with suspended or revoked licenses, and where feasible insurance information.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Every year, the Department of Transportation would report to this council and the public on what it found, what it recommends, what agencies have done about it, and whether dangerous driving is going up or down.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: I look forward to working with the chair and the committee to move Intro 113 forward.

chapters.summary: Brooks-Powers voices support for Intro 46 as an aunt of an autistic nephew and for Intro 1070, which she co-sponsors with Majority Leader Abreu. She thanks advocates and colleagues for work on street safety.
chapters.title: Brooks-Powers supports Intro 46 and Intro 1070

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: I also want to just take a moment to just issue my support for Intro 46 as a proud aunt of an autistic nephew.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: It's a very important piece of legislation that I hope to see voted on, as well as Intro 1070, which I'm a proud co-prime sponsor with Majority Leader Abreu, looking to bring the...

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: a low traffic neighborhood traffic program, pilot program rather, to the city of New York.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: I look forward again to working with my colleagues on these important pieces of legislation and thank the advocates for the work that they've done around this issue and for our combined

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: effort to make New York safer.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair.

chapters.summary: Abreu recognizes members present, including Brooks-Powers, Justin Sanchez, Wong, Santos-Suoso, and the Public Advocate. He calls on Council Member Santos-Suoso to present her bill.
chapters.title: Abreu recognizes members and calls on Santosuosso

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Thank you, Councilmember.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: I'd like to recognize that we've been joined by Councilmembers Lewis, Brooks-Powers, Justin Sanchez, and Wong, and Councilmember Santos-Suoso and the Public Advocate.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Councilmember Santos-Suoso, followed by Public Advocate Jumaane Williams.

chapters.summary: Council Member Santos-Suoso presents Intro 1153, the Stop Super Speeders Act, which would require chronic speeders with 16 or more school-zone speed camera violations in 12 months to install speed-limiting devices in vehicles registered to them. She says thousands qualify and the bill targets the worst offenders.
chapters.title: Council Member Santosuosso presents Stop Super Speeders Act

utterances.speaker: Kayla Santosuosso
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr.

utterances.speaker: Kayla Santosuosso
utterances.text: Majority Leader.

utterances.speaker: Kayla Santosuosso
utterances.text: Today we will hear my bill, Intro 1153, otherwise known as the Stop Super Speeders Act, which would require that drivers who are chronic speeders install a speed-limiting device in any vehicle that is registered to them.

utterances.speaker: Kayla Santosuosso
utterances.text: This legislation aims to crack down on our absolute worst offenders.

utterances.speaker: Kayla Santosuosso
utterances.text: It would target drivers who incur speeding tickets in speed in school zones, 16 or more of those violations in the span of 12 months.

utterances.speaker: Kayla Santosuosso
utterances.text: And it's tempting to think that there aren't enough drivers that would actually, in fact, qualify for that speed limiting device.

utterances.speaker: Kayla Santosuosso
utterances.text: But it turns out that there are thousands of them and they are the worst danger to us on the streets.

utterances.speaker: Kayla Santosuosso
utterances.text: And it is time for us to limit their ability to navigate their own vehicles, which they have proven they are unable.

utterances.speaker: Kayla Santosuosso
utterances.text: to do safely.

utterances.speaker: Kayla Santosuosso
utterances.text: I come to this bill as a pedestrian, as a cyclist, and as a driver, and I understand that this is not aiming at the drivers who have one or two speeding tickets, but are absolute worst offenders.

utterances.speaker: Kayla Santosuosso
utterances.text: And I am so grateful that we have been able to get a swift hearing, and that's with the support of Chair Abreu and so many of the advocates that have pushed this forward.

utterances.speaker: Kayla Santosuosso
utterances.text: So I look forward to hearing from DOT on the implementation of this bill, what kind of challenges it proposes, what you need in order to implement it.

utterances.speaker: Kayla Santosuosso
utterances.text: As you all know, this was started on the state level through State Senator Gennardis and Assemblymember Emily Gallagher and many others.

utterances.speaker: Kayla Santosuosso
utterances.text: And we look forward to sort of finishing the job here on the city level.

utterances.speaker: Kayla Santosuosso
utterances.text: And we want to see it as swift of passage as possible.

utterances.speaker: Kayla Santosuosso
utterances.text: So I look forward to hearing how we can make that happen by partnering with this administration.

utterances.speaker: Kayla Santosuosso
utterances.text: And I want to thank you for your efforts in focusing on this critical issue.

utterances.speaker: Kayla Santosuosso
utterances.text: Finally, thanks to the advocates.

utterances.speaker: Kayla Santosuosso
utterances.text: Thanks to the drafters who have turned this around quite quickly.

utterances.speaker: Kayla Santosuosso
utterances.text: And thank you again to the chair for hearing this bill.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Thank you, Councilmember.

chapters.summary: Public Advocate Jumaane Williams testifies that crash data on the city's open data portal has not been updated since June 2026 and cites recent fatal collisions, including hit-and-run deaths and cyclist deaths. He argues public awareness of the road crisis remains limited.
chapters.title: Public Advocate Jumaane Williams testifies on road crisis

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Public Advocate Jumaane Williams.

utterances.speaker: Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr.

utterances.speaker: Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: Chair.

utterances.speaker: Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: As I mentioned, my name is Jumaane Williams, Public Advocate, City of New York.

utterances.speaker: Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: I want to thank Chair Burrow as well as members of the Committee on Transportation Infrastructure for holding this important hearing and for the opportunity to share testimony.

utterances.speaker: Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: Public awareness of the city's road crisis still remains a little limited.

utterances.speaker: Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: partly because crash statistics on the city's open data portal have not been updated since June of 2026.

utterances.speaker: Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: Directly outside of the Dinkins Municipal Building on Center Street, a fatal collision occurred on July 29th involving a SUV and an individual riding an illegal e-bike.

utterances.speaker: Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: In August 2026, hit-and-run drivers took the lives of three cyclists within three days, bringing the total number of people killed by hit-and-run drivers to nine by the end of the month.

utterances.speaker: Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: Just earlier this month on Atlantic Avenue in Brooklyn, an unmarked NYPD vehicle ran a red light and struck a cyclist.

utterances.speaker: Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: Nine pedestrians were injured on October 9th when a driver reportedly attempting to beat a traffic light sped through a busy Bronx intersection.

utterances.speaker: Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: According to the Vision Zero eBay Imagine report, the DOT plans to use hardened daylighting or better treatments such as traffic signals, all-way stops, crosswalks, and leading pedestrian intervals.

utterances.speaker: Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: As the DOT moves forward with daylighting measures, we must emphasize the compromise visibility posed.

utterances.speaker: Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: Poses a direct threat to pedestrian, cyclist, delivery workers, and motorists alike.

chapters.summary: Williams urges DOT to integrate daylighting into planned milling and repainting, expand protected bike lanes, and penalize retailers selling non-compliant e-bikes. He also warns that aggressive enforcement should not target delivery workers and everyday e-bike riders rather than systemic harms.
chapters.title: Williams urges daylighting and e-bike regulation

utterances.speaker: Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: To keep expenses minimal relative to their overall budget, the DOT can integrate more daylighting into planned milling and repainting work executed by city staff rather than outside contractors.

utterances.speaker: Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: To regulate micro-ability and e-bike effectively, priorities must center on expanding protected bike lanes and infrastructure, penalizing retailers who sell non-compliant e-bikes engineered to exceed legal speeds.

utterances.speaker: Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: Especially with the increased ICE presence across the city under this federal administration,

utterances.speaker: Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: We want to make sure that if there's particularly aggressive enforcement, it's not focused on driver delivery work as cyclists and everyday e-bike riders, but the onus of regulation on individuals rather than the systems contributing to most of the harm.

utterances.speaker: Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: That doesn't mean we have to eliminate enforcement altogether.

chapters.summary: Williams supports expanding Sammy's Law speed limits beyond school zones to other designated areas and calls for immediate local implementation of the Stop Super Speeders program. He asks that speed-limiting devices be applied equitably.
chapters.title: Williams supports Sammy's Law expansion and Stop Super Speeders

utterances.speaker: Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: To further enhance safety, the city must expand the implementation of SAMI's law, lowering speed limits beyond school zones to include other designated areas.

utterances.speaker: Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: I don't know that I yet support across the entire city, but definitely some other areas outside of school zones.

utterances.speaker: Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: Furthermore, advocates are calling for immediate local programming of another state law, the Super Speed Initiative by Councilmember Santa Suoso.

utterances.speaker: Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: Did I say that correctly?

utterances.speaker: Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: Oh, praise God.

utterances.speaker: Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: Which mandates speed limiting devices for chronic reckless drivers.

utterances.speaker: Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: I just want to make sure that that will be applied equitably to everyone in the city.

utterances.speaker: Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: As noted by the mayor, reckless drivers account for nearly 40% of traffic fatalities and pose a significantly higher risk of causing severe collisions repeatedly.

utterances.speaker: Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: Building on the city's initiatives, we should prioritize legislative action that will prevent reckless driving.

utterances.speaker: Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: As motor vehicles crashes, which people have to remember, we talk about cycling and even horses, crashes by vehicles remain a significantly greater hazard than anything else in the city.

utterances.speaker: Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: And every time we try to move on it, we get a particularly vociferous response.

chapters.summary: Williams urges the Council to pass Council Member Julie Won's Intro 511 for universal daylighting and stronger accountability, noting support from over 200 organizations and 23 community boards. He calls for codifying no standing or parking within 20 feet of intersections.
chapters.title: Williams urges council to pass Intro 511 universal daylighting

utterances.speaker: Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: Specifically, I urge the council to consider and also pass a member, Councilmember Juan's bill, Intro 511, to implement universal daylighting and strengthen accountability on streets.

utterances.speaker: Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: The daylighting...

utterances.speaker: Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: Supported by over 200 civic streets, safety, and community organizations.

utterances.speaker: Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: Additionally, 23 NYC community boards have passed resolutions endorsing intersection daylighting as a key measure to enhance street safety.

utterances.speaker: Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: Enacting this bill and others will ensure that compliance is legally required and formally codified, not standing or parking within 20 feet of an intersection.

utterances.speaker: Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: Any crosswalk while establishing mandatory and annual benchmarks for DOT, including the target numbers for hunting intersections.

utterances.speaker: Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: This is a very important hearing, and I want to thank the chair again.

utterances.speaker: Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Public Advocate.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: I would like to recognize that we've been joined by Councilmember Marte.

chapters.summary: Committee counsel administers the oath to agency witnesses, asking them to affirm they will tell the truth and respond honestly to council questions. The witnesses are told to state their names and titles for the record.
chapters.title: Committee counsel administers oath to agency witnesses

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: I will now move to admin testimony and turn it over to the committee counsel to give the oath.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Please raise your right hand.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Do you affirm to tell the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth before the committee and to respond honestly to council member questions?

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: You may begin when ready, stating your name and title for the record.

chapters.summary: DOT Commissioner Mike Flynn introduces himself and his colleagues, Deputy Commissioner Eric Beaton and Chief of Staff Madeline Labadie. He says traffic deaths have reached historic lows, with the second fewest since 1910, and pedestrian fatalities at an all-time low.
chapters.title: DOT Commissioner Mike Flynn introduces Vision Zero progress

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: Good morning, Chair Abreu and members of the Committee on Transportation and Infrastructure.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: I'm Mike Flynn, Commissioner of the New York City Department of Transportation.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: With me today is Eric Beaton, Deputy Commissioner for Transportation Planning and Management, and Madeline Labadee, my Chief of Staff.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: Thank you for the opportunity to testify on behalf of Mayor Zoran Mamdani about Vision Zero and the administration's street safety strategy.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: October has been an exciting and busy month as the city's ramping up our reimagined Vision Zero approach.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: Vision Zero is a comprehensive multi-agency priority initiative to build multiple layers of protection to both prevent crashes in the first place and minimize severity when they do occur.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: Our strategy is working.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: Earlier this month, we announced that traffic deaths have reached historic lows over the first three quarters of 2026, with the second fewest traffic deaths since the city started tracking data in 1910.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: Pedestrian fatalities are at an all-time low, and to date, this is the second safest year on record for our streets.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: But we know that one death is one too many.

chapters.summary: Flynn describes Vision Zero Reimagined as a 10-year strategy with goals including implementing safety improvements on the most dangerous streets within three years, removing dangerous drivers and devices, encouraging safe travel modes, and using data and technology for smarter interventions.
chapters.title: Flynn outlines Vision Zero Reimagined goals

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: On top of the tremendous progress to date, the Mamdani administration is committing to Vision Zero through the new Vision Zero Reimagined Action Plan, citywide strategy for the next decade, because there's more work to be done.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: Our decades-long initiative has shown that building safer streets works to keep

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: More New Yorkers safe while traveling.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: And our newly released action plan continues the administration's commitment to expanding the deployment of proven safety interventions.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: While Vision Zero is a citywide effort, DOT is highlighting a variety of goals to support Vision Zero, which include

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: Implementing safety improvements for all of the city's most dangerous streets within three years by the end of the mayor's current term in office.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: Removing dangerous drivers and devices from our streets.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: Encouraging safe travel modes while discouraging oversized vehicles.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: Cultivating a safety...

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: Culture of accountability through education and enforcement, and leveraging emerging data, technology, and analysis for smarter interventions.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: Altogether, these efforts support a holistic citywide strategy with our sister agencies to eliminate traffic deaths and serious injuries by targeting behaviors, vehicles, and street conditions that inflict the most damage.

chapters.summary: Flynn says the administration made a historic funding commitment and DOT is hiring additional staff, expanding contractor capacity, and investing in facilities and equipment. He expects record output and asks the Council to preserve flexibility so DOT can focus on data-driven projects.
chapters.title: Flynn details DOT capacity and hiring ramp-up

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: The progress we've made under Vision Zero is remarkable, but we aren't satisfied.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: Not when New Yorkers are still losing their lives on our streets.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: When Mayor Mamdani announced my appointment as DOT Commissioner, he made clear our bold ambition to make our streetscape the envy of the world.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: And that starts with safety.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: In just nine and a half months, we've reinvigorated the work at our agency.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: We've advanced long-delayed street redesigns, we have ambitious new projects in the pipeline, and we're scaling up all the foundational resources we need to do more and do it faster.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: hiring additional staff, expanding work capacity with contractors, investing in new facilities and equipment, and so much more.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: I expect that this year we'll see record output at DOT in terms of both quantity and quality, and we'll set a new high-water mark each and every year.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: We have a clear roadmap for where we're headed and we're laser focused on delivering.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: We want to keep our eye on the ball by following the data, prioritizing the projects that will have the greatest impact, and directing resources towards where they're most needed.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: We see the Council as a vital partner in this work.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: We share your commitment to street safety and welcome ideas and oversight.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: However, discretion and flexibility are critical to our success.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: In order for DOT to keep improving safety outcomes on our streets, it's vital we preserve our focus on the projects and initiatives that have the greatest data-driven impact.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: In the past, we've seen well-intentioned mandates curb our ability to adapt to the changing needs of the city's streetscapes.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: We're excited to work with Council to strike that balance and implement the most impactful projects possible.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: My ambition for DOT, and it's shared throughout the organization, is simple, to execute with purpose and urgency because lives truly depend on it.

chapters.summary: Flynn supports the intent of Intro 46 to protect vulnerable road users but cites the federal MUTCD and studies showing too many signs create clutter and do not change driver behavior. He also warns the autism warning plaque system would require substantial staffing and funding.
chapters.title: Flynn states DOT position on Intro 46 autism plaques

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: Turning to the legislation before the Council today.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: First, Intro 46, sponsored by Council Member Areola.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: This bill would require DOT to install, at the request of a child's parent or legal guardian, warning signs with plaques to warn a motorist.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: of the presence of a child with autism.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: Being an attentive and safe driver, cyclist, or pedestrian is extremely important for everyone sharing the street in any neighborhood.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: We support the intent of protecting vulnerable road users, doing so is core to our agency's mission.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: However, guided by the Federal Manual on Uniform Traffic Control Devices, or MUTCD, we use signage carefully.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: Both the manual and independent studies demonstrate that too many signs create visual clutter, which increases the chances that drivers will actually ignore signs with critical information.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: It's also important to acknowledge that research shows that these specific types of signs don't make streets safer or change driver behavior.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: Finally, the system proposed would require substantial new staffing and funding.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: Without an effective removal process, we would be concerned to see these signs up on every block.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: We're happy to have further discussions with the Council about this bill and our rigorous process for street safety design interventions.

chapters.summary: Flynn supports Intro 113's annual study of driving behavior associated with crashes, injuries, and fatalities. He says DOT wants suggested amendments to ensure comprehensive reporting and supports targeted safety strategies.
chapters.title: Flynn states DOT position on Intro 113 dangerous driving study

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: Next, Intro 113, sponsored by Councilmember Brooks Powers.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: This bill would require DOT, in coordination with the police department and other appropriate agencies, to conduct an annual study of driving behavior to determine what behaviors are associated with traffic crashes, injuries, and fatalities.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: Our priority is enhancing street safety, which is driven by comprehensive data collection to inform the thoughtful implementation of new initiatives.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: By examining our streets, we're able to build safer streets that work to keep more New Yorkers safe while traveling.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: We support studies that help the city better understand equitable and targeted safety strategies and look forward to working with council on a few suggested amendments to ensure comprehensive reporting.

chapters.summary: Flynn responds to Intro 613, which would require 100 miles of protected bike lanes per year for six years. He says biking is getting safer but wants flexibility and conversations about efficient, equitable implementation rather than rigid mandates.
chapters.title: Flynn states DOT position on Intro 613 protected bike lane mandate

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: Next, Intro 613, sponsored by Councilmember Joseph.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: This bill would require DOT to install 100 miles of protected bike lane per year for the next six years.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: Biking in New York City is safe and getting safer.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: The rate of cyclist deaths is trending down, but of course we have more to do.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: As part of the mayoral administration, we're excited to build up our in-house capacity and to deliver more transformative and ambitious street redesign projects.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: As demand for safe and comfortable bike routes increases, we're responding by expanding opportunities beyond just protected bike lanes, ensuring the tools we use are appropriate for each respective corridor.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: We share the Council's goal to enhance safety by delivering protected bike lane miles citywide and look forward to conversations with the Council on how to best implement these designs in an efficient and equitable way.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: As I said earlier in my testimony, mandates don't always adapt to our evolving city.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: You have an administration and a DOT that is committed to achieving shared goals, so let's work together to deliver the greatest possible impact on street safety while preserving the flexibility needed to do so.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: As always, we're happy to meet to address specific corridors in your district that may need closer attention as well.

chapters.summary: Flynn supports the goals of Intro 1070 to establish a two-year low-traffic neighborhood pilot. He says reclaiming roadway for public space can improve safety and points to open streets and pedestrian plazas, while wanting more discussion on how to define and structure LTNs.
chapters.title: Flynn states DOT position on Intro 1070 low-traffic neighborhoods

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: Next, Intro 1070, sponsored by Chera Breu.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: This bill would require DOT to establish a two-year low-traffic neighborhood pilot program to direct traffic away from residential areas.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: With 6,300 miles of streets and 12,000 miles of sidewalk, DOT is responsible for a vast and vital portion of the city's public space.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: Safety is our top priority when determining design treatments, and reclaiming roadway into vibrant public spaces increases safety by enhancing pedestrian comfort and flow.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: We're always thinking creatively about how we can reimagine and transform our streets into public space open to all.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: We support the goals of this bill, which would expand upon proven initiatives like open streets, pedestrian plazas, and even trigger streets coming up this weekend to ensure that our streets continue to be a valuable local asset across neighborhoods citywide.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: We have thoughts on how best to define or structure low-traffic neighborhoods, and we're excited for future conversations on this subject.

chapters.summary: Flynn supports Intro 1153 and notes the administration backed Intelligent Speed Assistance in the state budget, authorizing a Stop Super Speeders pilot for owners with 16 adjudicated speed camera tickets in 12 months. He says ISA can prevent super speeders from speeding in the first place.
chapters.title: Flynn states DOT support for Intro 1153 intelligent speed assistance

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: Next, Intro 1153, sponsored by Councilmember Santusoso.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: This bill would require the city to establish a demonstration program for the installation and maintenance of intelligent speed assistance devices.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: The administration was proud to support the inclusion of Intelligent Speed Assistance, or ISA, in the state budget, which authorizes the city to implement a Stop Super Speeders pilot program, which would require a vehicle owner who racks up 16

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: finally adjudicated speed camera tickets in 12 months to install a speed limiter device.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: New York City has been a national leader in

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: combating traffic violence, and our automated traffic enforcement cameras have been an effective intervention.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: But a small group of recidivist speeders continues to flagrantly endanger themselves and others.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: Technology like ISA can target and preempt these super speeders'dangerous behavior as it prevents a vehicle from traveling fast enough to break the speed limit in the first place.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: Since local authorization is required under the state law to stand up a program, we support this bill and look forward to future conversations to ensure the success of the pilot program.

chapters.summary: Flynn concludes DOT's prepared testimony and thanks the Council for the opportunity to testify. He says the agency is ready to answer questions.
chapters.title: Flynn concludes DOT testimony and takes questions

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: In conclusion, I'd like to thank the Council for the opportunity to testify before you today.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: We would now be happy to answer any questions.

chapters.summary: Abreu recognizes newly joined members, including Pierina Sanchez and Ariola. He invites Council Member Ariola to give her opening remarks on Intro 46.
chapters.title: Abreu recognizes members and invites Ariola opening

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: We've been joined by Councilmember Pierina Sanchez and Councilmember Mariola.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: You want to give your opening now?

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: You can.

chapters.summary: Council Member Ariola presents Intro 46, which would allow parents and guardians to request warning signs alerting motorists to autistic children nearby. She calls it a common-sense safety measure and criticizes the Commissioner for calling the signs clutter.
chapters.title: Council Member Ariola presents Intro 46 autism warning plaques

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair Majority Leader Abreu and the Transportation Committee for hearing Intro 46.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: Intro 46 would allow parents and guardians of children with autism to request the warning signs.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: From the Department of Transportation to make motorists aware that there are autistic children living nearby.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: For some children with autism, busy streets and traffic can present unique challenges, safety challenges, and these signs would serve as an additional reminder for motorists to slow down and be alert.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: This simple

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: Common sense measure can give parents some added peace of mind and while doing so help them to keep their children safe.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: And his passage would be another step towards protecting the most vulnerable among us.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: For the Commissioner of Transportation to call the possible life-saving signs as clutter is sending the message to the families raising a child or children with autism

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: that New York City does not see you, does not understand the challenges you face, and is not willing to take reasonable steps to help their children stay safe.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: I do not believe that there should be a cost put on the children.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: on the safety of children, especially children with autism.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: Thank you for your consideration and the time to speak about my bill.

chapters.summary: Abreu begins questions on Vision Zero Reimagined, asking what measurable benchmarks DOT will use and how they differ from previous Vision Zero initiatives. Flynn cites numerical targets for daylighting and priority corridors and says DOT will create a Vision Zero dashboard.
chapters.title: Abreu questions DOT on Vision Zero Reimagined benchmarks

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Thank you, Councilmember.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: All right, let's head to some questions now.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: This should have some questions on Vision Zero Reimagined.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: In September 2026, the administration released Vision Zero Reimagined, a 10-year action plan outlining eight strategic goals, including stronger enforcement, safer street designs, and expanded use of technology.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: While the goals set forth in this new plan are laudable, the devil's in the details, and we must make sure that they are implemented effectively, transparently, and in a timely manner.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Commissioner, what specific measurable benchmarks would DOT use to evaluate progress under Vision Zero Reimagined, and how do these benchmarks differ from previous Vision Zero initiatives?

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: Yeah, you know, we absolutely agree that we can only measure success if we're tracking these kinds of things, right?

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: And that's why the plan includes a number of commitments that include numerical targets, whether it's implementing 1,000 intersections with daylighting or better, or addressing the

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: roughly 200 Vision Zero priority corridors.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: It also includes a commitment to creating a Vision Zero dashboard.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: That would be a place where you can find...

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: a whole lot of different kinds of information about the program and the results.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: Likewise related, we'll have an update to the streets plan coming out in the next couple months, and that'll include some additional targets and metrics that we'll be measuring.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: And we're certainly open to other ideas as well.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Thank you, Commissioner.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: And we'll get into those specific benchmarks, like daylighting later, for instance.

chapters.summary: Abreu asks what funding and staffing are necessary to implement Vision Zero Reimagined. Flynn says the mayor made a historic commitment and DOT has resources for most of the plan, ramping up staffing and capacity in FY27.
chapters.title: Abreu asks DOT about funding and staffing for Vision Zero plan

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: What funding and staffing levels are necessary to implement the Vision Zero Reimagined plan?

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: Yeah, so we're really excited that the mayor made a historic level of commitment to our safety and multimodal programs earlier this year.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: And we have the resources to move ahead with the bulk of the Vision Zero plan.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: It is a 10-year strategy.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: So if there's additional resources needed, we'll certainly be in constant communication with City Hall and OMB on that.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: And are these resources currently available?

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: We're ramping up, yeah.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: So the new resources that kicked in in FY27 in July, so we've been in that process basically of staffing up, of

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: expanding capacity of different mechanisms for implementing things that we need to do, and that's all pretty far along in progress.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: That's great.

chapters.summary: Abreu asks which positions and divisions DOT is expanding. Flynn says the hiring mix includes project development, implementation, and maintenance staff, with roughly 200 new headcount and over 100 already far along in the pipeline.
chapters.title: Abreu questions DOT hiring and divisions expanding capacity

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: And as part of the ramping,

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Can you give examples of certain positions you're hiring for, divisions, where are you expanding that capacity?

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: So it's a mix of the folks who develop the projects, the folks who implement them, and the folks who have to maintain it because you need all of that.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: But just, you know, given, I guess, an order of magnitude, there's roughly 200 new headcount, about, I think, a little over 100 of which is already pretty far along in the pipeline, and others are in progress.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: It takes time, obviously, to put out postings and hire, but we're moving quickly.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: And, yeah, those are distributed.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: It could be, you know, we have different groups focused on different aspects, but that gives you an idea.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Abreu asks how frequently DOT will publicly report on Vision Zero Reimagined implementation. Flynn says the dashboard will be the most frequently updated tool, and Abreu confirms it will track benchmarks regularly.
chapters.title: Abreu asks about public reporting and Vision Zero dashboard

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: How frequently will DLT publicly report on implementation of Vision Zero Reimagined initiatives?

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: So I think, like I mentioned, we'll be setting up the dashboard, and that's going to be, I think, the most frequently updated in terms of other things we can get back to.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: And then are you envisioning that dashboard to provide updates regularly on your agency's ability to meet these benchmarks?

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: Yeah, that's the idea.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: And of course, at hearings, you can share a lot as well, right?

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: Yes.

chapters.summary: Abreu asks how the forthcoming streets plan will incorporate Vision Zero Reimagined. Flynn says the streets plan will flesh out priority corridors and add specificity to the action plan's street design elements.
chapters.title: Abreu asks how streets plan will build on Vision Zero Reimagined

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: How will the forthcoming streets plan incorporate or build upon the Vision Zero Reimagine initiatives?

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: Yeah, so probably the biggest kind of jumping off point in the streets plan from the Vision Zero plan will be around those priority corridors.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: We're fleshing those out, basically, and we've been crunching the data.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: So the streets plan will include the new set of priority corridors that we're committing to redesigning, upgrading.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: It'll also add specificity to some of the ideas that are in the Vision Zero action plan.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: You know, the action plan, it's an action plan, right?

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: So it has a series of different things.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: Some of them are further along in development than others.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: So some of them will be able to share more in the streets plan.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: As a policy matter.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: How do you see the actualization of the streets plan?

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: How does that impact Vision Zero initiatives?

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: If I'm understanding, I mean, I think that the streets plan, you can see it kind of as an umbrella for multiple plans.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: So it will, it's one mechanism for fleshing out and implementing elements of the streets plan.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: But it also, you know, the same could be said for our bus plan, next stop, fast buses.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: And, yeah, I guess more of the street design-related aspects of the Vision Zero plan would be more articulated in the streets plan.

chapters.summary: Abreu asks how the Vision Zero Task Force agencies work together. Labadie describes biweekly meetings with DOT, NYPD, FDNY, MOPD, and public schools, sharing data and tracking fatalities and metrics, and cites the recent cease-and-desist work as a policy outcome.
chapters.title: Abreu questions Vision Zero Task Force coordination

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Vision Zero is incorporated.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: into the operations of all the agencies on the Vision Zero Task Force, which is a location, which is a coalition of agencies, including DOT and YPD

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: and the Business Integrity Commission, which I'll refer to as BIC for the rest of the hearing, that meets every other week to review upcoming and ongoing projects, study progress on key measures, and share agency updates.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Could you give us an overview of how the various agencies that are part of the Vision Zero Task Force work together?

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: What happens in these meetings?

utterances.speaker: Madeline Labadie
utterances.text: Happy to, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Madeline Labadie
utterances.text: My name is Madeline Labade.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Can you get closer to the mic?

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Sure thing.

utterances.speaker: Madeline Labadie
utterances.text: Madeline Labade, Chief of Staff at DOT.

utterances.speaker: Madeline Labadie
utterances.text: The biweekly meetings have all of the agencies under the umbrella, including additional agencies that have been added under this administration, including the Fire Department, the Mayor's Office for People with Disabilities, and formerly the Department of Education, New York City Public Schools.

utterances.speaker: Madeline Labadie
utterances.text: It is a coalition where every piece of the toolkit is employed when it comes to addressing the trends that all of us are seeing from the data of collisions on the street, our enforcement trends,

utterances.speaker: Madeline Labadie
utterances.text: novel policy discussions, really everything driven by what we are seeing and novel ways that we can address it.

utterances.speaker: Madeline Labadie
utterances.text: So imagine it is the full sort of kit and caboodle of government all working together.

utterances.speaker: Madeline Labadie
utterances.text: These meetings really do look at the fatality numbers.

utterances.speaker: Madeline Labadie
utterances.text: DOT provides a monthly fatalities dashboard and the Mayor's Office of Operations, which convenes the Vision Zero Task Force, tracks metrics for all agencies to ensure that we are on track for the commitments we have made publicly,

utterances.speaker: Madeline Labadie
utterances.text: as well as our general MMR level metrics as well.

utterances.speaker: Madeline Labadie
utterances.text: It is a highly collaborative group of staff members from each agency well positioned to work across agency and across the city in order to drive fatalities down.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: So it's fair to say there's a lot of data sharing happening?

utterances.speaker: Madeline Labadie
utterances.text: A ton of data sharing, yes.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: And are there updates regularly on project updates that you have?

utterances.speaker: Madeline Labadie
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: Madeline Labadie
utterances.text: So as there are large programs, you know, for example, from DOT, perhaps a large street reengineering project, one might say Queens Boulevard, a legacy capital project,

utterances.speaker: Madeline Labadie
utterances.text: updates on things like that, as well as discussions on novel issues such as crashes, you know, the one that has been discussed a lot lately, I believe in the public advocate's testimony and in past hearings that occurred in September,

utterances.speaker: Madeline Labadie
utterances.text: as well as the one in July, where there are notable trends, even small numbers.

utterances.speaker: Madeline Labadie
utterances.text: That is when the Vision Zero team gets together to really figure out how to address it and discuss the best path forward.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: And have you in this past year, have you seen these meetings lead to policy changes?

utterances.speaker: Madeline Labadie
utterances.text: Yeah, a great example is actually the cease and desist work that the mayor announced recently.

utterances.speaker: Madeline Labadie
utterances.text: That work was really driven by the task force monitoring the illegal device trends that we have seen both in enforcement and in collisions

utterances.speaker: Madeline Labadie
utterances.text: and really working together to see what additional tools can be brought to the fore, bringing in the law department to really expand the pie when it comes to ways that we can get at reducing traffic fatalities.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Abreu questions why Vision Zero-related moving summonses have fallen substantially below pre-pandemic levels. Flynn attributes the drop to pandemic disruptions, says enforcement is up over 40% since 2021, and argues quality and data-driven focus matter more than ticket totals.
chapters.title: Abreu questions NYPD on falling Vision Zero summonses

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: I'm now going to turn over to some questions on enforcement for NYPD and DLT.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Overall, Vision Zero-related moving summonses issued by YPD have significantly fallen in recent years.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Prior to the COVID-19 pandemic and fiscal years 2020,

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: 2018 and 2019, NYPD routinely issued nearly 700,000 Vision Zero-related moving summonses annually.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: However, according to data from the mayor's management reports, NYPD's summonses issuance has fallen below fiscal year 2019's level

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: every year since and is currently at just over 413,000 summonses.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: At FY 2026, a decline of about 41% from pre-pandemic levels.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Why has NYPD enforcement remained substantially low pre-pandemic levels?

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Is this attributed to staffing, deployment priorities, or a change in enforcement strategy?

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Can we please?

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: I'll also get another mic.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: Thanks very much, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: So, of course, the pandemic had enormous disruptions in a variety of areas, and in our traffic enforcement, that was no exception.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: And that did result in decreases both in 2020 and then into a low.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Can you please get closer to the mic, please?

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: So the pandemic did create a number of disruptions that led to decreases across a lot of areas, and one of those areas was traffic enforcement, and that led to a low in 2021.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: Since that time, we've been issuing more summonses every year.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: We're up 40%, over 40% from that low in 2021.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: The other thing I think I would note there is that we're not writing tickets just to write tickets.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: We're focusing our enforcement where it's going to have the most impact, the most material benefits.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: And we're seeing those increases year over year.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: And I think the results that we're seeing with fatalities being down reflect the quality of that work, the quality of the work being done.

chapters.summary: Abreu calls the 41% decline astronomical and asks if NYPD aims to return to pre-pandemic enforcement numbers. Flynn says NYPD does not set a specific summons target and deploys resources where data shows the greatest impact.
chapters.title: Abreu presses NYPD on pre-pandemic enforcement commitment

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: I mean, a decline of 41% is kind of astronomical.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Is it NYPD's goal to get back to the pre-pandemic numbers?

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: We don't set a specific number of summonses we're going to be issuing.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: We're driven by the circumstances.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: We're driven by what our officers see on the ground.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: focus on is deploying our resources where they're going to have the most impact.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: So we follow the data, we identify those areas where that impact is going to have the most benefit, and we deploy our resources there.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: So our enforcement is following from that data.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: So what I'm hearing is a lack of a commitment to get to pre-pandemic enforcement levels.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: I think what I would say is that the number of tickets being written, that's not the end goal here.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: Our enforcement is going to follow the data.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: We're going to look to where we need to go to deploy those resources to keep our streets safe.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: I mean, I think there's clearly an enforcement strategy that is changing here because we see enforcement areas go up in some areas, but it's going dramatically down.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: In this area, is it fair to say that there's a change in enforcement strategy here?

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: Well, as I said, across the board, we're following the data.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: And when it comes to issuing summonses, what we're looking at is the areas where that's going to have the most impact.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: So we look at our high visibility corridors, and we deploy our resources there, and our enforcement follows from that.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: We work at the precinct level to identify areas that are going to have the highest risk, and that's based on fatality data, collision data, traffic data.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: And we're deploying resources there.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: So our overall enforcement strategy is following that data.

chapters.summary: Abreu challenges whether the data shows fewer traffic law violations. Flynn says officers write tickets where they see violations and enforcement is up over 40% since 2021, while Chief Rivera begins explaining the changed traffic landscape.
chapters.title: Abreu challenges NYPD data on traffic law violations

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: So you're talking about following the data, right?

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Is your data showing that folks are not flouting traffic laws as much as they used to?

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: Well, I think what...

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Please answer the question.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: Thanks, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: Our data, our enforcement data is what you've seen and what's in front of you.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: Our officers are writing tickets where they see violations, when they see movement.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: They're not seeing violations?

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: They're seeing violations in the right levels.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: At the same levels of pre-pandemic levels or more?

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: Well, as I said, we...

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: I'm looking, I'm just talking about the data here.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: What are you, I want to know what the data is telling you now.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: The data is telling us that we're up, we're up over 40% since 2021 and we're increasing every year.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: But you're not committing to doing pre-pandemic numbers.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: So I understand you're going up since every 2021, but there's no commitment to get pre-pandemic levels.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: We don't think that writing tickets for tickets'sake, it's not the number of tickets, it's the quality of enforcement.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Do you think that with the current data that your officers are seeing, it would warrant 700,000 tickets a year?

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: Well, I'll let Chief Obey speak to what our officers see on the ground.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: My expectation would be that, yes, that the data you're seeing on the ground would warrant more than 700,000 tickets a year.

chapters.summary: Chief Philip Rivera acknowledges the decline in Vision Zero summonses but cites a changed traffic landscape, micromobility growth, and increased seizures of motorcycles and mopeds. He says traffic enforcement remains overwhelmingly focused on cars and SUVs because they cause the most serious injuries and fatalities.
chapters.title: Chief Rivera explains changed traffic landscape and micromobility enforcement

utterances.speaker: Philip Rivera
utterances.text: Morning.

utterances.speaker: Philip Rivera
utterances.text: Sorry, good morning.

utterances.speaker: Philip Rivera
utterances.text: So we do acknowledge the declining of Vision Zero summonses.

utterances.speaker: Philip Rivera
utterances.text: I do want to mention that our commitment to Vision Zero remains unchanged.

utterances.speaker: Philip Rivera
utterances.text: The traffic landscape in 2019, a reference to the report, changed significantly from what we see in 2025 or what we currently see in 2026.

utterances.speaker: Philip Rivera
utterances.text: As things change, we had to pivot and address traffic safety outcomes, changing travel patterns, new technology, and the department's wide enforcement responsibilities.

utterances.speaker: Philip Rivera
utterances.text: As we heard earlier in the testimony,

utterances.speaker: Philip Rivera
utterances.text: I just want to highlight a few things.

utterances.speaker: Philip Rivera
utterances.text: First is traffic fatalities and pedestrian safety.

utterances.speaker: Philip Rivera
utterances.text: That will always be our goal.

utterances.speaker: Philip Rivera
utterances.text: You heard you're in 2025.

utterances.speaker: Philip Rivera
utterances.text: We reported 210 traffic fatalities compared to 252 in 2024 and 220 in 2019.

utterances.speaker: Philip Rivera
utterances.text: When you look at pedestrian fatalities, again, you're to date through 1018.

utterances.speaker: Philip Rivera
utterances.text: That also dropped 73 versus 86.

utterances.speaker: Philip Rivera
utterances.text: We're concerned about our seniors.

utterances.speaker: Philip Rivera
utterances.text: That also we see a significant decline, 26 versus 41.

utterances.speaker: Philip Rivera
utterances.text: This places 2026 amongst the lowest year-to-date totals in the department's historical trends.

utterances.speaker: Philip Rivera
utterances.text: Again, when it comes to Vision Zero, our efforts are always centered around what we call the three E's, that's enforcement, engineering, and education.

utterances.speaker: Philip Rivera
utterances.text: Another pivot we had to do was the growth from 2019 to what we saw in 2025 and 2026.

utterances.speaker: Philip Rivera
utterances.text: And we talked about this a little at the last hearing, the growth of two motorized devices.

utterances.speaker: Philip Rivera
utterances.text: The landscape is totally different.

utterances.speaker: Philip Rivera
utterances.text: So post-pandemic growth in e-bikes, stand-up scooters, mopeds, motorcycles, and off-road vehicles required us to devote more attention to illegal vehicles and dangerous riding behavior.

utterances.speaker: Philip Rivera
utterances.text: So this, of course, on our end, enforcement, seizures, and inspections of retail, as we talked about this a little, retailers selling non-compliant devices.

utterances.speaker: Philip Rivera
utterances.text: Just very quick with data.

utterances.speaker: Philip Rivera
utterances.text: When you look at our two-wheel device enforcement, motorcycle seizures, again, comparing 2025 to 2019, motorcycle seizures in 2025, 5,567 versus 2,169 in 2020.

utterances.speaker: Philip Rivera
utterances.text: Moped seizures in 2025, 14,421 versus 1610 in 2019.

utterances.speaker: Philip Rivera
utterances.text: Motorcycle moving summonses, 57,090 versus...

utterances.speaker: Philip Rivera
utterances.text: Motorcycle moving summonses, 57,090 versus 23,942.

utterances.speaker: Philip Rivera
utterances.text: Moped moving summonses, 26,154 versus 1105 in year end 2019.

utterances.speaker: Philip Rivera
utterances.text: Traffic enforcement is focused overwhelmingly on cars and SUVs, as they are the biggest category in causing serious injuries and fatalities.

utterances.speaker: Philip Rivera
utterances.text: Year-to-date 2026, 81.2% of our moving enforcement is accounted to cars and SUVs.

utterances.speaker: Philip Rivera
utterances.text: When you look at 2025, micromobility enforcement, again, I mentioned at the last hearing, accounting for 10,115 e-bikes and 468 scooter moving violations.

utterances.speaker: Philip Rivera
utterances.text: Through September 21 of 2026, this is the point of sale initiatives,

utterances.speaker: Philip Rivera
utterances.text: 63 stores inspected, 57 sea summonses issued, and we work closely with our partners in the DOT in identifying and preventing legal devices from entering our streets.

utterances.speaker: Philip Rivera
utterances.text: Another way in which we've pivoted also is automated enforcement.

utterances.speaker: Philip Rivera
utterances.text: an emphasis on reckless behavior, including ghost plates.

utterances.speaker: Philip Rivera
utterances.text: You talk about automated enforcement now supplements enforcement around the clock on city streets.

utterances.speaker: Philip Rivera
utterances.text: New York City speed cameras began operating 24-7 in August 2022.

utterances.speaker: Philip Rivera
utterances.text: And a network includes more than 2,200 cameras in 750 school speed zones.

utterances.speaker: Philip Rivera
utterances.text: As of October this year, red light cameras were expanded to 600 intersections.

utterances.speaker: Philip Rivera
utterances.text: These systems support consistent enforcement at locations where our offices can focus on driver behavior, such as reckless driving, suspended or revoked driving privileges, and fraudulent identification.

utterances.speaker: Philip Rivera
utterances.text: Data for reckless behavior, again, we're going to compare 25 to...

utterances.speaker: Philip Rivera
utterances.text: I know you're going to cut me off.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: Philip Rivera
utterances.text: I know.

utterances.speaker: Philip Rivera
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: You are saying that, sorry about that, Chief Obey.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: You are saying that part of the decline in enforcement is due to an increase in micromobility enforcement.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
