utterances.text: But are many micromobility tickets considered Vision Zero summonses?

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: For example, a motorcycle moving violation is a Vision Zero summons.

utterances.speaker: Philip Rivera
utterances.text: So I just, the point here is to, because your question is why the drop?

utterances.speaker: Philip Rivera
utterances.text: As we saw changes, micromobility wasn't a big thing in 2019.

utterances.speaker: Philip Rivera
utterances.text: It's huge now in 2025 and 2026.

utterances.speaker: Philip Rivera
utterances.text: So it's a combination of micro-bullying enforcement, automated enforcement, and ghost plates.

utterances.speaker: Philip Rivera
utterances.text: We've seen a huge increase in those also.

utterances.speaker: Philip Rivera
utterances.text: We've also paid attention to pedestrian right-of-way collision injuries.

utterances.speaker: Philip Rivera
utterances.text: In right-of-way summonses and also old summonses.

utterances.speaker: Philip Rivera
utterances.text: So it's a combination of factors, high visibility to corridor.

chapters.summary: Abreu asks whether lower enforcement is due to increased camera enforcement. Rivera calls it a combination of factors, and Abreu notes moving summonses dropped in 2020 before cameras were widely used. Flynn adds that enforcement is up for pedestrian-injury-related violations like failure to yield.
chapters.title: Abreu questions NYPD on camera enforcement and timing of summons drop

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: So is the suggestion that there's lower enforcement because of increased camera enforcement, for example?

utterances.speaker: Philip Rivera
utterances.text: It's a combination.

utterances.speaker: Philip Rivera
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: This is surprising to hear because...

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: While enforcement cameras like red light and speed cameras have slowly come online for over the past few years, the moving summonses quickly dropped in 2020 and then plateaued.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: How do you explain this timing difference between when summons dropped and when cameras became more widely used?

utterances.speaker: Philip Rivera
utterances.text: So, again, it's not just the cameras.

utterances.speaker: Philip Rivera
utterances.text: It's a combination of things.

utterances.speaker: Philip Rivera
utterances.text: We just had to address these changes as we saw the traffic landscape change.

utterances.speaker: Philip Rivera
utterances.text: So with...

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: Yeah, Chair, I think one additional aspect I would highlight is that when we're looking at moving violations in our Vision Zero summons is that our most responsible for injuries, especially for pedestrian injuries, we're seeing enforcement up there.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: We're targeting enforcement there.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: So things like disobeying traffic signs, street signs were up almost 13 percent for improper turns up 8.6 percent for failure to yield the right of way to pedestrians.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: An extremely important aspect for pedestrian safety.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: We're up 4.4 percent.

chapters.summary: Abreu notes the Mayor's Management Report lists a summons metric with a desired upward direction, contradicting Flynn's statement that tickets are not the goal. Rivera says the MMR may calculate the metric differently.
chapters.title: Abreu questions NYPD on MMR summons metric

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: I appreciate that progress, but I have to get back to your point from earlier where you said higher summonses are not a goal.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Then why is it in the mayor's management report it does list Summons metric with desired direction of being up?

utterances.speaker: Philip Rivera
utterances.text: I think that's calculated differently from the way we do it.

utterances.speaker: Philip Rivera
utterances.text: I think that's calendar year and year to date.

utterances.speaker: Philip Rivera
utterances.text: So maybe a little difference there.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: All right.

chapters.summary: Abreu asks how NYPD prioritizes enforcement of speeding and failure to yield. Flynn says DOT and NYPD collaborate using fatality, collision, and injury data. Abreu asks if more officers are needed; Flynn says more resources would help but current headcount does its best.
chapters.title: Abreu asks how NYPD prioritizes moving violation enforcement

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: How does NYPD determine where to prioritize enforcement of speeding, failure to yield, and other dangerous moving violations?

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: We're looking, we work in collaboration with our partners at DOT to identify those areas where the risk is highest.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: And so that's looking at the data.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: As I said, we're looking at fatalities, we look at collisions, we look at injuries.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: And using that universe of information, we collaborate with DOT to identify the areas where enforcement is the most important.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: And do you need more officers to adequately enforce dangers?

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Moving violations, I understand.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: This past year, there was, you know, the request for 5,000 additional officers.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: I'm asking because if you need more resources, we want to make sure you get them, especially as we're approaching budget season next year.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: In a perfect world, we would want more officers, of course.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: In a perfect world, unconstrained by resources, we would want everything that we could have.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: But based on the number of officers we have now, based on our current headcount, we're absolutely certain we're able to do our best in terms of the enforcement we have.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: And with an additional 5,000 officers, you think you'd be able to reach 700,000 summonses a year?

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: I mean, with an extra 10,000 officers, 20,000 officers, the more resources we have available, the more we're going to be able to do.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: But we obviously understand that we don't live in a world where we can simply have whatever, you know, an unlimited number.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: We live in a resource-constrained world.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: But you would like more officers, is that right?

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: All right.

chapters.summary: Abreu asks whether DOT's authority could expand for certain traffic violations or crash investigations and whether towing capacity is sufficient. Flynn says DOT thinks creatively about enforcement and automated enforcement, and says towing capacity is sufficient but DOT wants to replace the lost Manhattan tow pound.
chapters.title: Abreu asks about expanding DOT enforcement authority and towing

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: I'm going to go ask a question on enforcement coordination now between the agencies.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: NYPD remains primarily responsible for enforcing moving violations while DOT oversees street design and much of the city's automated enforcement infrastructure.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Has the administration considered expanding DOT's authority to enforce certain traffic violations or investigate serious crashes?

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: Well, what I can say, Chair, is, you know, I think hopefully it's evident in the Vision Zero reimagined plan that we're always trying to think creatively about all aspects of Vision Zero, enforcement being one of them.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: We're really proud of the impact of the automated enforcement program, and we're giving a lot of thought to that as well.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: With the state legislative session ahead of us.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: And on manual enforcement, we collaborate really closely and really well with PD, as you just heard.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: What about towing capacity to enforce parking laws?

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Does DOT or NYPD need increased capacity?

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: I can say, maybe not specifically the parking laws, but just for what it's worth, when we're redesigning a street or repaving a street, we do have the capability at DOT to tow vehicles out of the way.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: I would defer to my colleagues at PD on that.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Do you need more towing capacity to get cars off the road?

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: The towing capacity we have right now is sufficient for our enforcement goals.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: And as you know, Chair, we had a tow pound in Manhattan that we lost several years ago because of a change in state law.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: We've been working to try to find a replacement location.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: That's a difficult thing to do, obviously, in Manhattan, given Manhattan real estate.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: It's something we're working actively towards.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: But with what we have now, we're able to do the work.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Are there any responsibilities that could be transferred from PD to DLT or vice versa?

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: So when it comes to towing capacity that y'all have spoken about,

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: I can't say we've had those conversations.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: All right, I have questions on...

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: What is the coordination?

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Wait, actually.

chapters.summary: Abreu asks how DOT and NYPD coordinate on crash investigations. Labadie describes co-location at the traffic management center, shared collision information, DOT field responses, and reengineering after crashes. Rivera adds that the agencies hold monthly Vision Zero meetings and education campaigns.
chapters.title: Abreu questions DOT-NYPD coordination on crash investigations

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: What does the coordination between DOT and NYPD currently look like?

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: How do you coordinate on crash investigations, for instance?

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: And how does DOT use its relationship with NYPD to implement street safety improvements?

utterances.speaker: Madeline Labadie
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: Madeline Labadie
utterances.text: Happy to discuss our collaboration.

utterances.speaker: Madeline Labadie
utterances.text: So one of the great parts about our Vision Zero partnership with NYPD is that we're co-located at our traffic management center in Queens.

utterances.speaker: Madeline Labadie
utterances.text: And so when information comes in that there has been a collision, we are there together and receive that information at the same time.

utterances.speaker: Madeline Labadie
utterances.text: NYPD obviously responds to do its investigations.

utterances.speaker: Madeline Labadie
utterances.text: DOT also responds in person in the field to assess the conditions on the ground, assess if there's any immediate fixes required to make the location safe, such as a downed sign or other sorts of issues that can be immediately repaired.

utterances.speaker: Madeline Labadie
utterances.text: And then, of course, we continue as NYPD collects more information, we receive that information.

utterances.speaker: Madeline Labadie
utterances.text: And in the stream of our data work, use NYPD's crash data to analyze and to find those trends and to assess individual crashes.

utterances.speaker: Madeline Labadie
utterances.text: DOT then works on any sort of reengineering plans or other sort of policy implementation after the fact for a given crash.

utterances.speaker: Madeline Labadie
utterances.text: But we work very closely both in the immediate, in the near term, as well as in the overall holistic work when we respond and how we share data and how we collaborate and how we respond both from a policy perspective as well as from a response perspective.

utterances.speaker: Philip Rivera
utterances.text: On the PD end, great partners in the DOT.

utterances.speaker: Philip Rivera
utterances.text: As you heard, co-located in the shared space, traffic management center, share the same data.

utterances.speaker: Philip Rivera
utterances.text: We have the monthly Vision Zero meetings on the education end, which is one of the three E's.

utterances.speaker: Philip Rivera
utterances.text: Every season brings its own challenges.

utterances.speaker: Philip Rivera
utterances.text: And we work with the DOT to inform the public about traffic safety initiatives.

utterances.speaker: Philip Rivera
utterances.text: So year to date, 21 education initiatives were scheduled, of which 18 of the 21 have been completed.

utterances.speaker: Philip Rivera
utterances.text: Right now we're working with them, and we have the wonderful, thanks to the DOT,

utterances.speaker: Philip Rivera
utterances.text: We have the Halloween traffic safety, working hand in hand with this.

utterances.speaker: Philip Rivera
utterances.text: I think about 30,000 flyers were created.

utterances.speaker: Philip Rivera
utterances.text: So there's a lot of work we're doing, and we appreciate the work that...

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Thank you, Chief.

chapters.summary: Abreu asks whether the monthly meetings Rivera mentioned are the Vision Zero Task Force. Rivera confirms, and Flynn adds there is also a separate monthly DOT-NYPD meeting to review the dashboard and specific locations.
chapters.title: Abreu clarifies DOT-NYPD monthly meetings

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: You mentioned monthly meetings.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Are you referring to the task force?

utterances.speaker: Philip Rivera
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Are those biweekly meetings?

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: So if I can add, in addition to the Vision Zero task force meetings, we have a specific DOT NYPD monthly meeting where we also talk through the dashboard in detail and look at whether there's specific locations that need additional.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: So it's in addition.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: We meet lots of times with lots of different groups, yes.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: All right.

chapters.summary: Abreu asks about the NYPD Collision Investigation Squad, which only investigates fatalities and critical injuries. Flynn says CIS is an elite unit that freezes the scene and gathers extensive evidence, and last year identified the vehicle in 75% of hit-and-run cases.
chapters.title: Abreu questions NYPD Collision Investigation Squad criteria

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: The NYPD's Collision Investigation Squad only investigates fatalities and critical injuries,

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: meaning only a very small percentage of total collisions are directed to the CIS, Collision Investigation Squad.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: What is the difference between how an instance of criminal road violence would be investigated by the CIS versus by a traditional precinct?

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: The CIS, as you said, is an elite unit that's focused on...

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Sorry, please speak closer to the mic.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: Sorry again, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: CIS is an elite unit that's focused specifically on this issue of these collisions that result in fatalities or the most serious injuries.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: And that work that they do is very, very extensive.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: The process for CIS when a case comes into them is going to involve freezing the street, gathering every piece of evidence off the street that they can, gathering every piece of video, reviewing every piece of video.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: It's a very intensive process, an extensive process, and it delivers fantastic results.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: Last year, 75% of hit-and-run cases, the vehicle was identified.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: is able to do all that work because we dedicate tremendous resources to that.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: Now, because it's such a resource-intensive process, it's a process that we're going to be using in those fatality cases and those most serious injuries.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: In the case of other investigations, those will be referred to the precincts.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: Those will go to the detective squads, and those cases will move forward under the detective squads.

chapters.summary: Abreu asks what qualifies as a serious injury for CIS. Flynn says CIS handles fatalities, likely fatalities, and critical injuries, with determinations generally made by EMS or a hospital.
chapters.title: Abreu asks what qualifies as serious injury for CIS

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: And what would you say qualifies as a serious injury?

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: So the cases that are going to CIS and Chief Owe can speak on more, but this is a case where there is a fatality, where there's a likely fatality, or there's a critical injury.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: And those are determinations that are made generally by EMS or by a hospital.

chapters.summary: Abreu cites nine hit-and-run deaths in August 2026 and asks how many recent cases have been resolved. Flynn says investigations can take six months or longer, cannot speak to specific cases, and will follow up with information.
chapters.title: Abreu questions NYPD on August hit-and-run cases

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: In August 2026, there was a string of deadly road violence in New York City that brought renewed scrutiny to the city's Vision Zero efforts.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Tragically, hit-and-run drivers killed nine people in the month of August, including three cyclists in just three days.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: And just this past week, a man riding an e-bike was hit and gravely injured by a hit-and-run driver in Crown Heights.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: How many of these recent hit-and-run cases have been fully investigated and resolved by NYPD?

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: So, Mr.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: Chairman, as I said, these cases are very extensively investigated.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: Those investigations can take up to six months or longer.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: So looking at those timelines, those investigations are likely to be ongoing.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: I can't speak to any specific investigation.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: What I can say is that CIS does thorough investigations of all of those cases and delivers the results they find.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: So all the investigators are currently being investigated.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: I can't speak to any of those specific investigations.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: What I can do is we can look into those and come back to that information for you.

chapters.summary: Abreu asks about the procedure for closing a CIS case. Rivera says CIS handles critical, likely fatal, and fatal cases, confers with the DA, and closes when wrapped up. Flynn says about two-thirds of identified cases result in arrest, noting some lack criminality.
chapters.title: Abreu asks NYPD procedure for closing CIS cases

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: What is the procedure for closing a case?

utterances.speaker: Philip Rivera
utterances.text: Serious injury, fatality, what?

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Regarding a case being investigated by CIS.

utterances.speaker: Philip Rivera
utterances.text: Okay, so with CIS, like Director Rappaccino mentioned, critical injury, likely to die, or fatal, fatal, where we actually have someone that's actually passed away.

utterances.speaker: Philip Rivera
utterances.text: I would say extensive work that's...

utterances.speaker: Philip Rivera
utterances.text: that involves conferral with the DA's office.

utterances.speaker: Philip Rivera
utterances.text: When that's all wrapped up at some point, then it's closed.

utterances.speaker: Philip Rivera
utterances.text: From start to finish, essentially.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Of the 75% of those that were identified as part of the CIS investigations, what percent of those resulted in an arrest?

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: I think it's about two-thirds of those cases are resulting in arrest.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: So two-thirds of the 75%?

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: Of the 75%.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: And I want to highlight there that in some cases, the fact that there's no arrest is because there might not actually have been criminality there.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: So a leaving the scene charge is going to be brought when somebody knows that they've struck another individual, that there's an injury, and then they struck the person and they've left the scene.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: In some instances, our investigation will reveal that the driver didn't have knowledge of the collision.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: So that accounts for some percent of those.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: So what's the breakdown of...

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: The percent of folks who engage in criminality versus those who didn't.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: I don't think that we have, I don't know that we have those numbers here, but we'll get those for you, Mr.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: Chair, and follow up.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: That would be great.

chapters.summary: Abreu probes the share of hit-and-run cases not identified and asks about criminality breakdown. Rivera provides 212 CIS cases year-to-date, with 167 fatal and 77 criminal, and says arrests are progressing. Flynn says these are difficult cases and will provide more data.
chapters.title: Abreu probes unresolved hit-and-run cases and CIS statistics

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: And then, so what happened with the other 25% that weren't identified?

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Why do you think that happened?

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: These are difficult cases.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: I mean, by definition, the perpetrator, the person who caused the collision is not on the scene.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: That presents significant challenges.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: We use every tool at our disposal in order to try to identify those individuals, in order to identify those vehicles.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: And as I said, that's a really extensive process.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: We throw everything we possibly can at it.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: Chief Obey, I don't know if you want to add any more to that.

utterances.speaker: Philip Rivera
utterances.text: So I'll go with the 26 numbers for CIS year to date through 1018, 212 CIS cases.

utterances.speaker: Philip Rivera
utterances.text: As we mentioned, the fatalities, 167 of the 212 were fatal and 45 of the 212 were non-fatal.

utterances.speaker: Philip Rivera
utterances.text: So these are just strictly CIS cases, 212 in 2026 year to date.

utterances.speaker: Philip Rivera
utterances.text: Year-to-date total criminal cases, 77 of the 212, about 36%, again, in conferral with the DA's office, were deemed to be criminal.

utterances.speaker: Philip Rivera
utterances.text: And total fatal criminal cases, the status is 63 of the 77, accounted for by 81% of all criminal CIS cases.

utterances.speaker: Philip Rivera
utterances.text: 40 of the 63 are close to arrest.

utterances.speaker: Philip Rivera
utterances.text: And total non-criminal cases.

utterances.speaker: Philip Rivera
utterances.text: This 14 of the 77, 9 of 14 are close to arrest.

chapters.summary: Abreu asks about trends in identifying hit-and-run drivers over five years. Rivera gives examples of a driver who fled abroad and another apprehended at JFK, and says the department will provide historical rates later.
chapters.title: Abreu asks trends in identifying hit-and-run drivers

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: What have the trends been in identifying those drivers involved in hit and runs over the past five years?

utterances.speaker: Philip Rivera
utterances.text: I can speak to two right off the top of my head.

utterances.speaker: Philip Rivera
utterances.text: January, just speaking to the extensive work that Director Pacino mentioned.

utterances.speaker: Philip Rivera
utterances.text: Without saying too much about this particular fatality, that in some cases, I'll speak very generally, some of these operators flee out of the country.

utterances.speaker: Philip Rivera
utterances.text: So in this one case, January, this particular operator fled to a particular country.

utterances.speaker: Philip Rivera
utterances.text: After six, seven months, again, working with partners, he was brought back to the country.

utterances.speaker: Philip Rivera
utterances.text: You know, to face justice.

utterances.speaker: Philip Rivera
utterances.text: And recently we had one, I know this was published, we had Ocean Parkway, and that particular operator was apprehended at JFK.

utterances.speaker: Philip Rivera
utterances.text: So this is the type of work that goes into the CIS cases.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: My question is, what is the trends right now, broadly, with respect to the police department identifying hit and run drivers?

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: I know you say it's a 75% has been trending upwards, downwards the past five years.

utterances.speaker: Philip Rivera
utterances.text: Identifying?

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: The drivers involved in hit and runs.

utterances.speaker: Philip Rivera
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Philip Rivera
utterances.text: So with hit and runs in general, again, we want to prioritize where we have our injuries.

utterances.speaker: Philip Rivera
utterances.text: The policy itself is officer gets there, assesses the scene.

utterances.speaker: Philip Rivera
utterances.text: If there's an injury, you call EMS.

utterances.speaker: Philip Rivera
utterances.text: If it is a serious injury, then that case is referred to.

utterances.speaker: Philip Rivera
utterances.text: A precinct detective squad, if it is critical or likely to die as determined by EMS, then CIS takes on that case.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: So last year, PD identified 75% of drivers involved in hit and runs.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: What was the rate the year before that and the year before that?

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: I'm just trying to see what the trend has been.

utterances.speaker: Philip Rivera
utterances.text: We can get that to you.

utterances.speaker: Philip Rivera
utterances.text: We don't have the numbers.

chapters.summary: Abreu asks whether all hit-and-run collisions should be diverted to CIS. Flynn says CIS investigations are resource-intensive and limited, so CIS focuses on fatalities and most serious injuries; other cases go to detective squads and are thoroughly investigated.
chapters.title: Abreu asks whether all hit-and-runs should go to CIS

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Would diverting hit-and-run collisions to the CIS help the NYPD close more cases?

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: So when the CIS gets a case, because of the intensive investigative resources that are put into that case, those rates are going to be higher.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: We, again, live in a world of not infinite resources.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: There are limits on everything that we can do.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: And so we identify those cases that are highest priority for us, those fatalities, those most serious injuries, and those are the ones that the CIS is taking on.

chapters.summary: Abreu describes the Vijay Bharadwaj hit-and-run, where the victim could not walk for six weeks and video existed, but the case was closed by a precinct and not escalated to CIS. Flynn cannot discuss the specific investigation, explains CIS criteria based on EMS or hospital determinations, and says NYPD will follow up.
chapters.title: Abreu questions why Vijay Bharadwaj hit-and-run was not escalated to CIS

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: So on June 23rd, 2026, Vijay Bharadwaj was struck in midtown by a turning vehicle.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: The driver fled the scene and Vijay was unable to walk for six weeks after being struck and run over.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: The crash.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: unlike many hit and runs, was caught on video.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: However, despite this evidence, the case was closed by a local precinct and not escalated to the CIS.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Why was this case not escalated to the CIS?

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: First, Chair, I want to say that that circumstance and what that individual suffered was horrible.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: I second want to say that I can't speak to the details about the investigation in that case.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: What I can say generally is that we are committed to using all the resources available to try to capture, to understand what happened in the case of a collision when there's a hit-and-run driver, to identify the individual responsible, and to bring justice and enforcement where it's appropriate.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: I mean, this sounds like a perfect case for a CIS.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: I mean, serious injury.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: There's a hit and run.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Likely some, that means, you know, leaving the scene of a crime.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: So there's a criminal implication there.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Would you agree that this is a perfect case for a CIS to be covering?

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: Under our current procedures, CIS is going to be taking cases overwhelmingly in instances where there's a fatality.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: Thankfully, this individual did not die.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: It was a likely fatality.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: Again, luckily, this was not what he was doing.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: He wasn't able to walk for six weeks.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: So those determinations.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: We were talking about earlier.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: I was trying to ask you about what a serious injury would be.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: This sounds to me like a very serious injury.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: So under our current procedures, that's generally defined as being a critical injury, and that's a determination that we don't make.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: That's a determination that's made by EMS or by a hospital.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: And do you know how the hospital make a determination?

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Are you saying it was a hospital's decision to label it a critical injury and therefore you didn't get involved?

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: I'm not trying to make a straw man.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: I'm trying to understand if that's the implication.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: So I can't speak to the specifics of this investigation, this case.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: We can look into that and get back to you.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: So how does NYPD know when there's a serious injury or not?

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: Well, so as a general matter, we'll be informed by the hospital or EMS that an injury is critical, it's fatal, it's likely to be fatal, and that's the case, the instance when CIS is taken.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: In this specific instance, are you aware of EMS or the hospital indicating that this individual had a serious injury?

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: I can't speak to the specific instance, but we can look into that and certainly get back to you.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: I would say as a general matter, if it's a critical injury, that's something that we would get from EMS.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: And if this is something that is transported to you in real time via the telephone, is there some receipt we can probably try to obtain to get more information on this?

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: Chief, do you know the form in which those are coming over?

utterances.speaker: Philip Rivera
utterances.text: I'm sorry, can you just...

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: My question is, I'm trying to understand how is it when PD learns, NYPD learns in real time whether or not an injury is critical.

utterances.speaker: Philip Rivera
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: And I'm trying to understand if there were some communication from EMS or from the hospital transported to you guys that made it such that this individual wasn't being perceived as having a serious injury.

utterances.speaker: Philip Rivera
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Because that way we can try to obtain the facts.

utterances.speaker: Philip Rivera
utterances.text: Like Director Pacino said, we can't speak to this particular case, but I will tell you.

utterances.speaker: Philip Rivera
utterances.text: At the scene of the incident, the initial scene when this collision happens, our officers respond.

utterances.speaker: Philip Rivera
utterances.text: EMS also is called, they respond.

utterances.speaker: Philip Rivera
utterances.text: If the injuries are serious enough where EMS determines, deems that this particular person is critical, likely to die, the person is dead, or critical, that...

utterances.speaker: Philip Rivera
utterances.text: Responding unit will call CIS.

utterances.speaker: Philip Rivera
utterances.text: They will respond.

utterances.speaker: Philip Rivera
utterances.text: We also have situations where people are conscious and alert and they die at the hospital.

utterances.speaker: Philip Rivera
utterances.text: In that case also, CIS is called.

utterances.speaker: Philip Rivera
utterances.text: So CIS will handle all critical, likely to die, all fatalities.

utterances.speaker: Philip Rivera
utterances.text: Serious injuries, we can't speak to this particular case.

utterances.speaker: Philip Rivera
utterances.text: We'll reach out to your office, speak to you a little more about it.

utterances.speaker: Philip Rivera
utterances.text: But to your question, with criticality, EMS determines, we respond, and CIS handles it.

utterances.speaker: Philip Rivera
utterances.text: But this case, we're going to have to get back to you on that.

chapters.summary: Abreu asks why CIS investigates only about 200-250 crashes per year despite many serious crashes. Rivera reiterates CIS criteria, while Flynn acknowledges a gap between serious and critical injuries and says resources are not unlimited. Abreu offers to partner on obtaining more CIS resources.
chapters.title: Abreu asks why CIS investigates only 200-250 crashes and whether it needs resources

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: So CIS investigates about 200 to 250 crashes per year, despite there being many more crashes in our city that result in death and serious injury.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Why is this number so low, and does CIS require more resources?

utterances.speaker: Philip Rivera
utterances.text: So the criteria, again, for CIS is this critical injuries, seriously likely to die or fatal.

utterances.speaker: Philip Rivera
utterances.text: Those are the cases that CIS will handle.

utterances.speaker: Philip Rivera
utterances.text: So what's the second half of the question?

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Despite there being many more crashes in our city that result in death and serious injury, why is this number so low?

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: Chair, I think, again, what I would point to is the space, perhaps, between a serious injury and what's designated as a critical injury.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: I don't want to in any way take away from how life-affecting a crash can be and how serious injuries can be in those instances.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: But the procedures that we have in place are for when that injury, that is a serious injury, crosses over to being a critical injury based on determinations that are made by EMS or at a hospital.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: And those critical injuries are those instances where those fatalities are likely to be fatal, where we're going to have CIS take over an investigation.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Do you believe that all hit-and-run cases should be placed under CIS investigation?

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: As I said earlier, Chair, and you might get sick of me saying it, but we are aware of the fact that we don't live in an instance where we have unlimited resources all the time.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: And that's not necessarily just PD resources that we're talking about here.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: A CIS investigation is a really intensive, extensive investigation that has widespread impact.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: We use that process.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: We use those resources in the most serious cases.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: That's the process that we have available.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: And that's not to take away from the investigation that goes on when CIS is not involved.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: Those cases are going to a detective squad.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: They are thoroughly investigated.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: And as I said earlier, I'm asking all these questions because I want to make sure that PD has the resources.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: resources.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Do you need more officers for CIS?

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: I mean, we want to make sure that the hit and runs are spiking.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: And we want to increase the identification rates.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: We want to increase the arrest rates.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: What do you need from us?

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: What should we advocate for?

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: So, Sharon, I want to say three things here.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: I think, first of all, I'd just reiterate, obviously, we would take everything that we can get in a perfect world.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: Second, with respect to decisions about how to allocate resources, how to do assignments in the departments, that's something that we're constantly looking at, reevaluating and making new determinations on to shift resources where they're needed most.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: And then third, with respect to upcoming budget, I mean, we'll be looking forward and the commissioner will be looking forward to being in touch with council about that process as we move into that process.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: And as we move into that process, I'm going to be looking for more enforcement on moving violations, CIS if you need more resources to beef up.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: You know, the pursuit of these hit and run drivers, you know, consider me a partner.

chapters.summary: Abreu raises ghost plates and obscured license plates, noting over a million speed camera violations were thrown out in early 2023. Rivera details joint bridge and tunnel operations, arrests, summonses, and vehicle seizures. Flynn says automated enforcement can free NYPD resources for manual enforcement.
chapters.title: Abreu questions NYPD on ghost plate enforcement

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: I have a lot more, I have a few more questions for PD and then I'll turn over to my colleagues is on ghost plates.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Obscured license plates and ghost plates are unfortunately frequently seen in New York City, allowing drivers to evade tolls and camera-based enforcement.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: In a 2024 report, the city comptroller found that between January and June 2023, over a million speed camera violations had to be thrown out due to obscured or ghost plates,

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: which represented 22% of all cameras.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: or based violations over that period.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: What kinds of targeted enforcement action does NYPD take against obscured or ghost license plates?

utterances.speaker: Philip Rivera
utterances.text: Okay, so I'll address the ghost rate operations that we conduct across bridges and tunnels in the city.

utterances.speaker: Philip Rivera
utterances.text: We work closely with other partners, TBTA, MTA, New York State Police, PAPD, just to name a few.

utterances.speaker: Philip Rivera
utterances.text: 2026 operations through 1018, we've had 31.

utterances.speaker: Philip Rivera
utterances.text: Joint operations resulted in 440 arrests, 18,805 summonses, 1937 vehicle seizures, and 64 motorcycle and moped seizures.

utterances.speaker: Philip Rivera
utterances.text: More generally, locally, on ground, our officers have addressed this reckless behavior.

utterances.speaker: Philip Rivera
utterances.text: And with obstructed plate moving summonses, you're in 2025.

utterances.speaker: Philip Rivera
utterances.text: I don't have the 26 numbers.

utterances.speaker: Philip Rivera
utterances.text: 43,058, obstructed plate parking summonses, mostly by our TEA agents, 219,890.

utterances.speaker: Philip Rivera
utterances.text: We also address reckless driving criminal summonses, reckless driving arrest, and fraudulent temper arrest.

utterances.speaker: Philip Rivera
utterances.text: So it's something that we take seriously, and we have great data to support the work.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: If I could just add.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: You know, I think also going back to an earlier point, this is an area that we recognize is a very critical path, addressing ghost plates.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: That's why it was included in the Vision Zero Reimagined as one of the initiatives.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: I think it's also an example where expanded use of automated enforcement can maybe free up NYPD resources to be able to focus on the things that really benefit from more manual enforcement, ghost plates being one of them.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Commissioner Flynn for the save.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: No, I'm kidding.

chapters.summary: Abreu asks what regulatory or legal changes the city should seek to combat ghost plates, including penalties, impoundment, and towing. Flynn says DOT welcomes innovations but has no specific proposal today. Rivera says enforcement locations are based on complaints and partnerships.
chapters.title: Abreu asks what legal changes needed to combat ghost plates

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: So what further changes in regulation or laws should the city seek in order to combat ghost plates?

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Should we pursue increased penalties, more frequent impoundment, greater towing capacity?

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: What should we be doing at the city, at the state level?

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: How can we do something in lockstep on this issue?

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Because I know it's something that you guys deeply care about.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: If you guys have any ideas, please.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: Well, Chair, as Chief Obey said, this is an issue that we take very seriously.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: We dedicate substantial enforcement resources to.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: We would welcome innovations in the law that could address these problems.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: I don't have anything to propose for you here today, but it's something we're very eager to engage on to try to solve this problem.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: And in terms of location, how does NYPD determine where to conduct targeted license plate enforcement actions?

utterances.speaker: Philip Rivera
utterances.text: Like I mentioned, we work closely with other partners around the city, locally also, local streets, stemming from complaints we have.

utterances.speaker: Philip Rivera
utterances.text: Our TEAs are also involved too.

utterances.speaker: Philip Rivera
utterances.text: So it just, we kind of go.

utterances.speaker: Philip Rivera
utterances.text: all over for the most part.

chapters.summary: Abreu thanks Chief Obey's team for targeted enforcement in his district and recognizes members present, including Hanif on Zoom, Dinowitz, and Ressler. He calls on Council Member Wong for questions.
chapters.title: Abreu thanks NYPD targeted enforcement and turns to Wong

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: And I have to say that, you know, your chief Obey, your team has been incredible with target enforcement actions in my district.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: And we have been seeing, we have seen results.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: So I'd like to recognize we've been joined by Councilmember Hanif on Zoom, Councilmember Dinowitz and Ressler.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: For questions, we begin with Councilmember Wong.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Followed by Santos Suoso.

chapters.summary: Council Member Wong describes a 12-year-old severely injured at 75th Avenue and 60th Lane and criticizes the 104th Precinct for incomplete collision reports and lack of basic police work. He asks Chief Obey to speak with precinct commanders about evidence gathering, accurate reports, and highway assistance.
chapters.title: Council Member Wong questions NYPD on 104th Precinct collision response

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: My questions is to Chief Obey and Chief O'Brien.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Chiefs, I thank you both for your help with the traffic enforcement in my district and for getting the collision investigation squad involved in the Glendale case.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: You've both been responsive, and I really, really appreciate it.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: But I'm very concerned and frustrated with my prison, the 104th.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: And as you know, two weeks ago, a 12-year-old child was severely injured at the corner of 75th Avenue and 60th Lane.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: He was hit by a motor vehicle speeding.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: And what we saw from the videos, which my office had to collect, not the precinct, the driver was at best running a yellow light or at worst going through a red light.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Basic police work was not done.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: The report was completed incorrectly with omissions and errors and has since been amended.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: and it still needs to be corrected.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: And that is unacceptable.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: And my office have to call your office to get additional help with the prison and should have been taking that initiative itself.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Frankly, I find it unacceptable.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Of the actions or lack of response from the 104th Precinct.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: And I appreciate being able to reach both of you, but families should not need their council members to call a chief to get the precinct to do their job.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: My question to Chief Obey is, could you speak directly with precinct commanding officers about what is expected when someone is seriously injured, nearly killed in this case, especially a 12-year-old child?

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: I think a conversation about gathering evidence, preparing accurate reports, and knowing when to request highway assistance would be helpful.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Please answer that.

utterances.speaker: Philip Rivera
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Philip Rivera
utterances.text: I can't speak to the particular case you referenced, but I can tell you that we do have a forum.

utterances.speaker: Philip Rivera
utterances.text: So it's called Traffic Stat, where we address concerns like this.

utterances.speaker: Philip Rivera
utterances.text: And I've also spoken to Chief Green and, you know, we work very closely with the borough.

utterances.speaker: Philip Rivera
utterances.text: So it is something that we take seriously and will continue to address.

chapters.summary: Wong asks how the 104th Precinct prepares and supervises collision reports and corrects errors. Rivera cites traffic safety team audits and says Highway CIS is handling the specific case. Wong asks for Traffic Stat records; Flynn says those are internal confidential NYPD meetings.
chapters.title: Wong questions collision report audits and Traffic Stat records

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Okay, I'll get to traffic stats in a minute, but I appreciate that Highway has now taken over the case.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: My concern with Highway...

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: How does the 104th Precinct handle collision reports generally?

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Could you review how those reports are prepared or checked by supervisors and corrected when errors identify?

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: How does that system work when you see errors?

utterances.speaker: Philip Rivera
utterances.text: So there's audits in place that traffic safety teams within precincts handle.

utterances.speaker: Philip Rivera
utterances.text: So in this particular case, it seems you're saying that there's a discrepancy in how the report was written.

utterances.speaker: Philip Rivera
utterances.text: So I think it's been handled, again, by Highway CIS, and I think it's prudent that we wait until they come to some resolution.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: As a follow-up question, since you mentioned traffic stat meetings,

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: I don't see any records, public records that I could review.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Are these like minutes or records available?

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Anybody know?

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: Yeah, those traffic stat meetings, like comstat meetings, are internal police department meetings.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: We need to have confidentiality in order to have the truly frank and honest conversations about exactly what needs to be done.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: That's an important part of our operational procedure.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: But the results that are coming out of those are things that will be communicated out as appropriate.

chapters.summary: Wong asks how dangerous intersections are escalated to the Traffic Stat priority list. Rivera says NYPD follows data on fatalities, injuries, and collisions, will speak with Queens North and the local precinct, but cannot speak to the specific intersection.
chapters.title: Wong asks how dangerous intersections reach priority list

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Then my follow-up question would be, when we identify dangerous intersections, like in this case where a child was hit,

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: community boards were notified, my office has been notified, and what is the process that gets escalated to the traffic stat priority list that an intersection needs work?

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: And then how would I know, or how would we know that it made it to your priority list?

utterances.speaker: Philip Rivera
utterances.text: So we take a look at data.

utterances.speaker: Philip Rivera
utterances.text: I haven't personally looked at that location, but we can certainly get back to your office.

utterances.speaker: Philip Rivera
utterances.text: But, you know, we'll speak to the borough itself, Queens North.

utterances.speaker: Philip Rivera
utterances.text: We'll speak to the local precinct and get a number of operations.

utterances.speaker: Philip Rivera
utterances.text: In place and will support the initiatives.

utterances.speaker: Philip Rivera
utterances.text: But typically we go where the data takes us, where we see spikes in fatalities, injuries, or collisions.

utterances.speaker: Philip Rivera
utterances.text: So I can't speak to this particular intersection where the collision happened, but that is typically our response.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Okay, thank you.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: I have a round two questions later.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: Sounds great.

chapters.summary: Council Member Santosuosso asks DOT about the timeline for implementing the Stop Super Speeders program, originally hoped for May 2027. Flynn says DOT is eager but cites software, back-end, DOF, and state DMV complexity and hopes to start early elements and testing.
chapters.title: Council Member Santosuosso questions DOT on Super Speeders timeline

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Councilmember Santos-Wilso, followed by Councilmember Justin Sanchez.

utterances.speaker: Kayla Santosuosso
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Kayla Santosuosso
utterances.text: Commissioner Flynn, thank you.

utterances.speaker: Kayla Santosuosso
utterances.text: First of all, again, thank you for the 17th Avenue Bridge.

utterances.speaker: Kayla Santosuosso
utterances.text: I'm going to keep thanking you because I'm thrilled.

utterances.speaker: Kayla Santosuosso
utterances.text: And thank you for sort of being of the same mind on the Super Speeders Act.

utterances.speaker: Kayla Santosuosso
utterances.text: You know, I think at this point, really, advocates are mostly concerned about timeline for implementation.

utterances.speaker: Kayla Santosuosso
utterances.text: The original hope was May from the state bill that was passed.

utterances.speaker: Kayla Santosuosso
utterances.text: Are we looking like that's possible?

utterances.speaker: Kayla Santosuosso
utterances.text: And if not, what barriers are there to timely implementation?

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: Thank you, Councilmember, and thank you for being such a great partner on this legislation.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: Yeah, we're really proud to have advocated and championed for the state legislation and appreciate the Council's partnership to move it forward.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: We're very eager to stand the program up as quickly as humanly possible.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: It is a new...

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: Very new program, right?

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: This is going to be really among the first in the nation and probably the largest at this scale.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: So there's a lot of complexity there.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: There's software and back end stuff.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: There's also things that are kind of dependent on partners we need to work with.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: And just generally the coordination with, for example, Department of Finance, the State Department of Motor Vehicles.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: And so there may be some aspects of the schedule that are more under our control than others.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: Our commitment is to do it as quickly as possible.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: I could talk a little more specifically about some of the other schedule aspects, but one thing we would like to do in any scenario is at least if there are things that are maybe out of our control for the full

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: program rollout, we think that we could at least get some early elements and testing going in the meantime.

chapters.summary: Santosuosso asks whether the city can order ISA installation for out-of-state registered vehicles and impose escalating fines. Flynn says yes for device orders and fines and can suspend New York driving privileges, but interstate re-registration is not possible. Labadie notes violations returnable to TVB.
chapters.title: Santosuosso questions out-of-state super speeders and ghost plates

utterances.speaker: Kayla Santosuosso
utterances.text: Okay, understood.

utterances.speaker: Kayla Santosuosso
utterances.text: And the other question that I have is a practicality question, and it goes back to the chair's question about ghost plates.

utterances.speaker: Kayla Santosuosso
utterances.text: So unfortunately, a large number of these super speeders have vehicles that are registered in another state.

utterances.speaker: Kayla Santosuosso
utterances.text: If I understand it, we can at least ensure that the escalated fine that results from failing to install a device.

utterances.speaker: Kayla Santosuosso
utterances.text: Well, first of all, we can order the installation of a device for a vehicle registered in another state, correct?

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: Kayla Santosuosso
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Kayla Santosuosso
utterances.text: And then the escalating fine that would be incurred if they fail to install such a device could also be...

utterances.speaker: Kayla Santosuosso
utterances.text: issued, correct?

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: Kayla Santosuosso
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Kayla Santosuosso
utterances.text: But otherwise, the piece of this that is missing is that clearly we can't withdraw the driver's ability to register a vehicle from another state.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: I think we can suspend their privilege to drive in New York State.

utterances.speaker: Kayla Santosuosso
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Kayla Santosuosso
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Kayla Santosuosso
utterances.text: So it could be a license suspension, in other words.

utterances.speaker: Kayla Santosuosso
utterances.text: Which, as far as I understand it, the legislation doesn't call for a license suspension.

utterances.speaker: Kayla Santosuosso
utterances.text: It calls for a license suspension.

utterances.speaker: Kayla Santosuosso
utterances.text: for a failure to register if you are registered in the state.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: It's a violation.

utterances.speaker: Kayla Santosuosso
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Kayla Santosuosso
utterances.text: Well.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: I'm not sure about that.

utterances.speaker: Madeline Labadie
utterances.text: So the violations are sort of returnable to TVB.

utterances.speaker: Madeline Labadie
utterances.text: So there's the ability to have an accountability measure.

utterances.speaker: Madeline Labadie
utterances.text: But to your point, obviously, these vehicles and their drivers are not registered within New York State.

utterances.speaker: Madeline Labadie
utterances.text: So if they are found in New York State, there is the potential for a violation and to go to traffic court.

utterances.speaker: Kayla Santosuosso
utterances.text: Got it.

utterances.speaker: Kayla Santosuosso
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Kayla Santosuosso
utterances.text: And so a true sort of interstate cooperation in terms of a failure, I'm sorry, a prohibition on a re-registration of a vehicle within another state is not possible at this point.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: I don't believe so.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: I know that there's some language in the law that allows DMV to basically account for the possibility of multiple vehicle registrations in New York State, but interstate, right, that's more complex.

chapters.summary: Santosuosso describes drag racing and street racing on the Belt Parkway in Southern Brooklyn, including a fatal crash with a vehicle over 100 mph, and says racing continued the next night. Deputy Chief Thomas Alps outlines NYPD's multi-bureau strategy, weekly meetings, LPR cameras, and enforcement results.
chapters.title: Santosuosso raises drag racing on Belt Parkway and asks NYPD for help

utterances.speaker: Kayla Santosuosso
utterances.text: Yeah, and it just makes the cracking down on the ghost plates just an even more critical piece of this, I think, which we already spoke about.

utterances.speaker: Kayla Santosuosso
utterances.text: I do want to turn the remainder of my time to the NYPD on a separate matter, which is the issue of drag racing, street racing.

utterances.speaker: Kayla Santosuosso
utterances.text: I represent Southern Brooklyn.

utterances.speaker: Kayla Santosuosso
utterances.text: It is a hotbed of drag racing and street racing, and particularly along the Belt Parkway, notably at the M.

utterances.speaker: Kayla Santosuosso
utterances.text: End of August, there were three teenagers who were killed in an extremely high-speed crash.

utterances.speaker: Kayla Santosuosso
utterances.text: One of the vehicles was registering over 100 miles per hour at the time of the crash.

utterances.speaker: Kayla Santosuosso
utterances.text: This may sound shocking to someone who does not live next to the Belt Parkway as I do, but what was even more shocking and distressing is that the night after three teenagers were killed in an act of street racing on the Belt Parkway, I could still hear

utterances.speaker: Kayla Santosuosso
utterances.text: the high speed taking place, the street racing taking place on the Belt Parkway the following night.

utterances.speaker: Kayla Santosuosso
utterances.text: And so my office and Senator Gennardis wrote a letter to the highway unit, I believe it's Highway Unit 2, asking what kind of enforcement was going to be going on, because this is a constant problem.

utterances.speaker: Kayla Santosuosso
utterances.text: And I am begging for help.

utterances.speaker: Kayla Santosuosso
utterances.text: And just if I could have 20 more seconds, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Kayla Santosuosso
utterances.text: Inspector Scholdus responded with a letter detailing some enforcement efforts, and it's one of those scenarios where I don't mean to question

utterances.speaker: Kayla Santosuosso
utterances.text: that work is being done, but I might be questioning that this work is not in fact solving the problem, because if I can hear it every single day from my window, something's wrong.

utterances.speaker: Kayla Santosuosso
utterances.text: And so I'm both begging for help and also asking...

utterances.speaker: Kayla Santosuosso
utterances.text: For some kind of change in what we are doing because it's clearly not working.

utterances.speaker: Kayla Santosuosso
utterances.text: And thank you for your time.

utterances.speaker: Thomas Alps
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Thomas Alps
utterances.text: Good morning, Deputy Chief Thomas Alps.

utterances.speaker: Thomas Alps
utterances.text: I'm the Executive Officer of Patrol Services Bureau.

utterances.speaker: Thomas Alps
utterances.text: What you're talking about, car meets, street takeovers, is a high priority for NYPD.

utterances.speaker: Thomas Alps
utterances.text: understand that it's a danger to public safety and traffic safety overall.

utterances.speaker: Thomas Alps
utterances.text: And, you know, sorry, I think we have to administer your oath.

utterances.speaker: Thomas Alps
utterances.text: So let's give us a second.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Please raise your right hand.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Do you affirm to tell the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth before this committee and to respond honestly to council member questions?

utterances.speaker: Thomas Alps
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: You may begin when you're ready.

utterances.speaker: Thomas Alps
utterances.text: So we understand that it can result in serious physical injury, death, in some cases property damage, and causes violent altercations.

utterances.speaker: Thomas Alps
utterances.text: And it's definitely a public nuisance.

utterances.speaker: Thomas Alps
utterances.text: So we understand the priority and the sensitivity behind that.

utterances.speaker: Thomas Alps
utterances.text: This, the strategy in regards to street takeovers mainly falls under my office, and then I chair a weekly meeting with executives across the borough.

utterances.speaker: Thomas Alps
utterances.text: We discuss deployment strategy and the latest intelligence.

utterances.speaker: Thomas Alps
utterances.text: So we gather information from sources of information as well as open sources.

utterances.speaker: Thomas Alps
utterances.text: And then we look to identify critical locations of where these incidents are happening.

utterances.speaker: Thomas Alps
utterances.text: In response to that, we've installed LPR cameras at these locations as well as covert cameras.

utterances.speaker: Thomas Alps
utterances.text: This will allow us to immediately identify that these groups are forming and we can respond quickly even before a 911 call comes in.

utterances.speaker: Thomas Alps
utterances.text: The LPR cameras are for...

utterances.speaker: Thomas Alps
utterances.text: Intelligence gathering, and prosecution on the back end to help us identify these individuals who are engaged in this illegal behavior.

utterances.speaker: Thomas Alps
utterances.text: So, you know, we also coordinate with our adjacent law enforcement agencies in Nassau County and Westchester County.

utterances.speaker: Thomas Alps
utterances.text: That's seamless because they're having similar problems that transcend and come into the city.

utterances.speaker: Thomas Alps
utterances.text: We have multiple bureaus that are attacking this issue to include Patrol Services Bureau, our community response teams, the intelligence bureaus heavily involved in it.

utterances.speaker: Thomas Alps
utterances.text: As well as we have tow trucks, we have drone teams, we have aviation, and we have our highway districts.

utterances.speaker: Thomas Alps
utterances.text: So it's a multi-bureau approach within NYPD addressing this.

utterances.speaker: Thomas Alps
utterances.text: What are the results?

utterances.speaker: Thomas Alps
utterances.text: You look at January 1st, 2026 to April 18th, 2026, NYPD responded to 271 documented street takeovers or car meetups.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Sorry, was that citywide?

utterances.speaker: Thomas Alps
utterances.text: Citywide.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: 271 in what period of time?

utterances.speaker: Thomas Alps
utterances.text: From January 1st to October 18th of this year.

utterances.speaker: Thomas Alps
utterances.text: So 271 total write-outs.

utterances.speaker: Thomas Alps
utterances.text: That's an 11% increase from last year.

utterances.speaker: Thomas Alps
utterances.text: We made 170 arrests.

utterances.speaker: Thomas Alps
utterances.text: We issued 1,572 summonses, and we seized 291 vehicles.

utterances.speaker: Thomas Alps
utterances.text: That's 161% increase in arrests, 246% increase in summonses, 104% increase in vehicle seizures, while again I said

utterances.speaker: Thomas Alps
utterances.text: that the number of car meetups and street takeovers have increased by about 11%.

utterances.speaker: Thomas Alps
utterances.text: So this is a high priority for us.

utterances.speaker: Thomas Alps
utterances.text: We do have dedicated teams.

utterances.speaker: Thomas Alps
utterances.text: that will go across borough boundaries and precinct boundaries, and we move throughout.

utterances.speaker: Thomas Alps
utterances.text: We can surge anywhere between 60 and 50 cars at a moment notice to take these over.

utterances.speaker: Thomas Alps
utterances.text: They're very dangerous to the police department.

utterances.speaker: Thomas Alps
utterances.text: We've had many instances, not a couple, many instances where these individuals ram our cars and physically assault our officers and ram our officers.

utterances.speaker: Thomas Alps
utterances.text: We had shots fired incidents.

utterances.speaker: Thomas Alps
utterances.text: So we understand the danger of it.

utterances.speaker: Thomas Alps
utterances.text: And the police commissioner has sent a directive.

utterances.speaker: Thomas Alps
utterances.text: This will be to us, and we are doing that.

utterances.speaker: Kayla Santosuosso
utterances.text: Okay.

chapters.summary: Santosuosso acknowledges NYPD's efforts but says the Belt Parkway in Bay Ridge remains unsafe and she can hear racing nightly. Abreu asks NYPD to bring attention to Bay Ridge and Coney Island and assist council members.
chapters.title: Santosuosso says Bay Ridge drag racing persists despite NYPD efforts

utterances.speaker: Kayla Santosuosso
utterances.text: And again, I see that the effort is taking place, but for some reason the Belt Parkway, at least in the Bay Ridge section, I can tell you by my ears every single night, it's not being solved.

utterances.speaker: Kayla Santosuosso
utterances.text: So I appreciate the efforts, but again, I'm not questioning whether work is happening.

utterances.speaker: Kayla Santosuosso
utterances.text: I'm saying, is it working for where, for my district?

utterances.speaker: Kayla Santosuosso
utterances.text: And I'm telling you it's not.

utterances.speaker: Kayla Santosuosso
utterances.text: So I don't know what further actions we can take, but it really is, you know, a dire, dire need.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Well, let's bring attention to Bay Ridge and to the council members'district, please.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Kayla Santosuosso
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: And to Coney Island as well.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Wherever it's taking place, please help out the council member, please.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Understood.

chapters.summary: Council Member Justin Sanchez asks what figures support DOT's claim that towing capacity is sufficient and requests tow request, completion, and response time data by borough. Rivera cites three tow pounds and says capacity is sufficient; Flynn defers enforcement towing to NYPD.
chapters.title: Council Member Justin Sanchez questions DOT and NYPD on towing capacity

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: All right, we're now going to move to Councilmember Justin Sanchez, followed by Dinowitz.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: I want to go back to towing capacity.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: First, you said that DOT's towing capacity is sufficient.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: What figures is DOT relying on when it says capacity is insufficient?

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: Enough.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: Can the agency give the council the number of tow requests last year, how many were completed, and the average response times by borough?

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: Thank you, Councilmember.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: Yeah, so just to clarify, again, we tow vehicles out of the way when we need to work on a street.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: For more enforcement-type towing, I would defer to PD.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: If you're asking, I guess, about the towing DOT does, I believe it's sufficient, but we could circle back.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: PD, same question.

utterances.speaker: Philip Rivera
utterances.text: I'm sorry, what's the question?

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: The question is, it was stated that the towing capacity is sufficient.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: So what figures is PD relying on when it says they have enough capacity?

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: Can the agency give the council the number of tow requests it had, how many were completed, and the average response times by borough?

utterances.speaker: Philip Rivera
utterances.text: Okay, so the second half will get to you after this, but I do want to say, as was mentioned earlier, we don't have a Manhattan toll pound, but we do have three toll pounds around the city, Brooklyn, Bronx, and Queens.

utterances.speaker: Philip Rivera
utterances.text: Brooklyn toll pound, vehicle capacity, 392.

utterances.speaker: Philip Rivera
utterances.text: That's the vehicle capacity.

utterances.speaker: Philip Rivera
utterances.text: Bronx toll pound, 350.

utterances.speaker: Philip Rivera
utterances.text: Queens toll pound, 250.

utterances.speaker: Philip Rivera
utterances.text: And it is sufficient.

utterances.speaker: Philip Rivera
utterances.text: If we're over, typically, in my experience, maybe about 60 plus vehicles, but again, I've testified to this.

utterances.speaker: Philip Rivera
utterances.text: For the most part, these vehicles are in and out.

chapters.summary: Sanchez cites 700 unlicensed tow trucks and challenges NYPD's assertion of sufficient capacity. Rivera says NYPD does not license tow companies, offers to visit the district, and says vehicles are towed for violations. Flynn says DOT tows when needed and wants to replace the Manhattan tow pound.
chapters.title: Sanchez challenges NYPD on unlicensed towing industry and sufficiency

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: So when we're talking about sufficiency, there is a rampant and growing unlicensed towing industry.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
