utterances.text: Gotham has found that there are 700 unlicensed tow trucks in the city.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: Would you agree that the size of this illegal fleet suggests that capacity isn't where it needs to be?

utterances.speaker: Philip Rivera
utterances.text: We don't handle that in the NYPD.

utterances.speaker: Philip Rivera
utterances.text: That doesn't fall under our...

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: Yeah, we don't do the licensing of tow companies.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: What I will say is what Chief Obey said, which is that when a summons is written, the vehicle needs to be towed.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: In those circumstances, we're able to tow the vehicle.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: We would love to be able to replace that Manhattan facility.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: It's something we're working hard to do, but it presents its challenges, some of which are very obvious.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: So if I'm understanding correctly, you're saying that the towing that we need in the borough, all of the cars that need to be towed that have, you know, kind of just sat there for time, we don't need to do anything about them.

utterances.speaker: Philip Rivera
utterances.text: I don't know if you want to speak to something specifically about.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: One of the biggest issues that all New Yorkers complain about, and I think the chair also brought it up, was that we just have cars that need to be towed, but they never seem like they are towed.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: And now we're hearing that we have the complete capacity.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: And I know when I'm dealing with trucks that need to be towed and I'm calling my PD station, I'm told that we don't have the sufficient capacity to tow all of these vehicles, to do all of this work.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: So I'm just confused on.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: What is sufficient?

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: Like what is sufficient, the number of cars that we have in the tow pounds, is sufficient the number of cars that we actually need to be towing?

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: What is sufficiency to the agency?

utterances.speaker: Philip Rivera
utterances.text: So two things I'll say.

utterances.speaker: Philip Rivera
utterances.text: First, we'll come visit you and take a look.

utterances.speaker: Philip Rivera
utterances.text: We'll walk through your district just to get a sense of what's happening there, and we'll help you with some towing issues.

utterances.speaker: Philip Rivera
utterances.text: The second thing is we don't tow just to tow.

utterances.speaker: Philip Rivera
utterances.text: We tow for violations for the most part.

utterances.speaker: Philip Rivera
utterances.text: So I talked about ghost plate enforcement.

utterances.speaker: Philip Rivera
utterances.text: Our tow operators will go out there, respond to community complaints.

utterances.speaker: Philip Rivera
utterances.text: And then we prioritize towing.

utterances.speaker: Philip Rivera
utterances.text: If you have a vehicle that's parked in front of a fire hydrant, that needs to go, rather than towing a vehicle that's parked in front of a expired meter.

utterances.speaker: Philip Rivera
utterances.text: So we prioritize it, but we don't tow just to tow.

utterances.speaker: Philip Rivera
utterances.text: We also can't tow our way out of the towing problem.

utterances.speaker: Philip Rivera
utterances.text: But we can certainly meet with you and we'll visit your district and work with you.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: I would appreciate that.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: I want to move on to...

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: Wait.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: You have 40 seconds.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: I want to move on quickly.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: I will need round two.

chapters.summary: Sanchez asks how DOT triangulates Empire bins with Vision Zero and daylighting and how drivers parking in daylighting zones are held accountable. Flynn discusses the new Office of Curb Management, DSNY coordination, flex-post curb extensions, and ongoing enforcement collaboration with PD.
chapters.title: Sanchez questions DOT on containerization and daylighting enforcement

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: I want to move on to containerization and Vision Zero.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: How does DOT triangulate Empire bins with the Vision Zero framework?

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: For example, a stationary on-street container looks like it could be in the daylighting areas.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: Have we or are we considering that?

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: What is happening there?

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: Also, can you talk to us about what's happening with daylighting parking?

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: How are we holding drivers accountable that are parking in these daylighting zones?

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: And what can we do?

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: Because you have put up these plastic little things, but they drive over it.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: Thank you, Councilmember.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: Yeah, there's a few dimensions there that you highlighted.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: I think, and in a way it also relates to the last conversation, I think, perhaps around some of the aspects of towing.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: There's so much happening at our curbside, right?

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: And that's why we're excited to be creating this Office of Curb Management, which we're currently putting together.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: We're going to have more to share there.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: But their job is really to be looking holistically at all these different dimensions, which in the past would have been handled at different parts of DOT.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: And so for containerization specifically, that's something that we're communicating with DSMY pretty constantly, actually.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: It's one of the bigger efforts going on right now that impacts us on the curb.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: And I'd say we have a great collaboration with them.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: I think some of the bins may be too high to actually put to use for Dayline because they would actually impede.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: the visibility.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: So it depends on the situation, but definitely we want to be thinking creatively every time we're putting something on the curb.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: Can it also serve a safety function or provide some other benefit?

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: So, you know, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: Can you just speak a little bit about what's happening to hold the cars accountable that are in the daylighting zones right now?

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: Yeah, and this is one of those things that we're always continually trying to sort of build upon, right?

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: We want to build.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: There's an urgency to rolling out safety improvements citywide, and to do that, it means building things quickly.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: But then when we build things quickly.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: They may have some of the issues that you mentioned.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: And so, you know, over the long run, we want to keep moving towards both a higher quantity, but also quality.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: And that's sometimes why I talk about this in the context of some of our discussions around different kinds of targets.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: We want quantity and quality.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: And so in this situation, we're always evaluating how is it being used?

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: How can we continue to improve upon it?

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: And, um,

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: So in the case of these painted curb extensions with the flex posts, maybe it's an enforcement thing we can work with PD on, or maybe there's a design solution we can keep innovating.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: It depends on the situation.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: Is there any enforcement right now?

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: We're continually collaborating with PD on enforcement.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: So is there a method for enforcement right now?

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: Like are cars getting tickets?

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: That seems like a question for PD to answer.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: daylighting cars that are parking in the daylighting areas.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: What is the enforcement looking like?

utterances.speaker: Philip Rivera
utterances.text: Okay, so...

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: Are they getting tickets or what is...

utterances.speaker: Philip Rivera
utterances.text: I can't speak to daylighting.

utterances.speaker: Philip Rivera
utterances.text: I can speak to enforcement generally.

utterances.speaker: Philip Rivera
utterances.text: So I don't know that we ticket vehicles as it pertains to daylighting, but just in general.

utterances.speaker: Philip Rivera
utterances.text: So maybe a conversation to be had with DOT.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: I think the council member raises a good point, especially as the administration is expanding daylighting, that we're also, in terms of increasing summonses and violations, that we're also accounting for ticketing for cars at daylighting.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: I'll now move it over to Councilmember Dynowitz, followed by Ressler.

chapters.summary: Council Member Dinowitz says DOT's testimony does not match his constituents' experience, citing lack of towing capacity on Webster and Goulden Avenues and unanswered requests for speed humps and stop signs. Flynn apologizes for communication gaps and says DOT will follow up.
chapters.title: Council Member Dinowitz criticizes DOT responsiveness to community requests

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: This is a very interesting hearing because I want to hearing testify today is extremely different than what I'm experiencing in my community and my constituents are experiencing.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: So it is interesting to hear that you have towing capacity because Webster Avenue, Goulden Avenue, the service road of Henry Ritz and Parkway are a mess.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: And we have heard that there's no capacity for towing or heavy towing.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: So I would love to continue that conversation with you further.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: And Chief Obey, why we are getting different reports from different people in PD about what is and isn't feasible to clean up our neighborhood.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: So I appreciate the testimony and look forward to speaking with you sooner.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: But I do want to ask the DOT.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: You know, there are, you testified, you're concerned about

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: certain legislation, you want the flexibility to be able to meet the needs of the city.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: And I appreciate that.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: And I think in normal circumstances, that would be normal testimony.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: If these ballot proposals pass, you will be given more authority to

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: in my view, ignore the community, which is actually the experience we have now.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: And it is deeply frustrating because we want simple things.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: We're not asking for hundreds of miles of bike lanes or bus lanes.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: We want some stop signs and we want some speed humps.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: We requested a speed hump on Richardson Avenue over a month ago.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: No response.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: No response from the Department of Transportation.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: We requested a two-way stop on the service road of Henrietta and Parkway about a month ago.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Not even acknowledgement of receipt.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: And of course, as I've mentioned at this hearing before, stop signs in North Ruda that were rejected.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: At a hearing just like this, it was committed to me that we would get data associated with that, including velocity.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: The speed of the cars.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: As to why those life-saving signs were rejected, we received no information despite follow-up.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: I am just simply wondering if there is an affirmative policy to ignore council member and community requests, or if that is a problem with the culture within the DOT.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: Thank you, Councilmember.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: And I want to apologize if there's been any gaps in communication.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: We really, we recognize just how critical community input and

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: Feedback is to the work we do because we know the work we do is so tangible and really does impact people's day-to-day lives.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: So we take, and I personally take that responsibility very seriously.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: That said, I know there's always room for improvement.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: So we're going to definitely take this feedback back.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: You know, with some of the specific traffic control requests you mentioned, we do get a large volume.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: And I know that, you know, there are criteria we have to use so that we can be objective.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: I believe that.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: I want to be clear.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: I'm not talking about the criteria.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Although in one case I am.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: In the cover letter, this was two years ago we got this report, I know before you.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: The cover letter said we considered velocity.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: The report itself did not list velocity.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: I asked for that data from this administration, did not receive it.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: And I'm not talking about what the data say in the other cases.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: I'm talking about acknowledging receipt and continuing a conversation, despite follow-ups from my office.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: We should absolutely be acknowledging receipt.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: So I'll certainly look into that later today.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: And it's a weird bare minimum to be asking to just acknowledge receipt.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: And as I've mentioned at this hearing before, it is unfortunate that the only time the DOE seems to act with urgency is when they want to do a project like a bike lane or a bus lane.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: And by the way, do not take community input into consideration.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Or if there is a crime, like a woman getting run over by a bus or a rape, which are the two instances I can remember.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: member of the DOT being responsive.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: And it shouldn't take that for the DOT to be responsive to a community.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: And we in my community are at our wits end to try to just get a few safety measures or at least start the conversation about that.

chapters.summary: Dinowitz says bus stops on 231st Street and Gun Hill Road are repeatedly blocked and automated enforcement is not enough. He requests manual enforcement to keep traffic moving, especially as the city considers a rezoning on Gun Hill Road.
chapters.title: Dinowitz requests enforcement on bus lanes and Gun Hill Road

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: I want to go back to enforcement.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: I would just like to note here that at 231st Street,

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: We've had meetings with DOT, NYPD, MTA about enforcement on 231st Street and Broadway

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: regarding cars parked or standing in the bus stop, contributing to a significant amount of traffic, slowing the buses down, which I know is a big priority of this administration and of my community members.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: And the response we got was, well, we'll do some enforcement, but we have automated bus enforcement, so we don't really need to.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: That was sort of the message that I got.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Every time I go by there, there is at least one car or truck or cart in the bus lane.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: I'm requesting here at this hearing enforcement.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: I'm also requesting enforcement on Gun Hill Road.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Where you installed a new bus lane.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: And we warned you people would be parking in double parking, clogging up traffic.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: The DUT told us it wouldn't happen.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Of course it's happening.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: We're requesting enforcement on Gun Hill Road to make sure traffic runs smoothly, especially, if I could just finish the thought, Chair, especially as we are considering a rezoning.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: On Gun Hill Road to provide much needed housing to our city and to our community.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: One of the big holdups is the traffic.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: When there is no enforcement,

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: It makes traffic work and it disincentivizes a community from getting on board to building additional housing and a denser neighborhood.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: So I cannot impress upon you how important it is for you all to be responsive to our community, to take our needs into consideration.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Thank you, Councilmember.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: We have Councilmember, first I'd like to recognize we've been joined by Councilmember Juan, Councilmember Ressler, followed by Juan.

chapters.summary: Council Member Restler thanks NYPD for responsiveness and asks when NYPD crash data on open data will be updated; Flynn promises an update this week. Restler asks if DOT supports expanding pedestrian space by a million square feet per year; Flynn expresses support but does not give a yes or no.
chapters.title: Council Member Restler questions DOT and NYPD on crash data and pedestrian space

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Thank you so much, Chair Abreu.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: You've been doing a terrific job with this committee and really appreciate your leadership.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Before I shift to DOT, I do just want to say when we reach out to the NYPD Transportation Division, we get really swift response.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: And so I really want to thank you, Chief Obey, for that.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: You've come out to my district several times.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: And I especially want to thank your XO, Chief O'Sullivan, who is like one of the most superb public servants I've had a chance to work with.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: So I really just want to thank you for everything you do and for being such a great partner.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: And Commissioner, good to see you and the team from DOT.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: I just want to highlight a few areas that have been of particular concern to me.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: And actually, you know, before I do, this is both a PDDOT question that we've been trying to get an answer.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: It's wrong.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: The NYPD crash data on open data hasn't been updated since June, I don't believe, unless there was an update in the last week.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: There is a note on the page saying there was an automation in progress and it was expected to be completed in August.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Does anybody at the dais have a timeline on when we're going to have that data back online?

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: And I'd love the answer to be today.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: We'll get back to you as soon as we can on that.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: It hasn't been updated in five months.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: Yeah, we'll look into that and get back to you as soon as we can.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: How soon?

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: As soon as we can, Councilmember.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Do you think you'll send me an email this week?

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: We'll give you an update about what that timeline looks like this week.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: Yes, we can get back to that.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: I'll accept that.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: I look forward to that.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Now we'll shift to fun DOT stuff.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Pedestrian space.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: The Vision Zero plan included some minor references to pedestrian space.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Expanding space around subways, bus stations, busy sidewalks is essential to making sure pedestrians have the space to move around our streets safely.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: More than half of New Yorkers do not own a car, myself included.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: But 75% of our streets are devoted to storing and moving vehicles.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Does DOT support expanding pedestrian space by a million square feet per year?

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Commissioner.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: Thank you, Councilmember.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: We're, as you noted, this is something we've been really prioritizing and working hard on the last few years, expanding pedestrian space, both actual full-time pedestrian space, but also, you know,

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: open streets and other creative use of space that may be more based on events or

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: different times of the year.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: And that's why we included it in the Vision Zero plan as one of the initiatives, is to really for the first time have an actual coordinated program around pedestrian districts and pedestrian priority zones.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: So we're very supportive of the idea of continuing to expand pedestrian space.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: I didn't hear a yes or no on the million square feet, but I heard an enthusiasm for pedestrian space, so we will keep working together on that.

chapters.summary: Restler asks if DOT is ready to comply with Local Law 178 of 2025, which requires sidewalk lighting on 300 commercial corridor blocks per year starting January 2027. Flynn says lighting is a focus but aging infrastructure creates challenges. Restler notes streetlight repair times rose from 5.3 to 8.5 days.
chapters.title: Restler presses DOT on streetlight and sidewalk lighting compliance

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: On lighting, this has been one of the areas that I will admit I have been most frustrated with the Department of Transportation.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: The Vision Zero plan includes some references to improving lighting.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Last year, we passed Local Law 178 of 2025 that requires DOT to install pedestrian sidewalk lighting on 300 commercial corridor blocks per year, places like Atlantic Avenue in Brooklyn.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: The law takes effect January 1, 2027.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Is DOT prepared to start installing lighting in compliance with this new law in January, and do you have the resources to do so?

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: Thank you, Councilmember.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: You know, I can say since I started in this role, it's become very clear to me just how much lighting affects the daily lives of New Yorkers.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: It's come up in almost all of my conversations with elected officials and partners, communities, and I hear that.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: You know, I think what I can say is that what we're seeing is that a lot of the infrastructure out there.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: Is showing its age and some fixes can be done very quickly and then others are more complex.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: Sometimes it's aging cables and bases to the lights.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: Some of them are just so old that they need a full replacement of the light.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: So we've been working to expand our contract capacity, and this has been a big area of focus for me and our team, is just really being able to be more nimble and expand our ability to fix the streetlights.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: I am happy to hear that it's been a priority for you.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: I will say I think it's one of the areas that...

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Undermines goodwill and confidence in DOT when lights don't get fixed in a timely manner.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: And when we have lights that are dark, it undermines our safety.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: And we light for the streets and not the sidewalks when most of us walk.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: And so I really think this is an area we need to prioritize.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: We have not yet heard whether DOT has the resources they need to comply with this new local law.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: So I would welcome a briefing on that and how you're improving lighting.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Similarly, we have significant challenges around street lights.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: So not the lights on the streets, but the lights at the intersections.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: If I made that distinction clear.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: In the MMR, the average number of days to repair a street light increased from 5.3 to 8.5 days.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: For years, years, it was under three days.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: What's the reason behind this unacceptable delay, and does DOT have a plan to bring that time back down?

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: So it's still a requirement that our contractors need to evaluate repairs within 10 days at each location.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: But like I said, some are more complex.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: We were having some challenges with some of our contracts and the ways that we fix streetlights.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: You know, I think what you said is spot on.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: If I would paraphrase, I think something the mayor says a lot, right?

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: It's like.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: The public needs to see that we can address the small things to trust us to do the big things, right?

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: And we take that very seriously.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: And that's why, yes, the answer to your question is yes, this is a focus area.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: And we're working very hard to improve here.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: If the chair allows, I'll come back for round two.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: I'll just say and conclude.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: I'll just say.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: We're thrilled about many of the street safety projects that are happening across our district.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Work started on Adam Street yesterday.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: McGinnis is just about completed, making the area in Eastern Greenpoint around PS 110 safer with the new innovative diverters that you all are installing.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: These are transformational projects that will save lives, dramatically improve safety across our communities, and I am deeply grateful for the leadership of DOT.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: For the first time in years, there's no political resistance at City Hall.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: You guys are able to just plow ahead and do the work and make the improvements happen that we all need to see around our districts.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: I do want to continue to harp on these operational issues, street lighting and the intersection, the street lights are really important issues that I don't think have gotten the attention they deserve at DOT over an extended period of time.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Fixing this stuff is hard, but it's really important, and I'm eager to see progress.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: The MMR did not yet show that progress, and so we're eager to get some updates from the agency on how we can turn things around.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: I'm going to come back for round two, but thank you so much again, Chair.

chapters.summary: Abreu agrees streetlight delays are a major issue and announces a public realm hearing in the coming months that will cover streetlights. Restler says installations often take 8-15 months after DOT approves an intersection analysis.
chapters.title: Abreu and Restler discuss streetlight delays and future public realm hearing

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Thank you so much, Councilmember.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: And, you know, these are conversations I've had with the commissioner regarding streetlights and the need to see and the eagerness on our part to see a change.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: We will be having a hearing on public realm in the next few months that will include streetlights.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: I'll just tell you, Chair, for your awareness, like...

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: We advocate for years to finally get DOT, to study an intersection, to analyze it.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: They'll approve it.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: And then it's another 8, 12, 15 months before the streetlight actually gets installed.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: It took me a few years to get a streetlight to be placed in front of a dog run, literally for like three years.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: And, you know, we will get to the bottom of this.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: It's a big area.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: It's related to crime.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: It's related to street safety.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: It's related to a host of other issues.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: And you're right, Commissioner, getting the small things done restores our faith and, you know, our constituents'faith in government that we can also get the big things done.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: So more on that to come in the next few months.

chapters.summary: Abreu says he will turn to BIC questions but first gives the floor to Council Member Julie Won.
chapters.title: Abreu transitions to BIC questions

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: I will have some questions now for BIC, for BIC.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: I'd like to turn over, before I do that, actually, Council Member Wan.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: My apologies, Council Member.

chapters.summary: Council Member Julie Won asks DOT to define what qualifies as 'daylighting or better' in Vision Zero Reimagined, what metrics are used, whether a leading pedestrian interval counts, and whether 1,000 intersections means all crossing locations. Flynn and Beaton describe context-specific treatments like new signals and pedestrianization.
chapters.title: Council Member Julie Won questions DOT on 'daylighting or better'

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: Okay, thank you so much, Chair Breu.

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: I want to bring it back to the Vision Zero Reimagined plan that the mayors were on Mondani revealed on September 15, 2026.

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: The advocates and I are still extremely disappointed that the mayor has walked back on his campaign commitment to support universal daylighting.

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: And I know that we're going to have the bill heard at another hearing.

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: But for the Vision Zero Reimagined plan, it commits to daylighting or better, in air quotes, verbatim, at a thousand intersections.

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: Per year.

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: Can you please define what better means?

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: and quantify it or qualify it and what metrics you are used to define that as daylighting or better.

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: And does this include non-physical infrastructure?

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: For example, would solely a leading pedestrian interval count?

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: And does 1,000 intersections mean safety treatments at all crossing locations within those 1,000 intersections?

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: Thank you, Councilmember.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: You know, I think the starting point to answering that is really about the outcomes, and that's really what we're after here.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: So with the daylighting or better, it's based on the actual analysis we've done on how these treatments can reduce crashes, basically, or reduce the severity of crashes.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: And a lot of that depends on the context of each location.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: If it's a narrow street, a wide street, one-way, two-way, we see, you know, basically the other things we're including there as under or better in certain situations could deliver even better crash reduction to daylighting.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: And that's why we're defining it that way.

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: Can you give us a clear example of what qualifies as better than daylighting?

utterances.speaker: Eric Beaton
utterances.text: Sure, and there's a longer list, but it could be a new traffic signal.

utterances.speaker: Eric Beaton
utterances.text: It could be pedestrianization of a street.

utterances.speaker: Eric Beaton
utterances.text: There's a very wide range of things that we've studied that, as the commissioner said, in the right circumstance can provide better outcomes than hardened daylighting.

utterances.speaker: Eric Beaton
utterances.text: So we absolutely have a strong commitment to doing more hardened daylighting and setting new highs for how much hardened daylighting we're going to.

utterances.speaker: Eric Beaton
utterances.text: We just want to be clear that it's not the only safety treatment that we have in our books, and we want to make sure that we're doing the right thing in the right places to get the maximum safety benefit.

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: And the 1,000 intersections are all crossing locations within those 1,000 intersections?

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: How are you quantifying 1,000?

utterances.speaker: Eric Beaton
utterances.text: So we would do a safety improvement at that intersection, and when we do that, we look at where is it needed most.

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: So that still doesn't answer my question.

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: How are you quantifying 1,000?

utterances.speaker: Eric Beaton
utterances.text: If we do safety improvements at that intersection, then it counts towards the 1,000 intersections.

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: But what we're asking is, does a thousand intersection mean safety treatments at all crossing locations?

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: I think it's going to depend on the intersection.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: As Deputy Commissioner Beaton said, we approach each location individually because we want to maximize the safety benefit.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: And so it's around looking at the crash history, the crash data, what kinds of crashes are happening.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: You know, is it...

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: Turning issues?

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: Is it like T-bone type issues?

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: That's going to suggest what the right treatments could be.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: And so at some intersections, it might be all the corners or all the approaches.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: At other intersections, it may be like a major road, you know, intersecting with a minor street.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: So that might look different.

chapters.summary: Won asks DOT to provide a process map or decision tree for choosing intersection treatments and asks how the plan will speed up concrete curb extensions. Flynn says curb extensions are valuable but challenging due to drainage and catch basin relocations, and more details will come in the streets plan.
chapters.title: Won asks DOT for decision tree and curb extension acceleration

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: So could DOT provide us with a process map or a decision tree on how you determine what is better and what should be treated per intersection?

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: For this new Vision Zero plan?

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: I'm happy to talk to the team.

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: Okay, great.

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: Concrete curb extensions are one of the most effective tools to reduce pedestrian crashes, slowing turns, daylighting corners, and shortening crossing distances.

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: They're extremely common in most cities, yet in New York City, installation has been extremely slow.

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: How does the Vision Zero Reimagine plan intend to speed up these vital concrete curb extensions?

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: That's a great question.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: Thank you, Councilmember.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: We love curb extensions as well because they really do deliver multiple benefits from safety to public space, potentially for greening and trees.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: And you're right that they're more challenging, right?

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: When we talk about our quick build toolkit, it often doesn't include that.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: And that's because by the nature of being at the curb, they affect drainage along the gutter and often the catch basins would need to be relocated.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: So something that I've talked about, and I think we'll have more to say about it in the forthcoming streets plan, is that we want to be able to do more, both quantity and quality.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: And part of that is how do we do more permanent type infrastructure with our in-house resources?

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: And that's something we're examining closely.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: We're having great conversations with DEP.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: And it's, yeah, that's an area of focus for us.

chapters.summary: Won asks whether DOT will prohibit vehicles from blocking curb cuts at unmarked crossings at T intersections. Beaton says it is not specifically in Vision Zero Reimagined, and Flynn says it was not on his radar but he will check with his team.
chapters.title: Won asks DOT to prohibit blocking curb cuts at T intersections

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: Under Vision Zero reimagined, will DOT commit to prohibiting vehicles from blocking curb cuts at unmarked crossings at T intersections?

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: If not, why not?

utterances.speaker: Eric Beaton
utterances.text: So that's not something that's specifically in the Vision Zero reimagined plan.

utterances.speaker: Eric Beaton
utterances.text: It's something that I know was brought up in the last administration, but the rule was not fully adopted.

utterances.speaker: Eric Beaton
utterances.text: And so it's something we can talk a little bit more about going forward.

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: So yes or no?

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: To be honest, that wasn't on my radar yet, so I think I need to check with my team and understand the history and happy to take a closer look at it.

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: Okay, we'll follow up.

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Abreu asks for the timeline for meeting annual daylighting commitments. Beaton says the 1,000-intersection target applies starting next year but DOT hopes to meet it this year. Abreu asks how many intersections have been daylighted since the report and how equity will be ensured; Flynn cites data and priority investment areas.
chapters.title: Abreu questions DOT on daylighting timeline and equity

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Thank you, Councilmember.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: I was going to go to BIC, but since we're on the topic of daylighting, I want to stay there for a second.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Can you walk me through the anticipated timeline for meeting the administration's daylighting commitments?

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: And by that I mean the annual commitments.

utterances.speaker: Eric Beaton
utterances.text: Right, so the 1,000 intersections are better.

utterances.speaker: Eric Beaton
utterances.text: While it technically would apply starting next year, we do expect that we'll be meeting it this year as well.

utterances.speaker: Eric Beaton
utterances.text: So this is something we want to do every year going forward.

utterances.speaker: Eric Beaton
utterances.text: And as the commissioner said, do more, do it better.

utterances.speaker: Eric Beaton
utterances.text: We think that this intersection safety is a critical part of delivering Vision Zero.

utterances.speaker: Eric Beaton
utterances.text: And we want to make sure that we're meeting or exceeding that target.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: So just making sure Vision Zero reimagined those target goals are set out beginning in 2027, not as of the announcement date.

utterances.speaker: Eric Beaton
utterances.text: Yeah, each goal might be a little bit different, but for a report that came out in the fall of 2026, it mostly looks ahead to future years.

utterances.speaker: Eric Beaton
utterances.text: But we have been working on it, and wherever we can, including on the 1,000 intersection number, we do want to meet it this year, too, and we are working towards that.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Since the report was released, how many additional intersections have been daylight?

utterances.speaker: Eric Beaton
utterances.text: We would have to get back to you on that specific number and timeline.

utterances.speaker: Eric Beaton
utterances.text: But we do track all of this.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: We hope it's happening.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: How many intersections have received daylighting at the entire intersection, and how many have received daylighting on a...

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: What are the benefits of installing daylighting on approach?

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: And when does the OT determine to use daylighting on approach?

utterances.speaker: Eric Beaton
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: Eric Beaton
utterances.text: And, you know, it always depends on the details of the intersection.

utterances.speaker: Eric Beaton
utterances.text: But in general, what we see the value of hardened daylighting is does tend to be on the approach to intersections because that's where the visibility is usually most limited.

utterances.speaker: Eric Beaton
utterances.text: So, you know, as we think about where we can best use our resources to provide safety, you know, that is one of the places that we focus on with hardened daylighting.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Six months from now, how many intersections can we expect to see daylight?

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Should we see 500?

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: Six months from now will be, I guess, sort of through the winter and early spring.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: So that's not typically when we're implementing as much.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: We tend to look at the year.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: So it's not prorated necessarily.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: I think it's hard to break it down that way because it's sort of like that over the course of the year.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: But we're fully committed to this commitment that we've made.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: So we're expecting 1,000 next summer.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: I don't want to hold you to that.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: Over the full year.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: Eric Beaton
utterances.text: Our construction timeline is between about April and early November, and so absolutely through the entire construction timeline.

utterances.speaker: Eric Beaton
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: And will the initial investments in daylighting be focused in particular geographic areas?

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: And how will DLT ensure that daylighting interventions are distributed equitably throughout the city?

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: So it's based on a combination.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: It's based on the data fundamentally.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: And so we want to put these treatments where they can have the biggest benefit.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: But the other core driver of our work program is what we call our priority investment areas, which is our equity framework.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: And we'll have a new map, basically, as part of the new streets plan.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: And we really prioritize the lion's share of our investments in, there's three tiers.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: So in the first two tiers in particular, and that's basically what's driving those investments.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: So it's a combination of the data telling us where can they be most effective, but also which neighborhoods really have been historically disadvantaged.

chapters.summary: Abreu notes other cities like Hoboken have implemented daylighting successfully and asks if DOT has communicated with peers. Flynn says DOT talks with industry peers and learns from Hoboken despite different local context.
chapters.title: Abreu asks DOT about learning from other cities on daylighting

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Other cities throughout the country have implemented daylighting to increase visibility, including ones with similar population density as New York, such as Hoboken, New Jersey.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: As the city begins to increase its daylighting commitments, has DOT been in communication with other cities?

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: There are cities that have had successful daylighting rollouts.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: Yes, we're always talking to our industry peers and we're always trying to learn from them.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: You know, I think Hoboken's done a lot of great things.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: They have some unique context things that are a bit different from us, but that doesn't mean we can't learn from them and we are.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Abreu turns to BIC and asks about truck side guards, noting a teenager was killed by a hydro excavation truck that had a BIC waiver. Elizabeth Crotty explains that waivers are granted when a vehicle cannot support side guards or has equipment like a fuel tank or toolbox closing the gap.
chapters.title: Abreu questions BIC on truck side guard waivers

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: I have some questions on enforcement questions.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Some questions on enforcement for BIC.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: I'd like to turn to truck side guards.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Side guards are lateral panels that cover the space between a truck's front and rear wheels to protect pedestrians and cyclists from being swept into the truck after a side impact collision.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Side guards are proven to keep vulnerable road users safe, and since 2023, they have been required on all tradeways vehicles in New York City with a gross vehicle weight rating over 10,000 pounds.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: On September 18 of this year, a teenager was killed and another was injured after they were hit by a hydro excavation truck while biking in the East Village.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: We later learned that the truck that had hit them did not have the required side guards because it had been granted a waiver from BIC.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: If side guards are such critical safety issues, as we know them to be, can you help me understand why BIC would waive that requirement for any truck under its jurisdiction?

utterances.speaker: Elizabeth Crotty
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Elizabeth Crotty
utterances.text: I'm happy to take the question.

utterances.speaker: Elizabeth Crotty
utterances.text: It was a horrible tragedy, this accident, and my heart goes out to the family of

utterances.speaker: Elizabeth Crotty
utterances.text: the young girl.

utterances.speaker: Elizabeth Crotty
utterances.text: We don't want any collisions like that to happen on New York City streets.

utterances.speaker: Elizabeth Crotty
utterances.text: And BIC, along with our Vision Zero partners, are doing all that we can to bring that idea, Vision Zero, into reality.

utterances.speaker: Elizabeth Crotty
utterances.text: As you said, side guards or rails or panels that you affix to a vehicle to help close that gap between the front axle and the rear axle.

utterances.speaker: Elizabeth Crotty
utterances.text: And side guards were not

utterances.speaker: Elizabeth Crotty
utterances.text: really a thing in the United States, New York is one of the pioneer cities to introduce side guards to various vehicle fleets, including the ones that BIC regulates.

utterances.speaker: Elizabeth Crotty
utterances.text: The national standards around, and side guards are just one of several tools to help ensure safety for these large, heavy vehicles.

utterances.speaker: Elizabeth Crotty
utterances.text: There are other safety requirements that BIC has, which complement side guards.

utterances.speaker: Elizabeth Crotty
utterances.text: Side guards can't prevent collisions.

utterances.speaker: Elizabeth Crotty
utterances.text: They can only mitigate the damage when a collision takes place.

utterances.speaker: Elizabeth Crotty
utterances.text: In this particular instance, a waiver was granted, and that's because the national standards around side guards recognize that while you want a side guard on a vehicle that does have that gap between the front and the rear axle,

utterances.speaker: Elizabeth Crotty
utterances.text: there are some vehicles that cannot support side guards, and there are some vehicles that already have infrastructure on the vehicle such that there is no gap between the front and the rear axle.

utterances.speaker: Elizabeth Crotty
utterances.text: In this particular case, the company that was involved in that collision had applied for a side guard waiver with BIC, and it had submitted information.

utterances.speaker: Elizabeth Crotty
utterances.text: We review each application individually.

utterances.speaker: Elizabeth Crotty
utterances.text: because every vehicle is different.

utterances.speaker: Elizabeth Crotty
utterances.text: And we confirmed that vehicle did have incorporated features between the front and the rear axle, so that there was not that same type of gap between the wheels and under the vehicle that we're usually concerned about with side guards.

utterances.speaker: Elizabeth Crotty
utterances.text: So that was an appropriate application of the waiver process.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: So in this instance, they had a different feature, you're saying, that justified the exemption?

utterances.speaker: Elizabeth Crotty
utterances.text: Yeah, this was not a vehicle that had a huge open space between the front and the rear axle and underneath.

utterances.speaker: Elizabeth Crotty
utterances.text: This was a vehicle that had devices, a fuel tank, a toolbox that...

utterances.speaker: Elizabeth Crotty
utterances.text: Eliminated that space between the wheels.

utterances.speaker: Elizabeth Crotty
utterances.text: And according to national best practices and industry standards, it was an appropriate candidate for a waiver of a side guard.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: And it was, despite the way that the truck was constructed, was a side guard not compatible?

utterances.speaker: Elizabeth Crotty
utterances.text: For this particular vehicle, each vehicle needs to be looked at individually.

utterances.speaker: Elizabeth Crotty
utterances.text: For this particular vehicle, a side guard, the vehicle would not support a side guard.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: It would not support a sidecar.

chapters.summary: Abreu asks whether the truck without a side guard was safe to operate. Crotty says she cannot comment on the specific incident but explains that if a vehicle cannot support a side guard, a waiver may be appropriate under national standards. She lists other BIC safety requirements like convex mirrors and daily inspections.
chapters.title: Abreu presses BIC on safety of truck without side guard

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Is it BIC's position that a truck without a side guard in this specific instance is safe to operate in New York City?

utterances.speaker: Elizabeth Crotty
utterances.text: I can't.

utterances.speaker: Elizabeth Crotty
utterances.text: speak to that particular incident.

utterances.speaker: Elizabeth Crotty
utterances.text: The collisions that happen on the road that end in fatalities, as we talked about earlier in this hearing, are investigated by the police department.

utterances.speaker: Elizabeth Crotty
utterances.text: But our view is that any vehicle, as you said, over that particular weight that's a trade waste vehicle should have a side guard because side guards help promote safety.

utterances.speaker: Elizabeth Crotty
utterances.text: But if the vehicle cannot support a side guard, then a waiver may be appropriate.

utterances.speaker: Elizabeth Crotty
utterances.text: But we want to make sure that all vehicles, whether they have a side guard or whether a waiver is appropriate, are also engaged in other safe practices.

utterances.speaker: Elizabeth Crotty
utterances.text: So BIC has requirements that govern convex mirrors.

utterances.speaker: Elizabeth Crotty
utterances.text: BIC has requirements that govern clearance in the windshield.

utterances.speaker: Elizabeth Crotty
utterances.text: BIC has requirements that drivers do a daily...

utterances.speaker: Elizabeth Crotty
utterances.text: Safety inspection of the vehicle before they go out on route every single day and they keep a copy of that report in the cab.

utterances.speaker: Elizabeth Crotty
utterances.text: So we have a full wrapper of safety requirements to help get us closer to the Vision Zero goal.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Thank you for that.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Would a truck that has a side guard be safer than the truck involved in this situation?

utterances.speaker: Elizabeth Crotty
utterances.text: Again, not appropriate for me to comment on that particular incident, but you could have a vehicle that has a wide open gap underneath it.

utterances.speaker: Elizabeth Crotty
utterances.text: And if there's nothing there and if the vehicle can support a side guard, a side guard should be installed.

utterances.speaker: Elizabeth Crotty
utterances.text: That's the harm that we're trying to prevent.

utterances.speaker: Elizabeth Crotty
utterances.text: But if you have a vehicle where the design of the vehicle

utterances.speaker: Elizabeth Crotty
utterances.text: can't support a side guard, and or where the vehicle has equipment, it could be an additional axle or two or three additional axles.

utterances.speaker: Elizabeth Crotty
utterances.text: It could be a toolbox.

utterances.speaker: Elizabeth Crotty
utterances.text: It could be a fuel tank.

utterances.speaker: Elizabeth Crotty
utterances.text: If it's eliminating that gap, if it's closing up that space, that is safer than a vehicle that has a wide open space underneath it.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Right, but is it safer than a truck with just a side guard?

utterances.speaker: Elizabeth Crotty
utterances.text: I'm sorry, can you repeat the question?

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: But is it safer than a truck with a traditional side guard?

utterances.speaker: Elizabeth Crotty
utterances.text: I think if what you're asking is if a truck with a traditional side guard is safer than a truck that has other equipment in that same zone, I couldn't comment on that.

utterances.speaker: Elizabeth Crotty
utterances.text: It's so truck-to-truck specific and it's incident-to-incident specific.

utterances.speaker: Elizabeth Crotty
utterances.text: We just want to make sure that there's as much coverage there as is possible to promote safety.

chapters.summary: Crotty gives other side guard waiver examples, including dump trucks with tri-axles that cannot support side guards. She says BIC reviews each application individually, may request mechanics letters, and has revisited waivers to require modified side guards.
chapters.title: Crotty explains other side guard waiver examples

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: So you were going into the bases for which BIC would issue side guard waivers, and this example is one of them.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Are there other examples where a side guard exemption would be appropriate?

utterances.speaker: Elizabeth Crotty
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: Elizabeth Crotty
utterances.text: Many of the trucks that fall under BIC's regulation are trucks that are used to remove construction and debris, not traditional waste, but we're talking about heavy-duty construction debris, and those are dump trucks.

utterances.speaker: Elizabeth Crotty
utterances.text: We regulate a large number of dump trucks.

utterances.speaker: Elizabeth Crotty
utterances.text: And if you look at the average dump truck, it doesn't just have a front axle, a rear axle, and lots of space in between.

utterances.speaker: Elizabeth Crotty
utterances.text: It usually has additional wheels, including something that's called a...

utterances.speaker: Elizabeth Crotty
utterances.text: like a third axle, a tri-axle, which is a wheel that is used to help the vehicle navigate uneven terrain.

utterances.speaker: Elizabeth Crotty
utterances.text: And so there's a series of these wheels.

utterances.speaker: Elizabeth Crotty
utterances.text: And a tri-axle vehicle, the vehicle moves in such a way that if you install a side guard,

utterances.speaker: Elizabeth Crotty
utterances.text: the side guard would break when the vehicle wheel turns or the wheel could get damaged.

utterances.speaker: Elizabeth Crotty
utterances.text: So one of the things that we require when we receive an application for a waiver is if we don't feel like we have enough information, we will ask the company for more.

utterances.speaker: Elizabeth Crotty
utterances.text: They may send us a mechanics letter that explains just what I explained to you, that the vehicle, the dump truck, for example, can't support a side guard.

utterances.speaker: Elizabeth Crotty
utterances.text: So that's one example of a type of vehicle that's different from the one involved at 14th Street.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Does BIC ever revisit or reevaluate a waiver after it has been issued, and has it ever been rescinded at any moment?

utterances.speaker: Elizabeth Crotty
utterances.text: We have revisited waivers that have been granted, and what it's allowed us to do is have an iterative, ongoing conversation with the company.

utterances.speaker: Elizabeth Crotty
utterances.text: So we may take another look at where we've given a waiver and said, you know what, there is still a one-foot space, for example, between the step to the cab and that gas tank.

utterances.speaker: Elizabeth Crotty
utterances.text: And can you install a modified side guard in that limited space?

utterances.speaker: Elizabeth Crotty
utterances.text: And we will keep working with the company until they do so.

utterances.speaker: Elizabeth Crotty
utterances.text: And we've had success in that regard.

chapters.summary: Abreu asks how many trucks under BIC jurisdiction have side guard waivers. Crotty says BIC regulates about 7,000 trucks and about half have waivers, mostly dump trucks. Abreu asks for collision data involving waived trucks; Crotty does not have it and will follow up.
chapters.title: Abreu asks how many BIC trucks have side guard waivers

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Sounds like you know a lot about side guards.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: How many trucks under a BICS jurisdiction currently have a waiver?

utterances.speaker: Elizabeth Crotty
utterances.text: Okay, so we have about 7,000 trucks under our...

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Sorry, say that again?

utterances.speaker: Elizabeth Crotty
utterances.text: We have about 7,000 trucks that are under our jurisdiction, that we have licensed, that we've given plates to.

utterances.speaker: Elizabeth Crotty
utterances.text: As I mentioned, the largest share of that are not traditional trash trucks that you throw a garbage bag into.

utterances.speaker: Elizabeth Crotty
utterances.text: The largest share are C&D, construction and demolition, what we call Class 2 vehicles.

utterances.speaker: Elizabeth Crotty
utterances.text: These are the heavy-duty vehicles.

utterances.speaker: Elizabeth Crotty
utterances.text: And most of those Class 2 vehicles are dump trucks.

utterances.speaker: Elizabeth Crotty
utterances.text: And those dump trucks, like I said, often have additional axles.

utterances.speaker: Elizabeth Crotty
utterances.text: So about half of the vehicles that we regulate have waivers.

utterances.speaker: Elizabeth Crotty
utterances.text: So those are these dump trucks.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: All right, so you're saying of the waivers given, most of them are dump trucks?

utterances.speaker: Elizabeth Crotty
utterances.text: Of the waivers given, the largest share are dump trucks.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: What are some other type of exemptions given for non-dump trucks?

utterances.speaker: Elizabeth Crotty
utterances.text: So, right.

utterances.speaker: Elizabeth Crotty
utterances.text: So the vehicle that was involved in the 14th Street incident, for example, was not a dump truck.

utterances.speaker: Elizabeth Crotty
utterances.text: It was a truck that had this, my understanding, and please correct me if I'm wrong, like a high-powered vacuum that's used, involved to kind of clean up street debris when there's construction or tearing up of a street.

utterances.speaker: Elizabeth Crotty
utterances.text: That had a toolbox and it had a fuel tank in that area.

utterances.speaker: Elizabeth Crotty
utterances.text: And that's why it couldn't support a side guard.

utterances.speaker: Elizabeth Crotty
utterances.text: There are many different designs of trucks.

utterances.speaker: Elizabeth Crotty
utterances.text: I don't want to give you broad categories.

utterances.speaker: Elizabeth Crotty
utterances.text: Dump truck is the easiest category because many of them do have those features I mentioned.

utterances.speaker: Elizabeth Crotty
utterances.text: But there can be a host of types of vehicles on the road where the manufacturer who builds the vehicle decides to put things underneath the truck in those spaces.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Do you know how many of those trucks that were granted waivers have been involved in collisions with pedestrians or cyclists since 2023?

utterances.speaker: Elizabeth Crotty
utterances.text: I do not have that information.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Or how it compares to those with not being granted a waiver.

utterances.speaker: Elizabeth Crotty
utterances.text: It's a good question, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Elizabeth Crotty
utterances.text: I will see if we have the data that allows us to break it down that way with respect to collision involvement and whether they had a side guard or a waiver.

utterances.speaker: Elizabeth Crotty
utterances.text: We'll have to get back to you.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: I think it's slightly disappointing to not have that information.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Very disappointing, actually, to not have that information.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Please get it to us as soon as you can.

chapters.summary: Abreu asks how BIC enforces the side guard requirement for trucks without waivers. Crotty describes yard and garage visits, joint Operation Safe Drive inspections with NYPD and state partners, 99% compliance, and fewer than 80 violations. Abreu requests violation and license revocation data.
chapters.title: Abreu asks BIC enforcement of side guard requirement

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: And how does BIC enforce the side guard requirement for trucks that do not have a waiver?

utterances.speaker: Elizabeth Crotty
utterances.text: We are regularly engaged in a variety of enforcement measures.

utterances.speaker: Elizabeth Crotty
utterances.text: So we regularly visit the yards and garages of companies that we regulate.

utterances.speaker: Elizabeth Crotty
utterances.text: And if we see a vehicle that looks like it should have a side guard and it does not, we will review and see was there an appropriate waiver here.

utterances.speaker: Elizabeth Crotty
utterances.text: And if it was not, then that can result in a violation.

utterances.speaker: Elizabeth Crotty
utterances.text: We do joint operations with NYPD, with the state, and with other agencies across the entire city.

utterances.speaker: Elizabeth Crotty
utterances.text: Operation Safe Drive is what we call it, where we will pick a high-traffic corridor and we will pull over trucks and we'll do a full vehicle inspection to see, do they have a side guard if they need one?

utterances.speaker: Elizabeth Crotty
utterances.text: Do they have a convex mirror?

utterances.speaker: Elizabeth Crotty
utterances.text: Are they filling out their daily inspection safety reports?

utterances.speaker: Elizabeth Crotty
utterances.text: So there's a lot of in-the-field work that we do to check, is this truck following all the safety regulations it's supposed to?

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: What is the number of violations, if you have any, for those?

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: For those who do not have a waiver and were found to not have a side guard.

utterances.speaker: Elizabeth Crotty
utterances.text: That's data I would have to get back to you.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: I would also need that information.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Do you know how many licenses have been revoked for those not having a side guard?

utterances.speaker: Elizabeth Crotty
utterances.text: I may be wrong, Chair, but my understanding is...

utterances.speaker: Elizabeth Crotty
utterances.text: One second.

utterances.speaker: Elizabeth Crotty
utterances.text: We have 99% compliance with the side guard waiver.

utterances.speaker: Elizabeth Crotty
utterances.text: So it would be very few where there have been violations of noncompliance with the side guard rule.

utterances.speaker: Elizabeth Crotty
utterances.text: It's been less than 80 over the past several years.

utterances.speaker: Elizabeth Crotty
utterances.text: We're talking about, again, 7,000 vehicles in the entire fleets that we oversee.

utterances.speaker: Elizabeth Crotty
utterances.text: Since the side guard rule went into effect, there have been less than 80 violations.

utterances.speaker: Elizabeth Crotty
utterances.text: So this demonstrates that the companies are either following the side guard rules.

utterances.speaker: Elizabeth Crotty
utterances.text: And we are working with them when we need an alternative like a modified side guard or a waiver.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Elizabeth Crotty
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: And I'll turn it over for questions for DOT.

chapters.summary: Abreu returns to DOT and asks about the discrepancy between record-low overall fatalities and an 86% increase in cyclist fatalities. Flynn says traditional cyclists are trending down while e-bike and scooter fatalities are up. Abreu asks about larger, heavier vehicles; Flynn says DOT advocates for smaller vehicles and shifting freight to cargo bikes, rail, and waterways.
chapters.title: Abreu questions DOT on cyclist fatalities and vehicle size

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: So this administration has touted its Vision Zero progress, citing record lows in overall traffic fatalities.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: However, traffic fatalities are up 86% for cyclists.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: How does the administration explain this discrepancy?

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Are streets getting safer for car drivers but more dangerous for cyclists?

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: So I guess just to be clear, we're seeing an overall downward trend for traditional cyclists, where we've seen that growth this year is for e-bikes and stand-up scooters.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: And that, as you know from the last hearing, is a big area of focus for us.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: Generally speaking, what we've been seeing is...

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: Crashes and fatalities from what you

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: might call traditional users have been trending in the right direction.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: And then as the industry evolves and things change, we have to keep evolving in response to those new challenges.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Recent trends in vehicles, such as larger hood sizes and heavier overall weight, make cars safer for those driving them, but more deadly for other road users.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: What is DOT doing in terms of advocacy, education, or other investments to address this issue?

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: I know we can't regulate size of vehicles in the city, but...

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: The harm to folks on our streets is it's pretty big.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: It's really alarming, Chair, yes.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: And I know the New York Times, for example, did a really good article on this topic a few months back where they visualized the growth in the average vehicle size over the last few decades.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: This is very much on our radar.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
