utterances.text: As you mentioned, it's something we have a little less control over, but we want to use our position to

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: advocate and to see where we do have some policy levers to really incentivize safer vehicles, which in general are smaller vehicles.

utterances.speaker: Madeline Labadie
utterances.text: And just to add, in terms of what's under DOT's control, obviously, you know, we're concerned about the role of the wear and tear on our assets as it relates to milling and paving and other repairs that need to be done.

utterances.speaker: Madeline Labadie
utterances.text: So we're thinking a lot about truck usage.

utterances.speaker: Madeline Labadie
utterances.text: So we are.

utterances.speaker: Madeline Labadie
utterances.text: We have a freight unit, and we are investing their work to help shift freight from large, heavy vehicles to other safer modes, such as cargo bikes, rail, and waterways through initiatives like the Blue Highways,

utterances.speaker: Madeline Labadie
utterances.text: and working with organizations such as IAHS to develop federal safety standards for freight vehicles as well to prioritize vulnerable road users.

chapters.summary: Abreu cites Transportation Alternatives' list of 50 boulevards of death, which make up 4% of street miles but over 20% of fatalities. Flynn says DOT focuses on Vision Zero priority corridors and points to a 90% fatality drop on Queens Boulevard. Beaton says DOT brings the whole toolbox to those streets.
chapters.title: Abreu asks DOT about boulevards of death

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Transportation Alternatives recently identified a list of 50 boulevards of death, streets that make up just 4% of the city's street miles but that account for more than 20% of traffic fatalities.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Have you studied these boulevards of death and do you have an understanding of why these particular streets are so deadly?

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: You know, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: Looking at the highest crash corridors and locations is really at the core of our Vision Zero work.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: And obviously, by its nature, it's always a moving target, right?

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: If we address one of the top most dangerous corridors, then you'll just keep going down the list.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: And so I think like Queens Boulevard is a really interesting example where it was the original, I guess, Boulevard of Death, right?

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: And there was a sustained effort both through quicker changes and then long-term capital projects to improve it.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: And we've seen a 90-plus percent drop in fatalities on Queens Boulevard since then.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: Obviously, big streets like that will continue, though, to be a challenge just by their nature.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: So it doesn't mean we won't come back and make more fixes.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: But the short answer to your question is yes.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: Really, that's the purpose of the Vision Zero priority corridors.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Can you speak to what DOT is doing to prioritize investments in the boulevards of death to make them safer for pedestrians and cyclists?

utterances.speaker: Eric Beaton
utterances.text: Sure, and this speaks to exactly why we put out and update our Vision Zero priority corridors, because it allows us to focus our work in those places where crashes are most frequent.

utterances.speaker: Eric Beaton
utterances.text: And so we bring the whole toolbox to those streets, right?

utterances.speaker: Eric Beaton
utterances.text: Those include physical redesigns.

utterances.speaker: Eric Beaton
utterances.text: It includes working with NYPD on enforcement.

utterances.speaker: Eric Beaton
utterances.text: It includes automated enforcement.

utterances.speaker: Eric Beaton
utterances.text: It includes looking at the traffic signal timing.

utterances.speaker: Eric Beaton
utterances.text: That when we have a street that has been identified as unsafe, we don't want to leave that untouched.

utterances.speaker: Eric Beaton
utterances.text: We want to make sure that we are always looking at those most crash-prone streets and doing everything we can to bring it down.

utterances.speaker: Eric Beaton
utterances.text: And if we bring it down, then there's another most crash-prone street, and we're going to go after that one.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: I mean, look, 20% is a big, it's pretty, pretty big for only 4% of the city street miles.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: And so it sounds like a worthy focus and worthy investment for our city.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: So I hope that this administration remains committed to addressing the 50 boulevards of death.

chapters.summary: Abreu notes leading pedestrian intervals reduce pedestrian casualties by 12.7% and asks how many signalized intersections have them. Flynn says DOT has installed over 6,000 LPIs and continues to prioritize locations with turning conflicts. Beaton says LPIs are focused on the most dangerous locations.
chapters.title: Abreu questions DOT on leading pedestrian intervals

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Leading pedestrian intervals, or LPIs, are when the crosswalk signal allows pedestrians to begin crossing before vehicles get a green light.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: This seems like a relatively straightforward and quick improvement that the council's data team found reduces pedestrian casualties by 12.7%.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: How many signalized...

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Intersections have received LPI treatment.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: We found LPIs to be one of the more effective and lower cost generally treatments in our toolbox.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: And we're really proud of how rapidly we've been able to roll them out across the city.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: What I will say is that just like any tool, the effectiveness will depend in part on the

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: context of that location, right?

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: They're really a tool that helps with turning conflicts more than anything.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: And so places where we have heavy turns and LPI can have the greatest sort of bang for the buck.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: And that, of course, there's also a finite number of intersections in the city.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: So eventually you start to kind of bump up against it.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: So I don't know, we could talk a little more about the specific numbers, but what I can say is that

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: Yeah, I guess to date we've done over 6,000 LPIs, and we continue to see that as an important tool and maximize our use of it.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: I'd like to note that we were joined by Councilmember Krishnan.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Given the speed at which LPIs can be implemented, their effectiveness, and that no physical...

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: That no physical infrastructure changes are needed.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Why haven't LPIs been installed at more intersections?

utterances.speaker: Eric Beaton
utterances.text: Well, it's really a good question.

utterances.speaker: Eric Beaton
utterances.text: And part of the answer is we are continuously installing more.

utterances.speaker: Eric Beaton
utterances.text: But part of the answer is also that we want to make sure we're focused on the most dangerous locations.

utterances.speaker: Eric Beaton
utterances.text: A little bit to your...

utterances.speaker: Eric Beaton
utterances.text: question before, not every intersection in the city, not even every signalized intersection, has the same crash rate, right?

utterances.speaker: Eric Beaton
utterances.text: There are parts of the city with fewer pedestrians, fewer turning conflicts, places where the LPI would not provide nearly as much benefit.

utterances.speaker: Eric Beaton
utterances.text: And so we want to make sure that our signal timing engineers are spending their effort

utterances.speaker: Eric Beaton
utterances.text: places that need the LPIs, but that they're also doing things like looking at how to make a correct progression so that cars aren't speeding, right?

utterances.speaker: Eric Beaton
utterances.text: There are other things that our signal engineers do, and we want to keep them focused on the places that really have the most crashes.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: I understand that LPIs are being done at the most dangerous intersections.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: How many are...

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: In terms of your body of work, what have you determined to be the dangerous intersections and how many more should we be expecting to address the outstanding dangerous corners?

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: And then I have a separate question, which is, are NLPIs better regardless of the benefit being less?

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: I mean, you know, what I'll say, I guess, and maybe this is sort of the overall theme is, right, in theory, we can do everything everywhere all at the same time.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: In reality, we need to focus our resources where we think they can have the greatest benefit.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: I think you can be everywhere at any time, Commissioner.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: I wish, I wish.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: So, you know, that's the short answer.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: I mean...

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: You mentioned also these high crash corridors or boulevards of death.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: That's another thing, right?

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: We're always trying to balance and figure out how we can have the greatest possible impact and save the greatest number of lives.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: And given that it's low cost, I would like to see a more rapid expansion of LPIs at these intersections.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: And I understand that we're talking about resources, and this is one of those things that doesn't require that much resource.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: So I think it's more of a question on the operationalizing of it.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: When can we get it done and by when?

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: So if you could just please keep us in the loop on that expansion and where they're going to be implemented, we would love to see more.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: Yeah, I'll absolutely huddle with my team on that.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: All right.

chapters.summary: Abreu notes most crashes occur at intersections and asks why New York City lacks protected bike intersections. Flynn says DOT sees value and is increasing use; Beaton says new bike lanes typically use protected intersection designs and older lanes are upgraded during repaving or redesign.
chapters.title: Abreu asks DOT about protected bike intersections

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Protected bike lanes keep riders safe for the length of a block, but then end at the intersection.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: With protected intersections, on the other hand, the bike lane is extended around the intersection, which offers a significant benefit for cyclist safety.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Other cities in the United States, like Seattle, Chicago, and San Francisco, implement these types of protections.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Given a majority of crashes occurring at intersections, why do we not have protected bike intersections in New York City?

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: And would you like to see more of that?

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: We certainly see the value of protected intersections.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: It is something that we've started to incorporate into our toolbox, and you can see examples of that around the city.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: I would say that we're increasing our use of it.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: I know it's a new thing, and I understand that it's all about a resource question.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: But let us know where.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Where you see that on the agenda when you do have the– if you can maybe answer it now, Mr.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Beaton, that would be great.

utterances.speaker: Eric Beaton
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: I like pronouncing your name.

utterances.speaker: Eric Beaton
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: I remember earlier this year I had fun pronouncing your name.

utterances.speaker: Eric Beaton
utterances.text: I like it too.

utterances.speaker: Eric Beaton
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Eric Beaton
utterances.text: But I would say there's two different things.

utterances.speaker: Eric Beaton
utterances.text: First, when we do new bike lanes, they are typically, we use the so-called protected intersection or Dutch-style intersection design.

utterances.speaker: Eric Beaton
utterances.text: And the places we don't use it are places that might have a very high number of turns where something like a split phase for traffic might make sense, right?

utterances.speaker: Eric Beaton
utterances.text: We want to make sure we're using the right thing at the right place.

utterances.speaker: Eric Beaton
utterances.text: We also are going back to many of the bike lanes that have older designs, and we go back and add the protected style intersection.

utterances.speaker: Eric Beaton
utterances.text: And, for example, when we repave a street that has a bike lane, we don't just put back exactly what was there.

utterances.speaker: Eric Beaton
utterances.text: We go and we make sure we're upgrading it to the latest designs.

utterances.speaker: Eric Beaton
utterances.text: And that takes work.

utterances.speaker: Eric Beaton
utterances.text: We don't get mileage credit for that kind of work, but we still think it's really important in delivering the safest bike network possible.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Moving forward, when you are...

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Constructing protected bike lanes and shovels already on the ground.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Is it fair to say that protected bike intersections could just be added as part of those projects without

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: being a significant cost.

utterances.speaker: Eric Beaton
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: Eric Beaton
utterances.text: When we're doing new lanes, we always want to do the safest thing possible at the intersection, which in many cases is that protected intersection.

utterances.speaker: Eric Beaton
utterances.text: Can we see that in future projects?

utterances.speaker: Eric Beaton
utterances.text: I think you see that in a lot of the projects going in right now, really all the projects going in right now, that it's incorporated into the work that we do, yes.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: And then retroactively, the protected bike lanes where they were not being implemented, was the...

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: agency's realistic ability here to go back and add these bike intersections, protected bike intersections?

utterances.speaker: Eric Beaton
utterances.text: So we certainly go back and add them anytime we're redoing the markings on the corridor, such as after resurfacing, or if we're seeing crash-related issues on a corridor, we'll go back and redesign as well.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: So as more streets get milled and repaved, are they being implemented?

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: We'll ask about that at the annual street hearing we do next year.

chapters.summary: Abreu raises Sammy's Law and asks about the expected scale of 20 mph neighborhood slow zones. Flynn says lower speed limits work best with traffic calming, DOT is developing a neighborhood-scale program, and it will complete lower-speed school zones by the end of the administration's first term.
chapters.title: Abreu questions DOT on Sammy's Law speed limit rollout

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Regarding Sammy's Law, Sammy's Law expanded New York City's authority to lower speed limits on certain streets.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Lower speed limits are a central component of Vision Zero and reducing the severity of crashes.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: 17 community boards representing nearly 2.5 million New Yorkers and 63 elected officials have now formally demanded SAMHSA's law slow zones in their districts.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: The Vision Zero Reimagined Plan commits to expand 20 miles per hour speed limits within entire neighborhoods or other defined zones.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: What is the expected scale of this rollout?

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: How large will the zones be and how many neighborhoods will get a slow zone each year?

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: Yeah, we're really excited about this one.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: You know, we, as we all know, speeding is one of the largest contributors to fatal traffic crashes.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: So we certainly support the goal of bringing speeds down across the city.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: Something we've learned through experience is that generally lowering the speed limit is most effective when it's paired with traffic calming improvements.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: And that's why we've kind of positioned it that way in the Vision Zero reimagined.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: As you know we took the big step of announcing that we will do these lower speed zones outside of essentially all New York City schools by the end of

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: the term of this administration the first term of this administration and we're excited to build on that and so yeah in Vision Zero Reimagined we talk about doing it at a neighborhood scale in terms of the actual

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: I guess, magnitude of that.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: It's something that's in development.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: This is a entirely new program, basically.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: So we're working out some of those details.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: But I think, you know, we want to do it at a scale that makes sense.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: And we want to learn from some of our global peers as well in terms of it should be a large enough scale that

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: You get that area-wide effect, but it should be also contained enough that we can put in the traffic calming that's going to make it most effective.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: And, yeah, I mean, I guess I would just– I didn't mention it.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: But, you know, it's been really, it's wonderful for us to see kind of this groundswell of support from community boards and to hear that this is something that so many New Yorkers want to see in their neighborhood.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: And we want to absolutely have that be a part of our decision-making process.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: We also want to follow the data and make sure that every neighborhood can benefit and that we're focusing these where they can have the greatest safety impact.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: So it's both.

chapters.summary: Abreu asks why DOT no longer accepts applications for new neighborhood slow zones. Flynn says the old program was phased out about 10 years ago and is a precursor to the new Sammy's Law zones, which pair lower limits with more intensive design treatments. Abreu notes the old data showed effectiveness.
chapters.title: Abreu asks why DOT stopped accepting neighborhood slow zone applications

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: So I have to ask, if the agency loves community board support and the community support more broadly, why is DOT no longer accepting applications for the creation of new neighborhood slow zones?

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Do you have any plans to reopen applications?

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: Well, the neighborhood slow zones, I think that's a program that was phased out maybe around 10 years ago.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: I guess you could see it in some ways as like an early precursor to these neighborhood Sammy's Law slower zones.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: I think the key difference, like I mentioned, is the...

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: A more intensive design treatment, basically, that complements the lower speed limit.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: And we would like to, you know, it's always a balancing act, right?

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: Like we want to be responsive where we're hearing the demand.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: We also want to make sure we're following the data.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: And we want to make sure that all neighborhoods, even those who maybe don't always have, we don't hear from as much, can benefit from these types of things.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: So it's all in the mix.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Yeah, your data.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: on neighborhood slow zones were actually showed that this was actually incredibly effective.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: So should we reopen applications for these?

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: I know that a lot of folks have been asking for it.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: I'm beating a dead horse.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: I understand.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: I mean, it's something we can look at.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: I think we should go back and look.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: And I'm sure the team has, but I get maybe a little more up to speed in terms of what the lessons learned were from the earlier program.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: But I'm sure that it's directly informing what we're developing right as we speak.

chapters.summary: Abreu asks how many streets have had speed limits reduced under Sammy's Law. DOT says it has done over 200 school slow zones this year and expects about 800 by year end, plus a few dozen other corridors. DOT commits to completing all eligible schools by the end of the term.
chapters.title: Abreu asks DOT how many streets reduced under Sammy's Law

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Going back to Sammy's Law, how many streets have had their speed limits reduced under Sammy's Law?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Well, I can say at least for the schools, and we have more detail here, but this year we've done over 200 of the 15-mile-an-hour slow zones,

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: and we're expecting to hit that roughly 800 by the end of the year in terms of the school ones.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: I know we've done it on other corridors.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: A few dozen.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: A few dozen other corridors.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: And these other corridors, these are neighborhood-based Sammy's Law zones?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: I think it's a...

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Yeah, a lot of the other uses have been in places where we have things like open streets or shared streets where there is some of that natural traffic calming built in already.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: And so we are doing it, as the commissioner said, both.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: We're doing all the schools, and that's something we've already committed to.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: We're also doing it in these other areas where we compare it with traffic calming.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: And sometimes that's on a street basis.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Sometimes it will be on a neighborhood basis.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: But we want to really put those together, that it's not, we're not just putting up signs, that we're really delivering a street design for slower traffic.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: So you mentioned that you've done 200 so far this year, 800 by the end of the year.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: What about next year?

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: How much do you expect to do by then?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Our commitment is to do all eligible schools, which is the vast majority or almost all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: It's 2,300 school locations, which has about 3,200 schools, and some are co-located by the end of this term.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Got it.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: So 800 by the end of this year, no number commitment for next year so far, but you're committing to doing all schools by the end of the term.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Yes.

chapters.summary: Abreu asks about barriers to broader Sammy's Law implementation. DOT cites state law exemptions for roads over three lanes outside Manhattan, the need to pair speed limit changes with traffic calming, and balancing data, equity, and community demand.
chapters.title: Abreu asks DOT about barriers to broader Sammy's Law implementation

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: What are the barriers?

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: What barriers are you finding you may have for broader implementation?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Of reduced speed areas?

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: I mean, yeah.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: If any.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Yeah, I think it's just, it's part of the same overall, you know, it's kind of what Deputy Minister Beaton and others we've been talking about.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Always trying to calibrate and target our investments to have the greatest impact.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: So, you know, again, it's, I don't know that there's any specific barriers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: I think it's more just about how do we balance that program with several dozen other approaches that we take to improve safety.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: You were sort of getting into the criteria that DOT uses to prioritize SAMHSA law locations like shared streets, open streets.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Can you speak to any other factors that DOT considers when prioritizing locations?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: And one of them is related to the barriers that you're talking about, one of which is the law itself does have specific.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Roads on which we are not allowed to do them, right?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: It's roads over three lanes outside of Manhattan.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: And those are often the most dangerous roads in those neighborhoods.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: So we do want to make sure that we are addressing the most dangerous roads, some of which are just, you know, we're not included, we're specifically exempted from the state law.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Beyond that, I think it's really we do want to look at the places where we're also doing the traffic calming at the same time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: I think what we've seen over time is that just putting up signs has a pretty limited

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: effect that, you know, we're lucky when New Yorkers see signs at all, if there's something on a couple blocks, you know, most people just don't notice it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: But we want it to be reinforcing with the street design itself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: So places where we want to do traffic calming, places where there's been crashes or neighborhood-wide issues, we want to do the speed limit changes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: And we want to pair it with the traffic calming that really makes it real.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Abreu asks how DOT is spending the $377,527 increase for Sammy's Law school zone implementation. DOT says funds go to inspection staff and sign shop production, including aluminum and reflective sheeting, and offers a tour of the sign shop.
chapters.title: Abreu asks DOT about Sammy's Law budget spending

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: The budget for SAMHSA's law implementation around school zones was increased by $377,527, with more in the out years to install signage and hire planners to assess signs'impacts on streets.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: How much of this has the OT already spent, and can you give us a breakdown of where the funds have gone?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Yes, so this is, we'll get you a breakdown of what has been spent to date exactly, but it goes to two main things.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: It goes to hiring staff who do, you can call it planning, we also call it inspections, where they just go and, like, this is the pole we need to put the sign on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: And then there's a crew in the sign shop that we buy the aluminum, we buy the retro-reflective sheeting material.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: We would love to take you on a tour of the sign shop sometime if you want, but there's a whole process where we produce these signs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: With you, Mr.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Behan, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: We have fabulous, dedicated staff who are so proud of the work that they do on signs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: It's really amazing.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: I would actually love to do that.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: That sounds great.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: But we find the places for the signs, we produce the sign, then we have a crew that goes out in a truck and goes up in a bucket and installs the sign.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: And so it's not a huge amount of money, but it's just all the steps along the way that get funded.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: All right, I have questions on low-traffic neighborhoods, and then after this set of questions, I'll turn it over to my colleague for round two questioning.

chapters.summary: Abreu turns to his low-traffic neighborhood bill and asks what volume reduction tools the administration envisions. DOT describes a spectrum including pedestrian priority zones, lower speed zones, and LTNs, says it is learning from London, and supports the goals while wanting a precise definition and structure.
chapters.title: Abreu questions DOT on low-traffic neighborhoods and volume reduction tools

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: So I'd like now to turn it over to my bill.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: So throughout the Vision Zero Reimagined report, the administration makes a range of commitments regarding the future of traffic management planning in the city, and particularly with respect to pedestrian-focused street design.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: For example, the administration states that it wants to establish pedestrian priority districts.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Quote, pedestrian priority districts.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Quote, shift New York City streets towards people rather than cars.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: And quote, expand and innovate the city's toolkit of transformative corridor and neighborhood designs.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: For example, like boulevards, slow zones, and other speed management and volume reduction tools.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Like with most aspects of the Visions That We Imagine report, these commitments sound great, but the devil's in the details.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: So to start, with respect to the administration's commitment to exploring, quote, other speed management and volume reduction tools, can you please describe what these tools are and do they include low traffic neighborhoods?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Yeah, I think there's sort of a family of treatments, right, that are kind of on a spectrum from

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: things that are really about reducing through traffic on local streets, things that are about reducing speed, which is similar, but...

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Also separate potentially, and then things that are about kind of creating more space for pedestrians.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: And it depends on the neighborhood, right?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: If you're looking at a dense commercial retail district where pedestrians are literally or figuratively spilling off the sidewalk, you know, you may want to look at treatments that actually create more space for pedestrians or give them more use of the entire roadway.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: In maybe like a lower traffic, quieter residential neighborhood, it may be more of a concern from the community around cut-through traffic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: And so there's kind of a range of treatments that are related here, whether it's pedestrian-only zones, pedestrian priority zones, lower speed zones, or low-traffic neighborhoods.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: And so we absolutely see the potential of LTNs as an important tool for keeping New Yorkers safe.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: We certainly are looking at and learning from...

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Our peers, in particular London, but also other places around the world that are employing these kinds of tools.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: And we're really excited.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: To be honest, some of these ideas are still in development.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: So, you know, it may be hard to provide specifics, but we're excited to share more and to talk more.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: I look forward to it.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Anything you have to share on this is really exciting.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: And I know in your testimony, you mentioned you're excited for future conversations on this subject and that you support the goals of the bill, which we really welcome.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: You also mentioned in your testimony that you have thoughts on how to best define or structure low-traffic neighborhoods.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Can you speak to that?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Yeah, I mean, I think it's just to my last point, it's helpful to be a little more precise around what we mean by that and what it includes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: You know, does it include how much of it is the speed management component, how much of it's the cut through traffic management?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: I think, you know, and then that way it'll be helpful to us, especially if we're going to sort of be reporting out on our progress or ask to, you know, have certain targets.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Look, I think we can definitely work with the administration on this.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: What we do want to make clear is this will be the first true LTN in the country.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: We want a true neighborhood approach, not just a few blocks.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: We want a true neighborhood approach.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: And so as long as we share that goal on a true neighborhood approach, I think we can land the plane on this.

chapters.summary: Abreu asks whether permanent school street swing gates could be used for low-traffic neighborhoods. DOT says swing gates have potential, it wants to evaluate the first use, and if successful it could scale them up.
chapters.title: Abreu asks DOT about permanent school street swing gates for LTNs

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: DLT recently announced the first permanent school street with swing gates to block vehicle traffic during the school day.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Thank you for the invitation to that.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Sorry I couldn't make it.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: I thought it was very cool looking at the photos.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Does DLT have plans to expand the use of this infrastructure?

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: infrastructure and could these gates be a viable option for low traffic neighborhoods throughout the city?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: I think it has a lot of potential.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: You know, I think what we've seen when we're starting new programs and as we're kind of evolving our toolkit, it's a big, complex city.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: And so things need to be kind of, I guess, for lack of a better term, battle tested, you know, or tested on the ground because it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: New York does put a lot of demands on infrastructure in terms of, you know, withstanding things.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: So in the case of school streets and other open streets, we've seen historically the use of what we call French barricades, these movable fences.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Those have some advantages, but they also have some challenges, right, in terms of storage and maintenance and who's moving it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: I think a swing gate has a lot of potential.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: We want to evaluate this first use.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: See how it works, and if it works, then it would be great to scale it up.

chapters.summary: Abreu asks what data DOT uses to analyze cut-through traffic. DOT says it uses anonymized cell phone and company data to identify trips that neither start nor end in an area, and notes many automated camera violations are from out-of-city vehicles. Diverters are already used, learned from London.
chapters.title: Abreu asks DOT about cut-through traffic data

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: LTNs have many benefits, but a key one is that they prevent cut-through traffic in residential areas, right?

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: While cut-through traffic is a problem all over the city, it is worse in certain communities.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: What data does DOT use to analyze cut-through traffic?

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: And how is that data used by DOT to inform street design interventions?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Yeah, and that's a really good question, Chair, because it is one of the things that other cities have used to really choose where they're doing things like low-traffic neighborhoods.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: And we don't have knowledge of where every vehicle is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: It is in the city at all times.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: What we're trying to do now is use some of the bigger data sources that use things like anonymized cell phone data to figure out where are there areas where there's vehicle trips that neither start nor end in an area, which is kind of a description of cut-through traffic.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Is there any way you can get data from Waze or these companies to help you study that better?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Yeah, without naming all the companies, that's the kind of things we're talking about.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Something I'll just add, you know, that I thought was pretty eye-opening is that a large chunk of our automated camera violations actually go to vehicles registered out of the city.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: So it does seem like, you know, if some New Yorkers or some neighborhoods are perceiving that there's folks cutting through their neighborhood, the data suggested that that is the case.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: So, you know, that just sort of underscores the potential here.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Are there any street design tools currently used by DOT that are primarily aimed at reducing cut-through traffic in residential areas?

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: That doesn't include an LTN.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: So, I mean, just Councilmember Ressler actually mentioned one that we implemented just a few weeks ago

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: in his district where we used what we call a diverter, where traffic is still allowed on every street in the intersection, but traffic from certain streets is forced to make a left or a right onto another street so that they can't just drive straight through.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: So, you know, that's an example, a thing that we've learned from places like London as being very effective.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: It's designed so that if you're on your own,

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: on a bike or you're walking, you can, of course, continue going straight.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: But that vehicle traffic cannot take such a direct route.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Have you all been in conversation with London folks or government leaders there?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Yeah, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: In fact, I got to see some of these in person not too long ago.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: And we've even had them come and sort of exchange knowledge with our team.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: So we're trying to soak up as much information as we can.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Great.

chapters.summary: Abreu asks what a before-and-after LTN report should include. DOT says safety is the minimum, but it also wants to measure emergency response times, bus speeds, and spillover effects on surrounding streets, citing London's evidence of no significant surrounding traffic increase or emergency response delay.
chapters.title: Abreu asks DOT what LTN before-and-after report should include

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: A critical piece of this legislation is reporting on the impacts of the LTN pilot areas.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: What would a before and after data report look like?

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: And what data does DLT think would be important for understanding success?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: And, you know, we can talk about everything that might go into a report, but it, of course, starts with safety, right?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: But I think everyone expects there's less traffic in an area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: It's likely to lead to safety.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: So that's kind of a minimum level.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: But we also want to look at things like making sure that we're not affecting emergency response times.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: We want to make sure that as traffic is diverted to other streets, it's not affecting bus speeds, say, on those other streets.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: We want to make sure that we're not benefiting one area at the cost of another.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: And again, some of the lessons from London are that you don't see those spillover effects.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: But as we measure it in New York, we want to know for ourselves and be able to tell not just what's happening in the immediate neighborhood, but also any surrounding area.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: And what we saw in London was that the surrounding neighborhood traffic did not increase or significantly.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: And so, you know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: There's variation from place to place, but generally it did not.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: And that's a positive.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: And also, what we also found was that emergency response times also didn't significantly, it didn't increase.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: And partly because you have less traffic, so it's easier, of course, to get around.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: And that's something that we saw over there and hopefully happens here.

chapters.summary: Abreu asks NYPD about illegal parking around police precincts, citing photographic evidence and academic studies showing worse pedestrian safety near precincts. NYPD says parking is challenging, its Standards and Assessment Section conducts daily command visits, and findings are reported to leadership.
chapters.title: Abreu questions NYPD on illegal parking around police precincts

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: I'm going to ask my last question of this hearing before I turn it over to my colleagues, and that's for PD.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: For years, there has been consistent photographic evidence that streets surrounding NYPD precincts are inundated with illegally parked cars.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: This parking behavior has cascading impacts in the surrounding community for pedestrians, residents, and local businesses.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: These problems have been so longstanding that there are now academic studies looking into the street safety issues surrounding our police precincts.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Unfortunately, but unsurprisingly, they are finding evidence that pedestrian safety is worse near police precincts.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: In my district on 100th Street, there's, kid you not, there's a sign

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: in spray paint telling the NYPD on that block the days of alternate side parking for the cars to be gone, and it signs off DSNY.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: I don't know if it's true that DSNY used spray cans to let another government agency that needs to move its cars on certain dates, but this is an issue.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: That is pervasive in our city.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: What is the agency's position on it?

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Do you recognize that it is a problem?

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: I'll start there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: So parking, obviously, in the city and around our precincts can be challenging.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: And it is something that we absolutely do recognize and take efforts to address.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Our standards and assessment section is conducting daily command visits.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: We're evaluating our parking compliance.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: We're evaluating that at department facilities.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: So it's something we look into and that we're trying to make sure that we meet all of our guidelines.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Where we don't meet those guidelines, the SAS, the standards and assessment section, is going to be documenting that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Those findings are reported to department leadership.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: What's being done to address, I mean, do you recognize that it is a problem?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: It's a real challenge to park in these areas.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: I mean, there's just a limited amount of space.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: It's a real issue.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: So when you say challenging, is that a justification for the illegal parking?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: No, and as I said, it's something that we take seriously.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: And as I just walked through, you know, there are steps that we take to try to make sure that we're in compliance.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: And when there's indications of misuse of parking permits, those parking permits can be revoked.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: There could be other discipline as well.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: What are you doing to address these issues?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: So I mentioned the standards assessment section is conducting those daily command assessments.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: All that information that they're collecting, that's going to be reported up to department leadership.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: So we're looking at this command by command.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Those are coming on a daily basis.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: We're looking at our parking and making sure that we're

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: We're in compliance with our guidelines.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: And whether it departures from that, that's something that gets escalated.

chapters.summary: Abreu asks why precinct parking was not mentioned in Vision Zero Reimagined and whether NYPD has action items. NYPD says it takes the issue seriously, documents issues, and welcomes council suggestions. Abreu offers to discuss specific precincts in his district.
chapters.title: Abreu asks NYPD why precinct parking not in Vision Zero Reimagined

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Why wasn't this issue mentioned in Vision Zero Reimagined?

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Are there any action items you're committed to pursuing to help address these problems going forward?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Well, so as I said, it is something that we are taking seriously, that we are looking at, we do look at every day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: We document issues when we find them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: We take action to correct them when we can.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: So it's something we absolutely do take seriously.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: We want to move forward on and would welcome any suggestions from the council about what we can be doing better.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: And, you know, to Councilmember Santos-Suoso's point earlier, like, I'm not doubting that no work isn't happening or that work is happening.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: But it's clearly not enough because the behavior on our– every police precinct in my district, I mean, they have part– maybe the 2-6 is better than the others.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: But every other police precinct in my district, the 2-4–

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: The 3-0 and the 3-3 is pretty bad.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Mr.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Chairman, we'd be happy to discuss with you about those specific instances you're seeing in your district.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Abreu turns to Council Member Pierina Sanchez for questions.
chapters.title: Abreu turns to Council Member Pierina Sanchez

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: With questions, we're going to begin with Councilmember Pierina Sanchez, followed by Wong.

chapters.summary: Sanchez notes DOT redesigned Bailey and Sedgwick Avenues but left the dangerous I-87/Major Deegan intersections at Burnside, Fordham Road, and 231st Street largely unchanged. DOT says highway-street interfaces are complicated and some are controlled by state DOT, which must come to the table.
chapters.title: Pierina Sanchez questions DOT on dangerous highway ramp intersections

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Thank you so much, Majority Leader, and thank you for this very important hearing.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: So I have two sets of questions.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: The first one, and apologies if this topic has been touched on, but Vision Zero, Vision Zero Reimagined, and the Streets Plan all charge the agency with redesigning streets to improve pedestrian safety, as we've been talking about today.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: including consideration of hardened daylighting.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: In my neck of the woods, DOT has made significant changes to Bailey Avenue and Sedgwick Avenue in recent years, including this year.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Yet the most dangerous intersections of all, where the street grid collides with the entrance and exit ramps of the I-87 or Major Deegan Expressway at Burnside, Fordham Road, and 231st Street, have remained largely unchanged.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: How do I explain to my constituents why no changes were made at the most dangerous intersections of all where there were significant redesigns?

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: And part two is help me what interventions exist to make these specific kinds of high conflict locations like highway entrances more safe?

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: And what should I be advocating that you do at these locations?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Thank you so much, Councilmember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: And I got to say, I had the pleasure of biking down Bailey just a couple weekends ago and seeing the new extension there and also seeing...

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: You should have came by and said, I live right by this.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Yeah, next time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Yeah, it was a weekend.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: I happened to be coming back from something in Marble Hill.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: But I also saw some of the challenges that you mentioned.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: I know that something we were pretty proud of at the northern end by Van Cortlandt Park, there's some ramps right from the highway there, and we were able to make some pretty significant changes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: I'm not sure if you want to speak about some of the others.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Yeah, and like these interfaces between the highway and streets.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Have been an increased focus.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: They tend to be complicated intersections.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: They also are a little bit more complicated because they involve people beyond us, like the Fordham Road exit off the Deegan is really controlled by state DOT.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: And so we've been in touch with them and expressed that that is a priority for us for them to redesign.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: But at the end, it's their bridge and their highway.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: So we need them to come to the table.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: We are happy to work with them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: And we have very creative designers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: But part of the reason those sometimes take longer is because it's not as much in our control as some of the school streets.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: And sorry, just because I'm limited on time, I have another question.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: What changes should I be advocating for when we do get state DOT at the table?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Sure, and it varies location by location, but essentially what we want to do is make sure we're protecting pedestrians and providing safe time for pedestrians to cross, and then make sure that the turning vehicles are properly managed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: We can talk to you separately in great detail, but obviously at Fordham and Deegan, one of the problems is that the left turns overlap tremendously so that people go around and make double and triple lefts.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: I've never done that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Yeah, me neither.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: But, you know, the intersection, sort of the design causes the bad behavior.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: And so, you know, there's different intersection designs that have happened since the 1950s that do better at that sort of thing.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Sanchez raises her community board's letter about streetlights out for 9-12 months, false complaint closures, and daylight-only inspections under the Hyland contract. DOT says lighting is very much on its radar and it is expanding contract capacity. Abreu notes a future public realm hearing will cover streetlights.
chapters.title: Sanchez asks DOT about Hyland lighting contract and backlog

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: And then my second question, and more to come on that because these areas are very dangerous.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Highland and the lighting contract, the DOT's lighting contracts.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: I have before me a letter that

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: My community board number eight sent over to the controller, CC, the Bronx commissioner and other DOT staff on regarding lights that have been out for nine months, 10 months, a year at a time.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: I also myself have reported lights around the Jerome Park Reservoir that have been out for months and months and months.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: And we understand that the agency is not able to hold Highland accountable.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: That is the interpretation we have in the community because...

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Reports are made, if it's not the exact address, then the lighting complaints are closed, which is a false closure.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Inspections are only happening in the daylight.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: How does the company know that the lights are still off?

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: And so much more.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: So can you just give us an update on the status of your contract with Hyland?

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: How many light complaints are in the backlog?

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: And when can we expect to have our lights back in functioning order in our communities?

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Because it's creating dangerous conditions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: I can say, you know, I'm not sure if we're equipped to address the specific contract today, but I can say, and I mentioned this, I think, earlier, you may have been out, lighting is something I've definitely heard a lot about in my time in this role.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: And, you know, it's clear communities, it really affects people's day-to-day lives.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: And I'll be honest, it's an area where we've had some challenges with, you know, as happens sometimes when you've got large operations.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: In this case, you know, we're working to really expand our contract capacity and be able to be more nimble and address.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: some of these lighting things quicker going forward.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: So I guess my point is it's very much on my radar and our radar, and it's something we're really focused on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Our street lighting division is actively working to kind of remediate some of these challenges.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: You can ask a follow-up, yes.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Just very quickly, this letter was sent last week.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: I hope that you all can send us a formal response.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: It was sent on October 21st, and so I would really appreciate the specifics on when our lights are going to...

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Yeah, happy to check with our traffic operations team and connect with you.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: And Councilmember Sanchez, we are going to have a hearing in the new year on public realm and streetlights where we're going to go into the details on that even more.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: As mentioned before, but Councilmember Ressler is an issue.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: I just got an email from Councilor Marano about this.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: It's an issue in every borough, and so we're going to take a close look at that.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Councilmember Wong, followed by Justin Sanchez.

chapters.summary: Council Member Wong asks whether DOT's traffic control studies near schools, daycares, and playgrounds capture arrival and dismissal periods. DOT says it uses 24-hour counters and peak-hour observations, relies on local input, and will follow up on expedited review criteria.
chapters.title: Council Member Wong questions DOT on school-zone traffic studies

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Thank you, Majority Leader and Chair.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: I requested a lot of traffic devices near intersections of schools, daycares, and playgrounds.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: And my question here is to DOT.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: DOT's reply usually says they need traffic control studies, which can take four to seven months, depending on the device under review.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: And my question is, when a request involves a school, daycare, or playground, how does DOT make sure it's

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Observations capture the periods when kids are actually crossing, and our studies conducted during arrival and dismissal while school is in session.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Please answer that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Sure, and that's a great question and something that we really do try to pay attention to.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Most intersections around the city, you try to capture the morning and the evening rush hour, but we know near schools or sometimes near parks, you get a different peak of when kids might be crossing the street.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Sometimes it's a Saturday afternoon right near a park.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: And so what we do is we put down counters that can give us like a 24-hour count as a starting place so that when we go and count pedestrians, we can make sure we're doing it at the peak hours for those locations.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: And then we look and we see, hey, there's a school right there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: We need to make sure that we're capturing school dismissal.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: We do try to be very aware.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Sometimes there's something that we might not know about a neighborhood, right?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: You don't know that there's a special event that happens midday is there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: And that's where we rely on input from local council members and other experts who can tell us, make sure you check this hour, and we will go and do that.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: As a follow-up, what conditions qualify a location for an expedited review or interim protection while a longer study is underway?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: So we'll have to get back to you because that's beyond my specific expertise.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: But one thing I will talk about is if there's been a recent history of crashes, right, and we're responding to some to like very recent events, then that's something that we have to take into account and make sure we're being.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Responsive to something newer going on.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Okay, thank you.

chapters.summary: Wong describes Amazon delivery trucks taking over residential parking spaces all day for package handoffs. DOT says post-pandemic delivery activity has surged and its new curb management and freight team is exploring micro hubs, shared lockers, and dedicated delivery space.
chapters.title: Wong raises Amazon delivery trucks occupying residential parking

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Second question, also on DOT.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: In my district, I have parking spaces that's been taken over by Amazon delivery trucks, where big trucks or packages pull in,

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: and then walkers, people walk up with dollies, with hand trucks, with all sorts of devices.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Pick up their packages, and they go their separate ways.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: They come back and they do it again.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Here's the problem.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: One, these trucks are not in these loading or unloading zones.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: They are in residential streets.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: They take over parking spaces.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: And now let me tell you how I know about it because they chose the intersection in front of my office.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: And they're there the whole day.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Like 8 o'clock all the way to 6 p.m.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: And I see it as a citywide problem because I see it in Jackson Heights, Corona, other parts of Queens.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: So my question to you is, are you allowing this to happen or is something you need to address because it's clearly a problem?

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: A problem because they're taking over our residential streets and our parking spaces.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Please answer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Thank you, Councilmember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Yeah, I mean, I think, you know, what we're seeing is really these trends that have accelerated, especially since the pandemic, in online shopping and online delivery

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: and just much higher delivery activity in residential areas than we saw historically.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: And I think that highlights, you know, the need for curb space and how we provide it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: We are doing a lot of innovative work.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: We have a whole freight team devoted to this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: That's part of our new curb management division.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: And, you know, they're trying a few different tools across the board, both because it's a little bit, there's two things in tension, right?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: We want less trucks circling all over the place to make deliveries.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: But if they're not doing that, then they're going to do what you described, which is basically what we would call micro distribution, right?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Where they stop in one place and then they use maybe hand trucks or they just walk or maybe use a cargo bike to make the final delivery.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: So we do have a micro hub pilot program.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: We're also looking at things like shared lockers where the deliveries can be made by Amazon, for example, to one set of lockers and then residents come and get it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: That also helps with theft, avoiding theft.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: So, you know, the short answer is it's very much on our radar and we're trying to explore a range of options to minimize all the truck circling and have dedicated space for deliveries.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: And I want to point out that as soon as the truck is empty, it pulls out, another one comes, pulls in, and so forth.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: People are doing a lot of online shopping.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Yeah, they're there the whole day, and that's clearly a problem, and it's a citywide issue.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Please look into it, and I'm happy to continue this discussion and come up with ideas.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: That would be great.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Yeah, we're always open to ideas, but definitely it's a priority.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Councilor Brooks-Powers, followed by Justin Sanchez and Hanif.

chapters.summary: Brooks-Powers asks whether the Vision Zero data warehouse will include conviction, license status, and insurance data for Intro 113. DOT supports the study concept but says it lacks access to insurance and conviction data; the data warehouse timeline is not available today.
chapters.title: Council Member Brooks-Powers questions DOT on Intro 113 data sources

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair, and thank you for the testimony today.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: I'm ping-ponging a bit today.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Regarding my bill, Intro 113, I wanted to ask, the administration's new plan makes removing dangerous drivers its first goal and says nearly half of traffic deaths involve a driver who

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: was unlicensed, previously suspended, or had multiple convictions.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Intro 113 asks DOT to study exactly those patterns and report on them every year.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: You may have stated this before, so I apologize if it's redundant because I was chairing another hearing, but wanting to know what DOT's official position is and will the plan visions

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Zero data warehouse include conviction, license status, and insurance data, and when will it be up and running?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Thank you, Councilmember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: So we very much support studies like this that help us better understand the trends that we're seeing out there and how we can do more equitable and targeted enforcement and other safety strategies.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: This is, in many ways, that's sort of the bread and butter, right?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: And I think anything we can do to better understand what's driving safety challenges is helpful.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: So we're excited to work with the council and yourself to ensure that, I guess, to kind of hone the legislation and how we can make it most effective in terms of the data warehouse.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Yeah, I think just some of our concerns with the bill is data sources we don't have access to as the city or as DOT.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: And so that falls into, I think, both the insurance data, which has been, I think, a longstanding issue.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Insurance firms have not provided that data to the city in the past, despite our deep desire to be aware of it, as well as the conviction data obviously living outside the mayoral control.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: So I think we're happy to continue conversations and think about are there novel ways that we can look for that data?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Because, you know, to your point, the data warehouse is a huge project that we're really invested in to make sure that all of the data from the hospital to the crash location are really talking to each other.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: And when will it be up and running?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: We'll have to get back to you on that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: I don't have it in front of me today.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Okay.

chapters.summary: Brooks-Powers asks what steps reduce crashes by dangerous drivers. DOT describes infrastructure first, automated enforcement, super speeder devices, and ghost plate enforcement. Brooks-Powers then asks NYPD about suspended/revoked license stops and reckless driving arrests; NYPD reports VTL 511 arrests up 9% and reckless driving arrest and summons numbers.
chapters.title: Brooks-Powers asks DOT what steps reduce dangerous driver crashes

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Intro 113 also asks relevant agencies to report on the steps taken to reduce accidents caused by dangerous drivers.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
