utterances.text: What steps are already in place to reduce those accidents, and what more do you feel can be done?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Yeah, it's really, it's sort of all of the above approach.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Infrastructure, you know, I think in our ideal world, all drivers would behave safely, right?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: And you wouldn't even necessarily need enforcement and folks could spend their violation money on better things, right?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: So we like to start with infrastructure and engineering and redesigning our streets.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: I love that.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Thank you for that.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: No, of course.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: You know what I mean?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Like that's, that's, that's.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: It's the most sustainable, right?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: It's the most sort of legible and elegant in a way.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: And so that's always our starting point.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: And so that's obviously following the data and innovating with new approaches to street design.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Sometimes that's not enough.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: And so that's where we start to look at some of the other tools.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: You know, we think that automated enforcement has been really effective and the stats are very compelling.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: And we could talk more about that, but that's certainly a key piece.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: And then there's sort of, you know, the question of, well, what happens with really the...

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: The folks for whom even that isn't a deterrent, right?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: The folks who are just racking up speeding tickets and red light.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: violations and that's where something like the super speeder program can be a great tool and things like we talked about earlier about looking at ghost plates and some of the other more systemic challenges.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: I appreciate that and my last question is for NYPD.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Hi Chief Obey.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Two questions for you.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: How many vehicles registered to people with suspended or revoked licenses does NYPD stop each year, and how many are caught on camera?

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: And in the past year, how many reckless driving and right-of-way law arrests were made, and how many led to convictions?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: I don't have the whole universe of what you're talking about, but I do have VTL 511 arrest.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: We are up 9%.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Year-to-date 2026 through 1018, 22,663 versus 20,799 from year-end 2025.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Reckless driving arrest, which is VTL 1212, 1815 versus 1784 from last year.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: And reckless driving C summons is issued 5819 versus 5290.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair.

chapters.summary: Council Member Justin Sanchez argues the Hub is a major destination and Bronx residents are more likely to be in crashes. He asks DOT to consider pedestrianization and a neighborhood study on pedestrian mobility, busway viability, and safety. DOT cites Bronx safety gains and is open to the study.
chapters.title: Council Member Justin Sanchez questions DOT on the Hub pedestrianization

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Councilmember Justin Sanchez, followed by Hanif.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: So the hub is the second largest, most visited place in the state of New York after Times Square on a daily basis.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: And additionally, a study of collision data found that the Bronx and its residents are more likely to be in traffic crashes than New Yorkers that live in any other borough, with the hub being a particular hotspot.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: Would DOT consider more of a time squarification of the hub that is pedestrianization of the area?

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: And can the agency commit to conducting a neighborhood study to address pedestrian mobility, busway viability, and ultimately address street safety?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Thank you, Councilmember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: You know, I know that in many ways the hub is sort of like the downtown, right, for the Bronx.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: And it has that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: And it is a hub, literally, right, where multiple modes come together.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: So, you know, I guess one thing I'll mention, I guess, on the safety side, something we're really proud of is we looked at the distribution of some of the safety gains we've seen in the last few years.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: And actually, the Bronx and the Queens have seen the greatest safety gains under our Vision Zero efforts in the last few years.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: But there's more to do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: The hub's a busy place.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: So definitely happy to sit down and brainstorm with you and your team around what that kind of study could look like.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Oh, you asked also sort of about the public space aspect.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: So I know Roberto Clemente Plaza was a big investment at the time and was a big change.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: to the hub.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: But in terms of further public space enhancements, we're definitely open to ideas.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: I think how it can really best support the community, support businesses, support commuters, it would be really exciting.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: I would really love to get this on the books sooner rather than later because we know how long these studies take to get done.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: And I hate studies.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: I just like action.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: Studies just delay us from getting to work.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: So really just would love to get that done.

chapters.summary: Sanchez asks whether DOT studies curb occupancy in the Bronx and how many parked cars are not local. DOT says it has looked at this through congestion pricing and Yankee Stadium studies and finds many cars parked long-term. On residential parking permits, DOT says RPP can help with out-of-state registration but has not dented demand elsewhere.
chapters.title: Sanchez asks DOT about parking permits and out-of-state plates

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: In terms of parking permits, has DOT studied how full the curbs are in the outer boroughs, particularly the Bronx, the South Bronx, and what share of parked cars don't belong to people or belong to people who don't actually live there?

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: And if DOT does not collect that data, does the agency have the capacity to gather such data in a piloted area?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: So this is something that we've looked at over the years.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: It was part of the congestion pricing parking study.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: It's also something we've looked at previously around places like Yankee Stadium that have had specific parking needs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: And you see two things, right?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: You can ask the question of, are the vehicles that you see parked on the street registered at the local address?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: And you get a little bit of a mixed bag there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: But when you look overnight, you see the same vehicles that tend to be parked there night after night after night, which suggests that even if the registration is elsewhere, they probably are actually

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: belonging to someone who is spending their time in that district.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: And this is a pattern we actually see all over the city is that a very, very large percentage of the vehicles parked in the free residential spaces do show that pattern of being there for very long stretches of time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: And we take that to mean our own by local residents.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: So we know that this is something that comes up, especially in busy business areas or where there is entertainment around.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: So it is a challenge where a lot of the problem is just that New Yorkers own a lot of cars, and that takes up a lot of the space on the street.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: Having said that, yes, there are a lot of cars that belong to people that live around there, but a lot of the times they're not registered to New York.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: They're not New York plates.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: And so ideally, wouldn't residential parking permit?

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: address that and also yes they're parked I think to your point they are parked for a very long period of time they're not moving during alternate side parkings hence we had to pass the green sticker bill

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: once more but because of this wouldn't residential parking also encourage people to actually have to move their cars

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: So I think, yeah, there's a range of tools that we could use that would really encourage, incentivize, or require folks to register their vehicle where they're supposed to register it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: If it's permits or if it's sort of the way that, you know, you charge for street space in areas that have paid parking, you know, you could have discounts for...

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Local residents whose vehicles are registered locally.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: There's different ways to look at that, I think.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: And that's, you know, that's exactly what our curb management group is going to be looking at those kinds of ideas.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: Do you, does DOT agree that residential parking permits are a good way to mitigate parking scarcity for resident New Yorkers?

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: Does the agency plan to advocate for a permit system in the state legislative agenda?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: So there's a range of things.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: I think with residential parking permits, what we've seen is that in other cities, at least, they're not priced in a way that it actually ends up freeing up parking because it's priced so cheaply on an annual basis that it's not actually managing the demand.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: So I think it can address, though.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: I think you made this point, Councilmember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: It can help with the issue of out-of-state registration.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: I think it could be helpful.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Like I said, I think there's also other ways to address that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: But RPP specifically, we haven't seen in other cities that they really made much of a dent in the actual demand for parking.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: Chair, do you mind if I ask one more question?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Please, go ahead.

chapters.summary: Sanchez cites armed turf wars in the towing industry and asks if BIC could regulate towing. BIC says its current jurisdiction covers trade waste, wholesale markets, and shipboard gambling, but its integrity and licensing model could be transposed to other industries if City Hall, budget, and Council legislation allow.
chapters.title: Sanchez asks BIC about towing industry and organized crime

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: This is for, thank you, this is for BIC.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: So BIC was created to drive organized crime out of the commercial waste industry.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: Recent reporting on towing describes armed turf wars between towing companies, including a Bronx body shop owner just sentenced to 19 years for killing a rival.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: Does BIC see parallels to the industries it already regulates?

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: Has BIC considered expanding its jurisdictional authority over the towing industry?

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: And could its model of integrity vetting and licensing work for towing?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Thank you, Council Member.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: As you noted, BIC's current jurisdiction covers the trade waste industry.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: It also covers the wholesale markets, which are in your district, as well as shipboard gambling.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: And that's our mandate by law.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: BIC's team is a talented, highly skilled team that is adept with respect to

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: identifying patterns of organized crime and engaged in licensing for businesses where we have concerns about criminality and want to keep criminality out of those businesses.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: That model could be transposed into...

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: to other industries.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: If the city believes that there is a risk of criminality in particular industries and BIC should come in, we're ready to have those conversations.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: There could be any number of industries that could be candidates for that, but that's a longer policy discussion that's going to have to include City Hall, that's going to involve some budgeting questions, and ultimately will require legislation by City Hall,

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: I'm sorry, legislation by City Council to give us the authority to move into whatever those new spaces are.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

chapters.summary: Council Member Hanif notes 17 community boards and 63 elected officials have called for Sammy's Law slow zones and asks why DOT lowers speed limits block by block instead of neighborhood-wide. DOT says the new neighborhood-scale program starts next year and will use speeding, cut-through traffic, crash data, and equity criteria.
chapters.title: Council Member Hanif questions DOT on neighborhood-wide slow zones

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Council Member Hani, followed by Juan.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair, and hello.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: Great to see everybody.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: Commissioner Flynn, this is for you.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: I wanted to come back to Sammy's Law.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: So 17 community boards representing nearly 2.5 million New Yorkers, along with 63 elected officials, have formally...

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: Called for SAMHSA's law slow zones in their neighborhoods, and I'm proud to be one of those elected officials.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: The city's own Vision Zero reimagined plan commits to expanding 20 mile per hour speed limits across entire neighborhoods, yet beyond the five existing SAMHSA's law slow zones,

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: DOT's largely limited speed reductions to short stretches in front of schools, very short stretches, I would add.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: Why are we lowering speed limits block by block when entire neighborhoods are demanding safer streets?

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: And can you tell us what's stopping DOT from implementing neighborhood-wide slow zones and when we can expect to see them?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Thank you, Councilmember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: And yeah, I mean, first, you know, I would reiterate that we've been thrilled to see that groundswell of demand and, you know, requests from New York City neighborhoods for lower speeds.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: We certainly see the value from a safety standpoint in reduced speed limits.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: You know, I guess your question around the school-related ones versus area ones, I think that there's room for both.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: They have, you know, somewhat different kind of goals or targets in mind.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: But we are really excited about the announcing and including in Vision Zero Reimagine rolling out these lower speed zones at more of a neighborhood.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: What's the timeline for that?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Well, this is an action plan.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: So this is a new program.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: We've just announced it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: We're developing the details of it now, but we'll be looking to roll it out starting next year.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: And that would include the neighborhood-wide.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: And could you share like what criteria is assessed in order to share which neighborhoods would be prioritized?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Yeah, I mean, I think we're kind of neck deep in developing this sizable program.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Like I mentioned earlier, you know, we want to strike a balance.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: We want to, it's really helpful for us to hear from communities that are asking for it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: And at the same time, we also want to use the data to make sure that we're...

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: But also, you don't actually have to hear from neighborhoods to know that this needs to get done, right?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Well, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: And we want to follow the data so that when we make these investments, it can have the greatest possible impact.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: And so we might look at things like where we're seeing speeding, where we're seeing cut through traffic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Anything you would add?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Those are some of the factors.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Crash data clearly is always kind of the baseline.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: Yeah, I would just push for expedition on this issue.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: Of course, having slower speed limits by school zones is necessary, but once kids are leaving the school, they're leaving that 150-foot slow zone area, and it's certainly not a substitute for a safer

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: neighborhood.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: And so I'd love to just know more details.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Yeah, I guess the one other thing I would add is, you know, that equity is a big component as well, right?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: So the new streets plan come.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: We're going to have a couple months.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: We'll have the new version of our priority investment areas.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: And we really try to focus a lot of our investments into the historically disadvantaged neighborhoods.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: So it's always a balancing act.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: But we're happy to talk more and share more when we can.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: And so when you say a couple months, we're talking December, we're talking January, are we talking March?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: For the streets plan?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: The deadline under the law is December 1st.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: And then that plan will lay out the proposals for the neighborhood-wide slow zones?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: I think we're excited to share.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: It's going to have more details on a number of initiatives, some of which were in Vision Zero plan, some maybe new.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: And yeah, we're excited to share more details.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Council Member 1.

chapters.summary: Council Member Julie Won asks what percentage of drivers yield to pedestrians at marked and unmarked crosswalks and what infrastructure improves yielding. DOT says it has not measured this citywide and will consider it. Won asks if Vision Zero Reimagined has a hard LPI commitment; DOT says no specific commitment but remains committed. Won requests a decision tree.
chapters.title: Council Member Julie Won questions DOT on crosswalk yield rates and LPIs

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: Thank you so much, Chair Abreu.

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: What percentage of drivers yield to pedestrians at both marked and unmarked crosswalks?

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: And what infrastructure improvements increase yield rates at pedestrian crossings?

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: And have these infrastructure improvements been considered in the Vision Zero reimagined plan?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: So I don't know that we have that specific data point, but we do know that yielding to pedestrians is an incredibly important thing, and that's something both we work on with PD from an enforcement perspective, but it's also something that we try to design into the street infrastructure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Just for example, you talked a little bit earlier about design of bike lanes at protected intersections, and one of the very specific ways that that improves safety

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: is by using the physical infrastructure to force drivers to turn more slowly and to turn at an angle where they can better see both cyclists and pedestrians.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: So what we want to do is have people turning slowly so that they can see pedestrians crossing and therefore yield.

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: So can you just clarify, you don't have the percentage of drivers for yielding to pedestrians at unmarked and marked crosswalks, or you don't have it with you right now?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: So that's not something we've measured on a citywide basis, no.

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: Is that something that you could consider measuring with the Vision Zero reimagined plan so that we have that data?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Let's talk about that and get back to you.

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: And leading pedestrian intervals, LPIs, are the cheapest intersection improvement given that they require no infrastructure changes.

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: Is Vision Zero reimagined aware that only half of the signalized intersections have LPIs?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Yeah, we've seen great results from LPIs, and we've put in over 6,000 to date.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: We continue to roll them out.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: You're right, Council Member, that they're really a...

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: much more easier on the wallet, I guess you could say.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: They're easier to roll out in that way.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Yeah, we remain committed to using it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: I think it's, you know, again, it's one of the tools that we have.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: And so it's part of the mix of all the safety improvements that we're making.

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: So is there a hard commitment from the mayoral admin of how many LPIs would be installed going forward with the Vision Zero reimagined plan?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Yeah, the Vision Zero reimagined doesn't include a commitment specifically around LPIs.

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: Would you be willing to add them?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: I mean, I think it's the treatment that we remain committed to.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: We, you know, as you mentioned, they're at, I guess, roughly half of signalized intersections.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: We prioritize them at locations where we think they can have the greatest benefit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: That's places where we're seeing a lot of turn conflicts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: So what happens over time is that the more intersections, you know, we put them at, the impact may be a little less.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Doesn't mean it's not a good idea.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: It just means like when we're balancing in a world of finite resources, you know, where to focus, we may find other things that will have a greater benefit.

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: So I guess what I'm struggling with is it's clear that we are aligned as a council and with the DOT on what your vision is for safety and what the advocates want.

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: But what I'm having a hard time understanding.

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: every single year is the decision tree or the process in which you make what safety measures are put into what intersections.

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: So if you could share that after this hearing as a follow-up to the chair as well as the members of this committee, it would be really helpful for us to really concretely understand what it is that you're quantifying and qualifying these decisions on.

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: Because there's so many tools in the toolbox, and we want to see all of them implemented.

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Thank you, Council Member.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: I'll meet with the team on that.

chapters.summary: Abreu relays Council Member Marte's question about whether the administration will pedestrianize Lower Manhattan, specifically FIDI, under the pedestrian priority districts initiative. DOT says the program is new, there is potential in high-pedestrian, low-vehicle areas, and more details will come next year.
chapters.title: Abreu asks DOT about pedestrian priority districts and FIDI

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Councilmember Chris Marte wanted me to ask a question on his behalf.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: As part of the visions that were reimagined, there were pedestrian priority districts mentioned.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Is the administration committing to pedestrianize lower Manhattan, specifically FIDI?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: We will have more details to share on that program.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: It's new.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: We're excited.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: We think there's a lot of potential in different neighborhoods where we're seeing high pedestrian volumes and lower vehicle volumes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: So there'll be more to share.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: The council member is very supportive of this project and just wanted to communicate that.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: I don't want to scoop you in your announcement, but when...

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Regardless of the neighborhood being selected, by when should we expect this pedestrian-only area to be done?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Well, we'd like to move quickly on any and all of the ideas in the Vision Zero reimagined.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Sometime next year?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: I'm sure we'll see movement on just about every initiative in that plan in some way, shape, or form by next year.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Well.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Councilmember Hanif has one more question, and then we'll close out.

chapters.summary: Council Member Hanif asks about a micro hub on Wyckoff Avenue near her district office that is causing double parking and constituent complaints. DOT says it is not officially part of the pilot but will look into it, explaining that micro hubs offer dedicated curb space in exchange for no double parking, with space removed if companies violate the agreement.
chapters.title: Council Member Hanif asks DOT about micro hub pilot on Wyckoff

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: So this is about the micro hubs.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: I'm really pleased to learn about this pilot.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: In my district, and I don't know if this is official, but on Wyckoff between Bond and Hoyt, right near my district office, there has been...

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: A hub, I'm not sure if it's official, would like to know what we can do to

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: either make that a part of the pilot, but I'm getting a lot of constituent complaints given that the truck, I mean, it seems like it's a subcontractor parked, double parked, and they're doing the deliveries, and it's caused a lot of pain.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: In the obvious residential neighborhood.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Sure, and I don't believe that that's officially part of the program, so we're happy to take a look and talk to you about it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: That would be great.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: And the idea behind it is that we offer something in terms of dedicated space at the curb to a company, and in doing that, they have to commit that they are not going to be double parking or driving around the neighborhood or doing these other bad behaviors.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: And if we see them doing that, the idea is we take that space away.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: So we've done it a handful of places now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: It's seemed to be effective.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: It has been across the city.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: I'd love to bump us up to the top because there's a ton of deliveries happening.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: And I've been in touch with Brooklyn Borough Commissioner Bray on this, but it's still unclear to me what the problem is.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: process is and if I think we've requested for a designated loading zone but it seems like this pilot is actually the solve.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Sure yeah well we and Commissioner Ray will talk to you more about that.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: Okay I appreciate it.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Thank you, Councilmember Hanif.

chapters.summary: Abreu excuses the administration panel and asks the room to quiet down. After a recess, he opens public testimony with rules: two minutes per speaker, appearance cards, no recordings from the witness table, and written testimony may be submitted by email within 72 hours.
chapters.title: Abreu excuses administration panel and opens public comment

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: This panel is hereby excused, and we'll open it up for public comment in a few minutes.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: If you guys can just keep it down in the committee room.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Sergeants, am I able to start?

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: I now open the hearing for public testimony.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: I remind members of the public that this is a formal government proceeding and that decorum shall be observed at all times.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: As such, members of the public shall remain silent at all times.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: The witness table is reserved for people who wish to testify.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: No video recording or photography is allowed from the witness table.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Further, members of the public may not present audio or video recordings as testimony, but may submit transcripts of such recordings to the Sergeant at Arms for inclusion in the hearing record.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: If you wish to speak at today's hearing, please fill out an appearance card with the Sergeant at Arms and wait to be recognized.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: When recognized, you will have two minutes to speak on the oversight topic and or legislation being heard today.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: If you have written statement or additional written testimony you wish to submit for the record, please provide a copy to the Sergeant at Arms.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: You may also email written testimony to testimony at council at nyc.gov within 72 hours of this hearing.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Audio and video recordings will not be accepted.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: I will now call the first panel.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: First panel, Ben Furness.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Julian Williams, Sarah Lynn, Amber Adler, Eric McClure, and Nyusha Masumi.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: All right, Ben, you may begin.

chapters.summary: Ben Furness, Executive Director of Transportation Alternatives, says over 150 New Yorkers have been killed in traffic this year and nine in hit-and-runs in August alone. He urges expanded daylighting, district-wide Sammy's Law speed limits, Stop Super Speeders by spring 2027, and safer city fleet vehicles.
chapters.title: Ben Furness, Transportation Alternatives, testifies on Vision Zero progress

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ben Furness
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Council Member.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ben Furness
utterances.text: Thank you for holding this hearing today.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ben Furness
utterances.text: My name is Ben Furness.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ben Furness
utterances.text: I'm the Executive Director of Transportation Alternatives.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ben Furness
utterances.text: When Mayor Bill de Blasio announced the launch of Vision Zero back in 2014, it seemed like a lofty, impossible goal.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ben Furness
utterances.text: Since then, traffic fatalities have dropped, but cities around the world show how much further we have to go.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ben Furness
utterances.text: Just so far this year, over 150 New Yorkers have been killed in traffic.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ben Furness
utterances.text: In August alone, nine New Yorkers were killed in hit and runs.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ben Furness
utterances.text: Hundreds held a die-in outside this very building in outrage.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ben Furness
utterances.text: All of these deaths were preventable.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ben Furness
utterances.text: We know this because peer cities have a

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ben Furness
utterances.text: eliminated or dramatically cut traffic deaths.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ben Furness
utterances.text: Per capita, New Yorkers are killed in traffic at double the rates of our global peers.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ben Furness
utterances.text: Coming in line with cities like London, Berlin, and Tokyo would cut our traffic deaths in half.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ben Furness
utterances.text: To get there, we must focus on the most common causes of death and injury.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ben Furness
utterances.text: Control vehicle speeds, fix the still deadly arterial streets, reduce cut-through traffic in residential neighborhoods, and make intersections safe.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ben Furness
utterances.text: City Hall already promised to implement daylighting or better at 1,000 intersections a year, a good start, but this must be dramatically expanded.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ben Furness
utterances.text: Broadly implementing Sammy's Law speed limits at district-wide levels could ensure safer streets throughout entire neighborhoods, saving lives, and creating more consistent rules for drivers.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ben Furness
utterances.text: And the city must slow down super speeders, ensuring the most reckless drivers are traveling at the speed limit.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ben Furness
utterances.text: Vehicles with 16 speeding tickets are twice as likely to be involved in a crash that leads to fatality or serious injuries, which is why we strongly support Councilmember Kyla Santosuoso's bill quickly launching the program by spring 2027.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ben Furness
utterances.text: New York City can also start at home by updating our fleets so that our city vehicles are safer.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ben Furness
utterances.text: Every year, New Yorkers are killed by city vehicles, seven and counting so far this year.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ben Furness
utterances.text: We must ensure that city vehicles save lives, not take them, by shrinking the fleet in total number and in vehicle size and implementing intelligent speed assist wherever possible and expanding the use of side guards.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ben Furness
utterances.text: We're closer to Vision Zero than we ever have, but there's still so much work to be done.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ben Furness
utterances.text: This is really a moment for global leadership.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ben Furness
utterances.text: The greatest city in the world should have the safest streets in the world.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ben Furness
utterances.text: We thank the council for holding this hearing.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Thank you, Ben.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Next.

chapters.summary: Eric McClure, Executive Director of StreetsPAC, notes a New Yorker is killed in traffic every 44 hours on average and marks five years since the committee's Rethinking Vision Zero hearing. He urges a bold streets plan, Sammy's Law citywide, focus on dangerous arterials, universal hardened daylighting, Stop Super Speeders, side guards, and focused enforcement, and supports Intro 1070, 1153, 613, and Res 687.
chapters.title: Eric McClure, StreetsPAC, testifies on Vision Zero implementation

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Eric McClure
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Deputy Majority Leader Abreu.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Eric McClure
utterances.text: Thank you for holding this hearing.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Eric McClure
utterances.text: My name is Eric McClure.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Eric McClure
utterances.text: I am the Executive Director of

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Let's, let's, can you please put the time back on?

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: And are we good with the setting up of the table?

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: No, no other?

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: All right, we're good.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Please start from the beginning.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Eric McClure
utterances.text: Sure thing.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Eric McClure
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Eric McClure
utterances.text: My name is Eric McClure.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Eric McClure
utterances.text: I'm the executive director of Streets Pack.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Eric McClure
utterances.text: New York City has had a Vision Zero strategy since 2014.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Eric McClure
utterances.text: In fact, Bill de Blasio earned Streets Pack's initial mayoral endorsement in 2013, largely based on his embrace of Vision Zero.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Eric McClure
utterances.text: But while the city has made progress toward zero traffic deaths over the ensuing years, we still have a long, long way to go.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Eric McClure
utterances.text: A New Yorker is killed in a traffic crash about every 44 hours on average, and many times that number are injured, often in life-altering ways.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Eric McClure
utterances.text: Today marks five years and a day since this committee held an oversight hearing entitled Rethinking Vision Zero.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Eric McClure
utterances.text: We testified that day that Vision Zero doesn't so much need to be rethought as it needs to be properly implemented, with a much greater emphasis on street design that can, and I quote, markedly reduce the frequency and severity of crashes, unquote.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Eric McClure
utterances.text: To be sure, we have made advances in design, and the present administration has shown a commitment to change that its Vision Zero era predecessors did not, as has this committee.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Eric McClure
utterances.text: But to really put a dent in traffic deaths and serious injuries, we need a bold new streets plan and a laser-focused, safe,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Eric McClure
utterances.text: safety first approach.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Eric McClure
utterances.text: To that end, we urge the following steps.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Eric McClure
utterances.text: First, implement Sammy's Law across the city, and I have more detail which I'll include in my written testimony.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Eric McClure
utterances.text: Secondly, focus on the most dangerous arterials and intersections.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Eric McClure
utterances.text: Thirdly, implement universal hardened daylighting.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Eric McClure
utterances.text: Fourthly, establish the Stop Super Speeders program authorized by Albany as soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Eric McClure
utterances.text: Fifth, mandate side guards for all trucks operating in New York City.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Eric McClure
utterances.text: And finally, to focus enforcement where it will have the greatest impact.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Eric McClure
utterances.text: On the specific legislation considered today, we strongly support Intro 1070, which would establish a low-traffic neighborhood pilot program.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Eric McClure
utterances.text: The LTNs have proved effective and politically popular in peer cities like London.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Eric McClure
utterances.text: They reduce cut-through traffic through simple design interventions, preserve access for emergency vehicles and city services and residents, and can be implemented with little to no parking reduction.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Eric McClure
utterances.text: We also support Intro 1153 and Intro 613, and we support Resolution 687.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Eric McClure
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Niusha Masumi, an Upper West Side resident and crash survivor, says her crash could have been prevented by daylighting. She says the crash changed her life even though she had no broken bones and urges the city to reinforce daylighting during repaving.
chapters.title: Niusha Masumi testifies as crash survivor about daylighting

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Niusha Masumi
utterances.text: Hi, thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Niusha Masumi
utterances.text: Thank you for your time and listening to a regular resident.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Niusha Masumi
utterances.text: My testimony is not regard the laws as a personal testimony.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Niusha Masumi
utterances.text: I'm one of the victims of car crash that my crash could have been easily prevented by daylighting.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Niusha Masumi
utterances.text: And I heard today that you were talking with NYPD with regard to the measure of the casualties and the

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Niusha Masumi
utterances.text: pain.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Niusha Masumi
utterances.text: In my incident, I didn't have any broken bones.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Niusha Masumi
utterances.text: I didn't require any surgery, but it changed my life.

chapters.summary: Sarah Lind, co-executive director of Open Plans, supports Intro 1070 to create low-traffic neighborhood pilots. She says LTNs use low-cost design like diverters and modal filters, preserve access, and reduce cut-through traffic; London evidence shows lower traffic, fatalities, pollution, crime, and more active transportation with no emergency response impact.
chapters.title: Sarah Lind, Open Plans, testifies in support of low-traffic neighborhoods

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sarah Lind
utterances.text: Good afternoon, dear.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: I think you came to my house, my office house event.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Niusha Masumi
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Nice to see you again.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Sarah?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sarah Lind
utterances.text: Hi, yeah, my name is Sarah Lind.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sarah Lind
utterances.text: I'm co-executive director of Open Plans, an organization advocating for a more livable city.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sarah Lind
utterances.text: Making our streets more safe and livable for every New Yorker should be our guiding star.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sarah Lind
utterances.text: Intro 1070, which would create low-traffic neighborhood pilots, or LTNs, would represent a significant step towards that goal.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sarah Lind
utterances.text: LTNs use smart street design and

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sarah Lind
utterances.text: and low-cost interventions, things like diagonal diverters, modal filters, or one-way streets that oppose each other, to correct a concerning trend.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sarah Lind
utterances.text: Every neighborhood street has become a cut-through to a final destination, no matter how small or residential that street might be.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sarah Lind
utterances.text: LTNs do not forbid car use, nor do they require removing parking.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sarah Lind
utterances.text: In an LTN, residents retain access to their homes by way of vehicles.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sarah Lind
utterances.text: Similarly, LTNs preserve access for deliveries, sanitation, emergency vehicles, and other critical city services.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sarah Lind
utterances.text: LTNs incentivize drivers who are not stopping in a neighborhood to use boundary roads, the roads around the LTN, to get to their destination rather than cutting through a quiet residential corridor.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sarah Lind
utterances.text: Critically, evidence shows that boundary roads do not experience an increase in traffic as overall driving trends downward.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sarah Lind
utterances.text: Evidence in London has shown that LTNs have so many benefits.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sarah Lind
utterances.text: Significantly lowered traffic volumes, up to 50% fewer traffic fatalities, lower air pollution, lower crime rates, more active transportation use, and more local businesses, all with no impact on emergency response time.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sarah Lind
utterances.text: Five community boards have already passed resolutions requesting an LTN in their neighborhood.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sarah Lind
utterances.text: We can feel the excitement neighbors have for LTNs, and we're delighted that the council has the opportunity to deliver on this.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sarah Lind
utterances.text: We've provided more data and details about why LTNs are right for New York City in our written testimony.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sarah Lind
utterances.text: We look forward to continuing to work with the council on making our streets more livable for all users, and we support the other bills mentioned by Streets Path.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Amber Adler
utterances.text: and transportation alternatives as well, and look forward to moving towards Vision Zero.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Well, the fact that we're hearing LTNs today is a true testament to the work that you're doing.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: I first discovered LTNs through your report, and I immediately put it in for legislative request very, very quickly, and I'm glad that we're finally moving on it.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Next.

chapters.summary: Amber Adler, a car crash survivor and member of Families for Safe Streets, says Vision Zero is achievable and cites traffic deaths including four-year-old Zachariah Padilla, Yvette James, Paulina Techchok, and her neighbor Natasha Sada and her daughters. She calls the deaths preventable with better infrastructure and policy.
chapters.title: Amber Adler, Families for Safe Streets, testifies on traffic deaths

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Amber Adler

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Amber Adler

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Amber Adler
utterances.text: It seemed like a noble but impossible goal.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Amber Adler
utterances.text: However, today it is highly accepted and significantly as a significantly viable route to safety and in many cities, a reality.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Amber Adler
utterances.text: From Oslo, Norway to Hoboken, New Jersey, we now have proof positive that Vision Zero is truly achievable.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Amber Adler
utterances.text: Underline achievable.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Amber Adler
utterances.text: That being said, this is a way to save lives.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Amber Adler
utterances.text: Cities are using this road design to make walking, biking, and driving safer, and it saves lives.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Amber Adler
utterances.text: Meanwhile, this year so far in New York, over 150 New Yorkers have been killed in traffic already.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Amber Adler
utterances.text: Including four-year-old Zachariah Padilla, who was killed by an SUV driver when he was walking with his mother.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Amber Adler
utterances.text: A 79-year-old woman, Yvette James, who was killed by an SUV driver that jumped the curve and hit her on the sidewalk.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Amber Adler

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Amber Adler
utterances.text: All of this is insanity.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Amber Adler
utterances.text: And of course, in 2024, the Ocean Parkway crash that killed my neighbor, Natasha Sada, and her two young daughters as they crossed the street on Shabbos after shul.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Amber Adler
utterances.text: That super speeder, may I note, Miriam Yurimi, sits behind bars, but will be back on the street as soon as next year.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Amber Adler
utterances.text: Three years was the minimum of her sentence.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Amber Adler
utterances.text: These deaths are preventable.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Amber Adler
utterances.text: And with different infrastructure design and policy changes, each one of these New Yorkers could, would still be alive.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Amber Adler
utterances.text: We know this because our peer cities around the world are dramatically safer.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Amber Adler
utterances.text: And in fact, New Yorkers are twice as likely to be killed in a traffic crash as compared to neighbors in London, Paris, Tokyo.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Amber Adler

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Amber Adler
utterances.text: I had a lot to say.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Amber Adler
utterances.text: It goes fast.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Amber Adler
utterances.text: Yeah, I know.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Amber Adler
utterances.text: I'm like.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Julian Williams, a member of Families for Safe Streets, testifies for his daughter Janiqua, killed in 2016 by a reckless driver blocks from her home in Lefrak City. He calls for Sammy's Law zones and implementation of the Stop Super Speeders program by spring 2027.

chapters.summary: Ligia Guallpa, Executive Director of the Workers Justice Project, supports Intro 613 and says streets are delivery workers' workplace. She cites a report showing 53% of delivery workers reported work-related injuries, mostly from car crashes or traffic crimes, and urges protected bike lanes, secure bike parking, charging, and rest areas.
chapters.title: Ligia Guallpa, Workers Justice Project, supports protected bike lanes

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ligia Guallpa
utterances.text: Yeah, okay.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ligia Guallpa
utterances.text: Thank you so much, Majority Leader and Chair, for the opportunity to speak today.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ligia Guallpa
utterances.text: My name is Ligia Walpin.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ligia Guallpa
utterances.text: I'm the Executive Director of the Workers'Justice Project.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ligia Guallpa
utterances.text: I'm really excited to be here in support of Intro 013, which will require the Department of Transportation to increase the pace of protected bike lanes.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ligia Guallpa
utterances.text: And also to highlight the importance of infrastructure for app delivery workers.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ligia Guallpa
utterances.text: For delivery workers, the streets are their workplace.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ligia Guallpa
utterances.text: Yet our streets lack the safe infrastructure workers need to do their job safely and return home safely.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ligia Guallpa
utterances.text: And I think today we heard about how cars are also the main cause of a lot of fatalities.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ligia Guallpa
utterances.text: And that's actually have been one of the biggest.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ligia Guallpa
utterances.text: issues that delivery workers have experienced.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ligia Guallpa
utterances.text: In our recent report with CUNY, driven by algorithms, 53% of delivery workers reported work-related injuries, and most of those injuries were related to car crashes.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ligia Guallpa
utterances.text: Or traffic crimes.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ligia Guallpa
utterances.text: Most of, so workers face pressure also from apps to deliver faster while navigating dangerous streets.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ligia Guallpa
utterances.text: More enforcement and more policing, we strongly believe, will not solve the infrastructure crisis that our city is facing.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ligia Guallpa
utterances.text: We need safer streets, stronger protections, but also an infrastructure that meets the reality of working New Yorkers, particularly delivery workers.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ligia Guallpa
utterances.text: So we urge the council to increase the pace, not only the installation of bike lanes, but also bike parking, secure bike parking,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ligia Guallpa
utterances.text: safe e-bike charging, and other essential street infrastructures, prioritizing neighborhoods where the need is greater.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ligia Guallpa

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ligia Guallpa

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ligia Guallpa

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ligia Guallpa

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: I would love that.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: I would love that.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: And I agree with you that the city.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: All right, next.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu

chapters.summary: Yadira Sanchez, Organizing Director of Los Deliveristas Unidos, supports Intro 613 and says delivery workers face serious risks, especially where protected bike lanes are missing or blocked. She calls for protected bike lanes, secure parking, and charging infrastructure with the same urgency as enforcement and warns increased police interactions can harm immigrant workers.
chapters.title: Yadira Sanchez, Los Deliveristas Unidos, supports Intro 613

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Yadira Sanchez

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Yadira Sanchez
utterances.text: We look forward to continue working with you all together and build safer streets for delivery workers and for New Yorkers.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Yadira Sanchez
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Celo Balde, a delivery worker and organizer, supports Intro 613 and its goal of 100 miles of protected bike lanes per year for six years. He describes dangerous intersections, portal and double-parked vehicles, and the need for secure parking, charging, rest, and dignity.
chapters.title: Celo Balde, delivery worker, supports 100 miles of protected bike lanes
